From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

"Castles in Spain" redirects here. For other uses, see [Castles in Spain (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castles_in_Spain_(disambiguation) "Castles in Spain (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Segovia%2C_situado_en_la_Ciudad_vieja_de_Segovia._Patrimonio_Mundial_por_la_UNESCO.jpg/330px-Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Segovia%2C_situado_en_la_Ciudad_vieja_de_Segovia._Patrimonio_Mundial_por_la_UNESCO.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Segovia,_situado_en_la_Ciudad_vieja_de_Segovia._Patrimonio_Mundial_por_la_UNESCO.jpg)

Dating back to the early 12th century, the [Alcázar of Segovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Segovia "Alcázar of Segovia") is one of the most distinctive [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") castles in Europe. [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney "Walt Disney") was inspired by this site in building [Cinderella's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella_(Disney_character) "Cinderella (Disney character)")[castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella_Castle "Cinderella Castle").

The **castles in Spain** were built mainly for [the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain")'s defense, particularly with respect to fortification. During the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), northern Christian kingdoms had to secure their borders with their Muslim southern neighbours, thus forcing both Christian and Muslim kings to grant border [fiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") to their [liege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homage_(feudal) "Homage (feudal)") noblemen so as to keep and maintain defensive fortresses. When the [Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista") advanced, those border castles lost their initial purpose, and, as in the rest of medieval Europe, they were used as noble residences and fief-keeps. Sporadic threats of war maintained their initial military purposes as enemy invasions were common. In some locations, such as the [Basque country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basque_Country_(autonomous_community) "Basque Country (autonomous community)"), fiefdoms did not exist as such, and noble families could not afford nor did they need huge fortresses, giving rise to many [tower houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_houses "Tower houses"). In Muslim Spain many castle-palaces were built: the petty _[taifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa "Taifa")_ kingdoms that arose after the fall of the [Caliphate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") were militarily weak thus castles began taking on a more aesthetic purpose. During the late Middle Ages, Christian kingdoms had secured and enriched themselves well enough to support a more courtly lifestyle, so more residential castles were built, such as the [Alcázar of Segovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Segovia "Alcázar of Segovia"), which was used as the main residence of the [kings of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile"), whereas the [Castle of Olite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palacio_Real_de_Olite "Palacio Real de Olite"), built in a luxurious gothic style, was the seat of the [Kingdom of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Navarre "Kingdom of Navarre")'s royal court.

After the [Conquest of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Granada "Conquest of Granada") in 1492, the [Catholic monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_monarchs "Catholic monarchs") ordered all the castles in their realms to be handed over to the Crown. Although the order was not completely carried out, the [War of the Germanias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German%C3%ADa "Germanía"), a rebellion against king [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") in the early 16th century, forced the new Spanish Habsburg dynasty to continue the process, and many castles were demolished as well. Most of the castles in Spain were successively abandoned and dismantled, Spanish kings fearing noble and peasant revolts, especially in the newly conquered lands. Accordingly, some of them are nowadays in a state of decay, and although some restoration work has been done, the number of former castles is so large that the Spanish government lacks both the resources and the will to restore them all.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

"Castles in Spain" redirects here. For other uses, see [Castles in Spain (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castles_in_Spain_(disambiguation) "Castles in Spain (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Segovia%2C_situado_en_la_Ciudad_vieja_de_Segovia._Patrimonio_Mundial_por_la_UNESCO.jpg/330px-Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Segovia%2C_situado_en_la_Ciudad_vieja_de_Segovia._Patrimonio_Mundial_por_la_UNESCO.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Segovia,_situado_en_la_Ciudad_vieja_de_Segovia._Patrimonio_Mundial_por_la_UNESCO.jpg)

Dating back to the early 12th century, the [Alcázar of Segovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Segovia "Alcázar of Segovia") is one of the most distinctive [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") castles in Europe. [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney "Walt Disney") was inspired by this site in building [Cinderella's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella_(Disney_character) "Cinderella (Disney character)")[castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella_Castle "Cinderella Castle").

The **castles in Spain** were built mainly for [the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain")'s defense, particularly with respect to fortification. During the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), northern Christian kingdoms had to secure their borders with their Muslim southern neighbours, thus forcing both Christian and Muslim kings to grant border [fiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") to their [liege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homage_(feudal) "Homage (feudal)") noblemen so as to keep and maintain defensive fortresses. When the [Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista") advanced, those border castles lost their initial purpose, and, as in the rest of medieval Europe, they were used as noble residences and fief-keeps. Sporadic threats of war maintained their initial military purposes as enemy invasions were common. In some locations, such as the [Basque country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basque_Country_(autonomous_community) "Basque Country (autonomous community)"), fiefdoms did not exist as such, and noble families could not afford nor did they need huge fortresses, giving rise to many [tower houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_houses "Tower houses"). In Muslim Spain many castle-palaces were built: the petty _[taifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa "Taifa")_ kingdoms that arose after the fall of the [Caliphate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") were militarily weak thus castles began taking on a more aesthetic purpose. During the late Middle Ages, Christian kingdoms had secured and enriched themselves well enough to support a more courtly lifestyle, so more residential castles were built, such as the [Alcázar of Segovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Segovia "Alcázar of Segovia"), which was used as the main residence of the [kings of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile"), whereas the [Castle of Olite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palacio_Real_de_Olite "Palacio Real de Olite"), built in a luxurious gothic style, was the seat of the [Kingdom of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Navarre "Kingdom of Navarre")'s royal court.

After the [Conquest of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Granada "Conquest of Granada") in 1492, the [Catholic monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_monarchs "Catholic monarchs") ordered all the castles in their realms to be handed over to the Crown. Although the order was not completely carried out, the [War of the Germanias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German%C3%ADa "Germanía"), a rebellion against king [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") in the early 16th century, forced the new Spanish Habsburg dynasty to continue the process, and many castles were demolished as well. Most of the castles in Spain were successively abandoned and dismantled, Spanish kings fearing noble and peasant revolts, especially in the newly conquered lands. Accordingly, some of them are nowadays in a state of decay, and although some restoration work has been done, the number of former castles is so large that the Spanish government lacks both the resources and the will to restore them all.

The **Alcazaba** (Spanish:[[alkaˈθaβa,alkaˈsaβa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); from [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): القَصَبَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-qaṣabah_, pronounced[[alˈqasˤaba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Arabic "Help:IPA/Arabic"); lit.'[citadel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasbah "Kasbah")') is a palatial fortification in [Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), built during the period of Muslim-ruled [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus"). The current complex was begun in the 11th century and was modified or rebuilt multiple times up to the 14th century. It is one of the best-preserved _[alcazabas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba "Alcazaba")_ in Spain. The Alcazaba is also connected by a walled corridor to the higher Castle of [Gibralfaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibralfaro "Gibralfaro"), and adjacent to the entrance of the Alcazaba are remnants of a [Roman theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_theatre_(structure) "Roman theatre (structure)") dating to the 1st century AD.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Gibralfaro and the hill on which the Alcazaba is built was previously occupied by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia") since around 600 BC, and remains of a Phoenician fortification wall have been uncovered there.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2) During the [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") period of the city (after 205 BC), the area was occupied by a [Roman villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_villa "Roman villa") and industrial facilities.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1) A Roman theater, excavated and visible today, was built into the western slope of the hill in the 1st century AD.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-3) After the Muslim conquest of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula") in the early 8th century, historical sources mention the existence of a fortress on the hill, constructed by [Abd ar-Rahman I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahman_I "Abd al-Rahman I") (r. 756–788) and including a mosque inside.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1)

The current Alcazaba was begun by the [Hammudid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammudid_dynasty "Hammudid dynasty") in the early 11th century, probably under the reign of Yahya I (r. 1021–1036), from which time some of the preserved palace architecture may date.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5) Following the [capture of Malaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirid_conquest_of_M%C3%A1laga "Zirid conquest of Málaga") by the [Zirids of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Granada "Taifa of Granada") in 1056, some additions were made during the reign of [Badis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badis_ibn_Habus "Badis ibn Habus") (d. 1073), possibly the double-walled fortifications or a wider reconstruction.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4) In the early 14th century, when Malaga was under the control of the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"), the Alcazaba was largely rebuilt by the [Nasrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty") emir [Muhammad II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_II_of_Granada "Muhammad II of Granada"), including the fortifications and the palatial residences.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:8-6)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2) The Castle of Gibralfaro, on a higher hill to the east, was built by the Nasrid emir [Yusuf I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusuf_I_of_Granada "Yusuf I of Granada") (r. 1333–1354), also on the site of previous fortifications. Yusuf also built a walled corridor connecting the castle with the lower citadel, creating a nearly impregnable fortified complex.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:9-7):159[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-8)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)

In a crucial event near the end of the _[Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_, the Spanish monarchs [Ferdinand and Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs_of_Spain "Catholic Monarchs of Spain") captured Málaga from the Muslims during the [Siege of Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_M%C3%A1laga_(1487) "Siege of Málaga (1487)"), which began on 6 May 1487 and ended with the surrender of the city on 18 August that same year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:9-7):159–163 After their victory, the monarchs raised their standard at the _Torre del Homenaje_ in the inner citadel.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Starting in the 18th century, the Alcazaba's military function ceased. It was occupied by civilian residents and became a marginal neighbourhood of the city. Starting in 1933, under the direction of [Leopoldo Torres Balbás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldo_Torres_Balb%C3%A1s "Leopoldo Torres Balbás"), the residents were evacuated and restorations of the Alcazaba began, along with [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") investigations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:0-9)

## Layout and architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Layout and architecture")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_001.JPG/250px-Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_001.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_001.JPG)

Model of the Alcazaba (displayed on site)

The Alcazaba of Málaga is built on a hill in the centre of the city, overlooking the port, and comprises two walled enclosures, one contained within the other. Each enclosure is defended by a wall fortified with towers. The inner enclosure occupies the summit of the hill and contains the palaces. Along with the double-layered fortifications, a total of five gates had to be crossed in order to reach the palace areas.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10) This design contrasts with the earlier sprawling palace complexes that were built during the [Umayyad Emirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Emirate "Umayyad Emirate") and [Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") periods of Al-Andalus (such as [Madinat al-Zahra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madinat_al-Zahra "Madinat al-Zahra")), and demonstrates the importance of military impregnability for the rulers of this period.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4) The fortress was formerly connected to the city [ramparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall") which formed a third defensive wall.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] According to architect restorer, [Leopoldo Torres Balbás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldo_Torres_Balb%C3%A1s "Leopoldo Torres Balbás"), the Alcazaba of Málaga is the prototype of [military architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture#In_Al-Andalus "Moorish architecture") in the [Taifa period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus") of [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus"), with its double walls and massive entry fortifications.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:0-9)

### Outer (lower) citadel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Outer (lower) citadel")]

The outer entrance to the citadel is via a climbing passage that passes through multiple gates and doubles back on itself twice (known as a "[bent entrance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bent_entrance "Bent entrance")"), a design intended to make progress difficult for attacking forces. Part-way up, the passage goes through the _Puerta de la Bóveda_ ('Gate of the Vault'), which forms one of the bends, and then through the _Puerta de las Columnas_ ('Gate of the Columns'), which is a simpler straight passage.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11) The name of the latter gate comes from the two Roman-era [columns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column "Column") and [capitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_(architecture) "Capital (architecture)"), reused from the nearby Roman theatre, that are integrated into the gate's façade.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11) In the 18th century, the mayor or governor of the Alcazaba built his residence on top of this gate. Over time houses and residences were built along much of the entrance passage and covered it, so that by the 19th century it was known as the "Alcazaba Tunnel" (_Túnel de la Alcazaba_).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11)

After the _Puerta de las Columnas_, another narrow space enclosed by walls continues upward towards the _Arco del Cristo_ ('Arch of the [Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus")', also called the _Torre del Cristo_, 'Tower of the Christ'), another bent-entrance gate that finally leads into the outer citadel enclosure.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10) The gate and its tower are so-named because one of the chambers in the tower was used as a chapel during the 19th century and housed an [altarpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altarpiece "Altarpiece") depicting Christ.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11) Beyond the gate, a short distance to the west and inside the outer citadel enclosure, is an open space now known as the _Plaza de las Armas_ ('Place/Square of Arms'), now occupied by gardens. No original remains are extant in this area, but archeological work uncovered remains of a former parish church, probably from the time of Ferdinand and Isabella (right after the city was captured), which was built on top of a former mosque.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12) Some parts of the outer enclosure are closed to the public today, including a large [well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well "Well"), known as the _Pozo Airón_, which cuts into the bedrock to a depth of 30 meters, where a natural water source was used to supply the inhabitants of the citadel.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12)

### Inner (upper) citadel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Inner (upper) citadel")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_-_Torre_del_Homenaje_001.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_-_Torre_del_Homenaje_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_-_Torre_del_Homenaje_001.jpg)

The _Torre del Homenaje_

The inner or upper enclosure can only be accessed through the _Puerta de los Cuartos de Granada_ ('Gate of the Granada Quarters', also known as the _Puerta de los Arcos_) a heavily-fortified gate on the western side of the enclosure. This gate is flanked by towers and has a straight passage with two doorways, between which is a small space open to the sky where defenders could attack intruders from above.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12) The gate fell into ruin over the centuries and was largely demolished in 1854; the current structure was reconstructed in the 20th century with the help of historical illustrations.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12) On the eastern side of the inner citadel is the large _Torre del Homenaje_ ('Tower of Tribute'), built during the 11th century but rebuilt in the Nasrid period. During the 20th-century restoration campaigns the tower was preserved instead of reconstructed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) Inside the inner citadel is a series of courtyard residences known as the _Cuartos de Granada_ (Quarters of Granada) which served as the home of the kings and governors.

#### Taifa-period palace

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Taifa-period palace")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/31.12.2021_-_Rundgang_durch_die_Maurische_Festung_in_Malaga._11.jpg/250px-31.12.2021_-_Rundgang_durch_die_Maurische_Festung_in_Malaga._11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:31.12.2021_-_Rundgang_durch_die_Maurische_Festung_in_Malaga._11.jpg)

The southern pavilion of the Taifa palace (seen from the courtyard side)

The Taifa palace

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga.jpg/330px-Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga.jpg)

[Caliphal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_Cordoba "Caliphate of Cordoba")-style [horseshoe arches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_arches "Horseshoe arches") at the entrance of the main hall

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-17.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-17.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga,_July_2017-17.jpg)

Intersecting [multifoil arches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multifoil_arch "Multifoil arch") in the side annex

The first (southernmost) of them is the only one that dates to the Taifa period (11th century).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:5-14) The northern wing of this palace has disappeared and is replaced by trees today.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) Only the southern wing or pavilion remain standing, though it was also heavily restored by Leopoldo Torres Balbás in the early 20th century. This pavilion has an inner façade (facing north to the former courtyard) and is entered via a wide [portico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portico "Portico") with arches, restored by Torres Balbás in a Nasrid style but possibly standing on top of original remains.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5) Behind this is a small rectangular chamber entered via another [arcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_game "Arcade game") with three horseshoe arches. The arches are supported by two columns in the middle and two engaged columns on the sides and are decorated with carved [arabesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabesque "Arabesque") decorations, with alternating plain and decorated [voussoirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voussoir "Voussoir"). This arcade reflects the earlier caliphal style of Madinat al-Zahra (10th-century), but in a much smaller and simpler form.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:8-6)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:5-14) This element may date from the early days of Hammudid rule in the city, under Yahya I (r. 1021-1036).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5)

Adjacent on the southwest side of the main chamber and portico is a small annex. A square chamber at the entrance of this annex is surrounded on all four sides by pairs of intersecting multifoil arches, although the arches on the southwest side (looking towards the city and the sea) were created by Torres Balbás.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5) These multifoil arches are similar to the precedents found in the 10th-century expansion of the [Great Mosque of Cordoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Cordoba "Great Mosque of Cordoba") but they are simpler and serve a more strictly decorative purpose, foreshadowing the more elaborate arches of the later 11th-century [Aljaferia Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aljafer%C3%ADa "Aljafería") in [Zaragoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaragoza "Zaragoza").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4)

Directly behind the southern pavilion is an outer fortification tower known as the _Torre de Maldonado_, which was remodeled by the [Almohads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") in the 12th-13th century, with vestiges of decoration from this era.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) Across from it, to the northeast, is a large chamber dating from the 16th century (after the Christian conquest) and featuring a wooden [Mudéjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") ceiling. Today it houses a model of the Alcazaba.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13)

#### Nasrid palace and houses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Nasrid palace and houses")]

The Nasrid palace

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-40.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-40.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga,_July_2017-40.jpg)

The _Patio de los Naranjos_

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Alcazaba_M%C3%A1laga_-_Patio_de_la_Alberca_2.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_M%C3%A1laga_-_Patio_de_la_Alberca_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_M%C3%A1laga_-_Patio_de_la_Alberca_2.jpg)

The _Patio de la Alberca_

The rest of the area northeast of the Taifa palace is occupied by a Nasrid palace with various rooms and porticos arranged around two rectangular courtyards. Most of this palace was reconstructed or restored in the 20th century on the basis of archeological remains.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) The first (southern) courtyard, known as the _Patio de los Naranjos_ ('Courtyard of the Orange Trees'), has preserved two original pools and their paved [tile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tile "Tile") decoration. The second (northern) courtyard, known as the _Patio de la Alberca_ ('Courtyard of the Pool'), has one long central pool, again surrounded by original tile paving.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) On the northeast side of this section is another courtyard, the Patio del Aljibe, which may or may not have been part of the Nasrid palace as well. It is now occupied by the restoration workshop of the Alcazaba. It is named after a cistern built under it with an area of approximately 25 square metres (270 sq ft).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13)

The rest of the space between the Nasrid palace and the _Torre del Homenaje_ is occupied by the so-called _Barrio Castrense_ ('Military District'), thought to date from the 11th century and to have been inhabited by the ruler's other officials and servants. It is one of the best-preserved areas of the citadel due to the fact that it was not rebuilt or repurposed in later centuries, but it is not open to the public today.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) The area contains eight houses connected by narrow streets. Some of the houses were reconstructed in the 20th century while others were preserved and are sheltered by a protective roof. One of the largest houses has its own [hammam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammam "Hammam") (bath facility) and toilets.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13)

The **Alcazaba** (Spanish:[[alkaˈθaβa,alkaˈsaβa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); from [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): القَصَبَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-qaṣabah_, pronounced[[alˈqasˤaba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Arabic "Help:IPA/Arabic"); lit.'[citadel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasbah "Kasbah")') is a palatial fortification in [Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), built during the period of Muslim-ruled [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus"). The current complex was begun in the 11th century and was modified or rebuilt multiple times up to the 14th century. It is one of the best-preserved _[alcazabas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba "Alcazaba")_ in Spain. The Alcazaba is also connected by a walled corridor to the higher Castle of [Gibralfaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibralfaro "Gibralfaro"), and adjacent to the entrance of the Alcazaba are remnants of a [Roman theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_theatre_(structure) "Roman theatre (structure)") dating to the 1st century AD.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Gibralfaro and the hill on which the Alcazaba is built was previously occupied by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia") since around 600 BC, and remains of a Phoenician fortification wall have been uncovered there.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2) During the [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") period of the city (after 205 BC), the area was occupied by a [Roman villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_villa "Roman villa") and industrial facilities.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1) A Roman theater, excavated and visible today, was built into the western slope of the hill in the 1st century AD.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-3) After the Muslim conquest of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula") in the early 8th century, historical sources mention the existence of a fortress on the hill, constructed by [Abd ar-Rahman I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahman_I "Abd al-Rahman I") (r. 756–788) and including a mosque inside.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1)

The current Alcazaba was begun by the [Hammudid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammudid_dynasty "Hammudid dynasty") in the early 11th century, probably under the reign of Yahya I (r. 1021–1036), from which time some of the preserved palace architecture may date.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5) Following the [capture of Malaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirid_conquest_of_M%C3%A1laga "Zirid conquest of Málaga") by the [Zirids of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Granada "Taifa of Granada") in 1056, some additions were made during the reign of [Badis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badis_ibn_Habus "Badis ibn Habus") (d. 1073), possibly the double-walled fortifications or a wider reconstruction.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4) In the early 14th century, when Malaga was under the control of the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"), the Alcazaba was largely rebuilt by the [Nasrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty") emir [Muhammad II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_II_of_Granada "Muhammad II of Granada"), including the fortifications and the palatial residences.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:8-6)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2) The Castle of Gibralfaro, on a higher hill to the east, was built by the Nasrid emir [Yusuf I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusuf_I_of_Granada "Yusuf I of Granada") (r. 1333–1354), also on the site of previous fortifications. Yusuf also built a walled corridor connecting the castle with the lower citadel, creating a nearly impregnable fortified complex.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:9-7):159[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-8)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:24-2)

In a crucial event near the end of the _[Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_, the Spanish monarchs [Ferdinand and Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs_of_Spain "Catholic Monarchs of Spain") captured Málaga from the Muslims during the [Siege of Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_M%C3%A1laga_(1487) "Siege of Málaga (1487)"), which began on 6 May 1487 and ended with the surrender of the city on 18 August that same year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:9-7):159–163 After their victory, the monarchs raised their standard at the _Torre del Homenaje_ in the inner citadel.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Starting in the 18th century, the Alcazaba's military function ceased. It was occupied by civilian residents and became a marginal neighbourhood of the city. Starting in 1933, under the direction of [Leopoldo Torres Balbás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldo_Torres_Balb%C3%A1s "Leopoldo Torres Balbás"), the residents were evacuated and restorations of the Alcazaba began, along with [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") investigations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:7-1)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:0-9)

## Layout and architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Layout and architecture")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_001.JPG/250px-Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_001.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_001.JPG)

Model of the Alcazaba (displayed on site)

The Alcazaba of Málaga is built on a hill in the centre of the city, overlooking the port, and comprises two walled enclosures, one contained within the other. Each enclosure is defended by a wall fortified with towers. The inner enclosure occupies the summit of the hill and contains the palaces. Along with the double-layered fortifications, a total of five gates had to be crossed in order to reach the palace areas.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10) This design contrasts with the earlier sprawling palace complexes that were built during the [Umayyad Emirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Emirate "Umayyad Emirate") and [Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") periods of Al-Andalus (such as [Madinat al-Zahra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madinat_al-Zahra "Madinat al-Zahra")), and demonstrates the importance of military impregnability for the rulers of this period.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4) The fortress was formerly connected to the city [ramparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall") which formed a third defensive wall.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] According to architect restorer, [Leopoldo Torres Balbás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldo_Torres_Balb%C3%A1s "Leopoldo Torres Balbás"), the Alcazaba of Málaga is the prototype of [military architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture#In_Al-Andalus "Moorish architecture") in the [Taifa period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus") of [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus"), with its double walls and massive entry fortifications.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:0-9)

### Outer (lower) citadel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Outer (lower) citadel")]

The outer entrance to the citadel is via a climbing passage that passes through multiple gates and doubles back on itself twice (known as a "[bent entrance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bent_entrance "Bent entrance")"), a design intended to make progress difficult for attacking forces. Part-way up, the passage goes through the _Puerta de la Bóveda_ ('Gate of the Vault'), which forms one of the bends, and then through the _Puerta de las Columnas_ ('Gate of the Columns'), which is a simpler straight passage.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11) The name of the latter gate comes from the two Roman-era [columns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column "Column") and [capitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_(architecture) "Capital (architecture)"), reused from the nearby Roman theatre, that are integrated into the gate's façade.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11) In the 18th century, the mayor or governor of the Alcazaba built his residence on top of this gate. Over time houses and residences were built along much of the entrance passage and covered it, so that by the 19th century it was known as the "Alcazaba Tunnel" (_Túnel de la Alcazaba_).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11)

After the _Puerta de las Columnas_, another narrow space enclosed by walls continues upward towards the _Arco del Cristo_ ('Arch of the [Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus")', also called the _Torre del Cristo_, 'Tower of the Christ'), another bent-entrance gate that finally leads into the outer citadel enclosure.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:1-10) The gate and its tower are so-named because one of the chambers in the tower was used as a chapel during the 19th century and housed an [altarpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altarpiece "Altarpiece") depicting Christ.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:2-11) Beyond the gate, a short distance to the west and inside the outer citadel enclosure, is an open space now known as the _Plaza de las Armas_ ('Place/Square of Arms'), now occupied by gardens. No original remains are extant in this area, but archeological work uncovered remains of a former parish church, probably from the time of Ferdinand and Isabella (right after the city was captured), which was built on top of a former mosque.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12) Some parts of the outer enclosure are closed to the public today, including a large [well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well "Well"), known as the _Pozo Airón_, which cuts into the bedrock to a depth of 30 meters, where a natural water source was used to supply the inhabitants of the citadel.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12)

### Inner (upper) citadel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Inner (upper) citadel")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_-_Torre_del_Homenaje_001.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_-_Torre_del_Homenaje_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_de_M%C3%A1laga_-_Torre_del_Homenaje_001.jpg)

The _Torre del Homenaje_

The inner or upper enclosure can only be accessed through the _Puerta de los Cuartos de Granada_ ('Gate of the Granada Quarters', also known as the _Puerta de los Arcos_) a heavily-fortified gate on the western side of the enclosure. This gate is flanked by towers and has a straight passage with two doorways, between which is a small space open to the sky where defenders could attack intruders from above.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12) The gate fell into ruin over the centuries and was largely demolished in 1854; the current structure was reconstructed in the 20th century with the help of historical illustrations.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:3-12) On the eastern side of the inner citadel is the large _Torre del Homenaje_ ('Tower of Tribute'), built during the 11th century but rebuilt in the Nasrid period. During the 20th-century restoration campaigns the tower was preserved instead of reconstructed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) Inside the inner citadel is a series of courtyard residences known as the _Cuartos de Granada_ (Quarters of Granada) which served as the home of the kings and governors.

#### Taifa-period palace

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Taifa-period palace")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/31.12.2021_-_Rundgang_durch_die_Maurische_Festung_in_Malaga._11.jpg/250px-31.12.2021_-_Rundgang_durch_die_Maurische_Festung_in_Malaga._11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:31.12.2021_-_Rundgang_durch_die_Maurische_Festung_in_Malaga._11.jpg)

The southern pavilion of the Taifa palace (seen from the courtyard side)

The Taifa palace

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga.jpg/330px-Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga.jpg)

[Caliphal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_Cordoba "Caliphate of Cordoba")-style [horseshoe arches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_arches "Horseshoe arches") at the entrance of the main hall

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-17.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-17.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga,_July_2017-17.jpg)

Intersecting [multifoil arches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multifoil_arch "Multifoil arch") in the side annex

The first (southernmost) of them is the only one that dates to the Taifa period (11th century).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:5-14) The northern wing of this palace has disappeared and is replaced by trees today.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) Only the southern wing or pavilion remain standing, though it was also heavily restored by Leopoldo Torres Balbás in the early 20th century. This pavilion has an inner façade (facing north to the former courtyard) and is entered via a wide [portico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portico "Portico") with arches, restored by Torres Balbás in a Nasrid style but possibly standing on top of original remains.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5) Behind this is a small rectangular chamber entered via another [arcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_game "Arcade game") with three horseshoe arches. The arches are supported by two columns in the middle and two engaged columns on the sides and are decorated with carved [arabesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabesque "Arabesque") decorations, with alternating plain and decorated [voussoirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voussoir "Voussoir"). This arcade reflects the earlier caliphal style of Madinat al-Zahra (10th-century), but in a much smaller and simpler form.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:8-6)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:5-14) This element may date from the early days of Hammudid rule in the city, under Yahya I (r. 1021-1036).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5)

Adjacent on the southwest side of the main chamber and portico is a small annex. A square chamber at the entrance of this annex is surrounded on all four sides by pairs of intersecting multifoil arches, although the arches on the southwest side (looking towards the city and the sea) were created by Torres Balbás.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:32-5) These multifoil arches are similar to the precedents found in the 10th-century expansion of the [Great Mosque of Cordoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Cordoba "Great Mosque of Cordoba") but they are simpler and serve a more strictly decorative purpose, foreshadowing the more elaborate arches of the later 11th-century [Aljaferia Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aljafer%C3%ADa "Aljafería") in [Zaragoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaragoza "Zaragoza").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:4-4)

Directly behind the southern pavilion is an outer fortification tower known as the _Torre de Maldonado_, which was remodeled by the [Almohads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") in the 12th-13th century, with vestiges of decoration from this era.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) Across from it, to the northeast, is a large chamber dating from the 16th century (after the Christian conquest) and featuring a wooden [Mudéjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") ceiling. Today it houses a model of the Alcazaba.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13)

#### Nasrid palace and houses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Nasrid palace and houses")]

The Nasrid palace

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-40.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga%2C_July_2017-40.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga,_July_2017-40.jpg)

The _Patio de los Naranjos_

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Alcazaba_M%C3%A1laga_-_Patio_de_la_Alberca_2.jpg/250px-Alcazaba_M%C3%A1laga_-_Patio_de_la_Alberca_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazaba_M%C3%A1laga_-_Patio_de_la_Alberca_2.jpg)

The _Patio de la Alberca_

The rest of the area northeast of the Taifa palace is occupied by a Nasrid palace with various rooms and porticos arranged around two rectangular courtyards. Most of this palace was reconstructed or restored in the 20th century on the basis of archeological remains.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) The first (southern) courtyard, known as the _Patio de los Naranjos_ ('Courtyard of the Orange Trees'), has preserved two original pools and their paved [tile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tile "Tile") decoration. The second (northern) courtyard, known as the _Patio de la Alberca_ ('Courtyard of the Pool'), has one long central pool, again surrounded by original tile paving.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) On the northeast side of this section is another courtyard, the Patio del Aljibe, which may or may not have been part of the Nasrid palace as well. It is now occupied by the restoration workshop of the Alcazaba. It is named after a cistern built under it with an area of approximately 25 square metres (270 sq ft).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13)

The rest of the space between the Nasrid palace and the _Torre del Homenaje_ is occupied by the so-called _Barrio Castrense_ ('Military District'), thought to date from the 11th century and to have been inhabited by the ruler's other officials and servants. It is one of the best-preserved areas of the citadel due to the fact that it was not rebuilt or repurposed in later centuries, but it is not open to the public today.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13) The area contains eight houses connected by narrow streets. Some of the houses were reconstructed in the 20th century while others were preserved and are sheltered by a protective roof. One of the largest houses has its own [hammam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammam "Hammam") (bath facility) and toilets.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_M%C3%A1laga#cite_note-:6-13)

The **Alcázar of Seville**, officially called **Royal Alcázar of Seville** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Real Alcázar de Sevilla or Reales Alcázares de Sevilla_),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-1) is a historic royal palace in [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") and one of the official residences of the [Spanish royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_royal_family "Spanish royal family"). It was formerly the site of the [Islamic-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus") citadel of the city, begun in the 10th century under the [Umayyads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_state_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Umayyad state of Córdoba") and then developed into a larger palace complex by the [Abbadid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbadid_dynasty "Abbadid dynasty") (11th century) and the [Almohads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") (12th to early 13th centuries). After the [Castilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile") conquest of the city in 1248, the site was progressively rebuilt and replaced by new palaces and gardens. Among the most important of these is a richly decorated [Mudéjar-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") palace built by [Pedro I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") during the 1360s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:0-3)

The palace is a preeminent example of Mudéjar style in the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula") and also includes sections with [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") and [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture") elements. The upper storeys of the Alcázar are still occupied by the [royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_royal_family "Spanish royal family") when they visit Seville and are administered by the [Patrimonio Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrimonio_Nacional "Patrimonio Nacional"). It was registered in 1987 by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"), along with the adjoining [Seville Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral") and the [General Archive of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Archive_of_the_Indies "General Archive of the Indies").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-unesco-4)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The Spanish term _[Alcázar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar "Alcázar")_ (pronounced[[alˈkaθaɾ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) comes from [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): اَلْقَصْر, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-qaṣr_ ([اَلْقَصْر](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%82%D8%B5%D8%B1#Noun "wikt:قصر"), "a large stone building from which power is projected"), which is ultimately from Latin _[castrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castrum "Castrum")_ "fort".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Houtsma1993-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-al-Q%C5%AB%E1%B9%AD%C4%AByahJames2009-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-BloomBlair2009-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

### Islamic era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Islamic era")]

In the year 712, Seville was conquered by the [Umayyad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate"). In the year 913–914, after a revolt against the government of Córdoba, the first [emir of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_state_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Umayyad state of Córdoba"), [Abd al-Rahman III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahman_III "Abd al-Rahman III"), built a fortified construction in place of a [Visigothic Christian basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigothic_art_and_architecture "Visigothic art and architecture").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9) It was a quadrangular, roughly square enclosure about 100 metres (330 ft) long on each side, fortified with walls and rectangular towers, and annexed to the city walls.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

In the 11th century, during the [Taifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa "Taifa"), the [Abbadid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbadid_dynasty "Abbadid dynasty") ruler [al-Mu'tamid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mu'tamid_ibn_Abbad "Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad") expanded the complex southwards and eastwards,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10) with a new southern enclosure measuring approximately 70 by 80 metres (230 by 260 ft).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) This new palace was called _al-Mubarak_ "the Blessed" (المبارك).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) Various additions to the construction such as stables and warehouses were also carried out.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9)

Towards 1150, the [Almohad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") began to develop [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville") as their capital in al-Andalus. The Almohad governor extended the fortified complex to the west, nearly doubling its size. At least six new courtyard palaces were constructed in the old enclosures, and nine palaces were added in the western extensions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) In 1163 the caliph [Abu Yaʿqub Yusuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Yaqub_Yusuf "Abu Yaqub Yusuf") made the Alcazar his main residence in the region.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) He further expanded and embellished the palace complex in 1169, adding six new enclosures to the north, south, and west sides of the existing palaces. The works were carried out by architects [Ahmad Ben Baso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Ben_Baso?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ahmad Ben Baso (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad%20Ben%20Baso "es:Ahmad Ben Baso")] and Ali al-Ghumari.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) With the exception of the walls, nearly all previous buildings were demolished, and a total of approximately twelve palaces were built.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10) Among the new structures was a very large garden courtyard, now known as the _Patio del Crucero_, which stood in the old Abbadid enclosure. Between 1171 and 1198, an enormous new [congregational mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_mosque "Congregational mosque") was built on the north side of the Alcazar (later transformed into the current [Cathedral of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral")). A shipyard was also built nearby in 1184, and a textile market was established in 1196.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

There are few remnants of these Islamic-era constructions today. Archaeological remains of the Al Mubarak Palace are currently preserved under the _Patio de la Monteria_. Several wall painting fragments were found that are now exhibited in the _Palacio del Yeso_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9) The courtyard buildings now known as the _Palacio del Yeso_ (or _Patio del Yeso_), the _Palacio de la Contratación_, and the _Patio del Crucero_ all preserve remains from the Almohad period.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Palacio_g%C3%B3tico_001.jpg/250px-Palacio_g%C3%B3tico_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Palacio_g%C3%B3tico_001.jpg)

The _Sala de las Bóvedas_ preserves elements of [Alfonso X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile "Alfonso X of Castile")'s [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") palace (13th century).

### Christian era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Christian era")]

Seville was [conquered in 1248](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Seville "Siege of Seville") by [Ferdinand III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_III_of_Castile "Ferdinand III of Castile") of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile"). The former Moorish palace-citadel was taken over by the Castilian monarchs and underwent significant reconstruction and modification, such that most of the Islamic-era structure has since disappeared.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Urqu%C3%ADzar-Herrera2017-12)

A [Gothic-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") palace was built on the site in 1258 for [Alfonso X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile "Alfonso X of Castile") (Ferdinand's successor).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:0-3) It stood on the site of the present-day _Patio del Crucero_, incorporating and preserving parts of the Almohad-era courtyard that was found here, including the Islamic-style garden divided into quadrants by two intersecting paths. Over these paths and around the courtyard, Gothic-style vaults and pointed arches were added, along with a hall divided into several naves. Corners towers containing spiral staircases granted access to an upper terrace.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13) Of the Gothic palace today, only the upstairs _Sala de las Bóvedas_ and the _Baños de María de Padilla_, with their Gothic [cross-ribbed vaults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault "Rib vault"), have been preserved or partially preserved.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13)

In the mid-14th century, [Alfonso XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XI_of_Castile "Alfonso XI of Castile") commissioned the construction of a new throne hall known as the Hall of Justice, which commemorated his victory at the [Battle of Río Salado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_R%C3%ADo_Salado "Battle of Río Salado") (1340).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) It is attached to the _Patio del Yeso_, an Almohad-era courtyard, and also serves as its antechamber. This new addition was made in a [Mudéjar style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_style "Mudéjar style"), with [stucco decoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stucco_decoration_in_Islamic_architecture "Stucco decoration in Islamic architecture") and an overall arrangement of elements directly based on contemporary [Islamic Andalusi architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Bild_fr%C3%A5n_Johanna_Kempes_f._Wallis_resa_genom_Spanien%2C_Portugal_och_Marocko_18_Mars_-_5_Juni_1895_-_Hallwylska_museet_-_103318.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Bild_fr%C3%A5n_Johanna_Kempes_f._Wallis_resa_genom_Spanien%2C_Portugal_och_Marocko_18_Mars_-_5_Juni_1895_-_Hallwylska_museet_-_103318.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bild_fr%C3%A5n_Johanna_Kempes_f._Wallis_resa_genom_Spanien,_Portugal_och_Marocko_18_Mars_-_5_Juni_1895_-_Hallwylska_museet_-_103318.tif)

1895 photo of a [Mudéjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar "Mudéjar") room in the palace

In the 1360s, much of the complex was rebuilt by [Pedro I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") in an ornate Mudéjar style.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The palace includes a monumental façade, a courtyard (the present-day _Patio de las Doncellas_), and a great domed hall known as the Hall of the Ambassadors (_Salon de los Embajadores_). A Latin inscription on the palace façade includes the year 1364 while an Arabic inscription in the Hall of Ambassadors gives the year 1366, which indicate the probable dates for the start and completion of construction, respectively.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The architecture of Pedro I's palace has strong similarities to the contemporary [Nasrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty") palaces of the [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra") in [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada "Granada"), although the complicated chronology of construction and renovations at both sites makes it difficult to determine what roles they might have played in influencing each other's designs.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) It is likely that Muhammad V, the Nasrid ruler of Granada and Pedro I's ally, sent craftsmen to Seville to help assist in the palace's construction and decoration.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-14) Under the [Catholic Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs_of_Spain "Catholic Monarchs of Spain"), [Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") (d. 1504) and [Fernando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") (d. 1516), the upper floor of the palace was extended and transformed into their main residence.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9)

The palace was the birthplace of [Infanta Maria Antonietta of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infanta_Maria_Antonietta_of_Spain "Infanta Maria Antonietta of Spain") (1729–1785), daughter of [Philip V of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Spain "Philip V of Spain") and [Elisabeth Farnese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Farnese "Elisabeth Farnese"), when the king was in the city to oversee the signing of the [Treaty of Seville (1729)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Seville_(1729) "Treaty of Seville (1729)") which ended the [Anglo-Spanish War (1727)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Spanish_War_(1727) "Anglo-Spanish War (1727)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10) Much of the old Gothic Palace of Alfonso X was destroyed during the [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13)

The Real Alcázar is situated near the [Seville Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral") and the [General Archive of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Archive_of_the_Indies "General Archive of the Indies") in one of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia")'s most emblematic areas.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10)

### Tiles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Tiles")]

The palace is renowned for its ornate tile decoration, with tiles being either _arista_ or _majolica_. In the arista technique, each tile is created by pressing clay into a mould—a process which creates tiles that have raised ridges and a three dimensional effect. By contrast, majolica tiles are flat and are created by painting design and color directly onto an opaque white background glaze. This technique was developed later than the arista process, during the 15th–16th centuries. As an important trade center, Seville had easy access to a wealth of producers of tiles which were mainly of geometric design inspired by arabesque ornamentation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-de_Viguerie_et_al_2019-15)

In the 16th century, the Catholic Monarchs commissioned an Italian artist from Pisa, Francisco Niculoso (called Pisano) to make two majolica tile altarpieces for their private chapel in the palace.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-(N.M.)2003-16) One still exists in the oratory of the royal apartments, the other one is missing. Later, the artist Cristóbal de Augusta created a tile-work in the Palacio Gotico. It features animals, cherubs and floral designs and gives the palace a bright tapestry look.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-17)
