### Puerta del León

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Puerta del León")]

The Puerta del León (Gate of the Lion), located in the outer wall of the complex, is the main access to the enclosure. Between the [lintel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lintel "Lintel") of this gate and under a machicolation there was a painting of a lion, whose origin is unknown, although it appears in the drawings made by [Richard Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Ford_(English_writer) "Richard Ford (English writer)") in 1832.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-19) The painting was likely painted over in 1876 when [Joaquín Domínguez Bécquer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaqu%C3%ADn_Dom%C3%ADnguez_B%C3%A9cquer "Joaquín Domínguez Bécquer"), the director of the painting and gilding at the time, may have considered it to be in bad condition and beyond repair.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Ignacio-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Gestoso1889-21)

In 1892 the painting was replaced by a panel of [azulejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azulejo "Azulejo") designed by Manuel Tortosa y Fernández, with the historical advice of [José Gestoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Gestoso_y_P%C3%A9rez?action=edit&redlink=1 "José Gestoso y Pérez (page does not exist)"). The azulejo was made in the [Mensaque factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Mensaque_y_Vera?action=edit&redlink=1 "José Mensaque y Vera (page does not exist)")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Mensaque-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-23) and also represents a lion,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Mensaque-22) in Gothic style, which appears holding a crucifix with its right claw and with a flag under its left claw. On the chest there is a [tefillin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tefillin "Tefillin") reading in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")_Ad utrumque_, which means "for one thing and for another", the word 'paratus' would be missing; _Ad utrumque paratus_,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Ignacio-20) thus meaning "prepared for one thing and for another".

The name "Puerta del León" dates to the 19th century and derives from the heraldic lion in this panel of tilework which is above the gateway and under a defensive [machicolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolation "Machicolation").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-N%C3%BA%C3%B1ezMorales199914-25) Historically, this gate had been known as Puerta de la Montería (Gate of the Hunt).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Amador_de_los_R%C3%ADos1884-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Amador_de_los_R%C3%ADos1876-27) According to [Ortiz de Zúñiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Ortiz_de_Z%C3%BA%C3%B1iga "Diego Ortiz de Zúñiga") (17th century) it was named this way as it was the gate used by King [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") and his men when they went hunting.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-29) The fact that Peter's father, [Alfonso XI of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XI_of_Castile "Alfonso XI of Castile"), was an avid hunter who even wrote a book on hunting lends credence to this hypothesis. According to José Gestoso, the gate's name derives from the hunting-themed decoration that is found here.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-30) On the left side of the arch there are reliefs of two worn poly-lobed medallions. One of them depicts what appears to be a four-legged animal. After passing through the gate, one enters the [Patio del León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patio_del_Le%C3%B3n?action=edit&redlink=1 "Patio del León (page does not exist)"). At the back of the courtyard, facing the entrance, is a stretch of Almohad defensive wall pierced by three arches. This wall has a masonry facade behind which is found unfaced rubble. The two outer arches were originally horseshoe-shaped arches which were transformed into rounded arches during the Christian period. Theatrical plays from the Spanish Golden Age were performed in a theatre, the Corral de Montería (Enclosure of the Hunt), that once stood here. It was established in 1625 and destroyed by a fire on 3 May 1691. Behind the stretch of wall is the Patio de la Montería, which faces the Palacio del Rey Don Pedro.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-N%C3%BA%C3%B1ezMorales199914-25)

### Sala de Justicia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Sala de Justicia")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Sala_de_la_Justicia.jpg/250px-Sala_de_la_Justicia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sala_de_la_Justicia.jpg)

Sala de Justicia

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Sala_de_la_Justicia%2C_Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_techumbre.jpg/250px-Sala_de_la_Justicia%2C_Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_techumbre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sala_de_la_Justicia,_Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla,_techumbre.jpg)

[Artesonado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artesonado "Artesonado") of the Sala de la Justicia, Mudéjar hall ordered to be built by Alfonso XI of Castile[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-31) (1340). First Mudéjar structure in Seville[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Colum-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33)

The Sala de Justicia (courtroom of Justice) is accessed through the Patio del León.

It has a square floor plan, is [Mudéjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") in style and was built in the reign of [Alfonso XI of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XI_of_Castile "Alfonso XI of Castile"). It is a square room with an [artesonado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artesonado "Artesonado") ([qubba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubba "Qubba")). In it there is a shield of the [Order of the Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Band "Order of the Band"), created by Alfonso XI around 1340. The room would have been built in 1340.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Colum-32) However, although the room was dated in the reign of Alfonso XI thanks, among other details, to this shield, the shield of that order also appears in other parts of the palace decorated in the reign of his son, [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile"). It is similar to the Sala de Comares of the [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra"). In the 16th and 17th centuries it was known as the Sala de los Consejos.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-34) It is most likely that it was an Almohad room[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-35) used to gather a council (_maswar_) and that it was reformed with [Mudéjar art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") by the Christians, who continued to use it for the same purpose. This was probably the room where the court presided by Peter was located, although there are other hypotheses about its possible location. In this court there were three brick steps with a stone throne, although this structure was demolished before the visit of [Philip II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain") in 1570. This action displeased Philip II, who was a great admirer of King Don Peter and who was the first to indicate that he should be called "the Avenger".

In the centre of the hall is a fountain with a shallow drain down to the Patio del Yeso, and round the walls are brick and tile benches.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33)

### Patio del Yeso

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Patio del Yeso")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Patio_del_Yeso_%28P%C3%B3rtico%29._Reales_Alc%C3%A1zares_de_Sevilla.jpg/250px-Patio_del_Yeso_%28P%C3%B3rtico%29._Reales_Alc%C3%A1zares_de_Sevilla.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patio_del_Yeso_(P%C3%B3rtico)._Reales_Alc%C3%A1zares_de_Sevilla.jpg)

The south portico of the Patio del Yeso (Courtyard of the Plaster), one of the few remaining elements from the [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate")-era palace (end of the 12th century).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

From the Sala de Justicia one enters the Patio del Yeso, which was built at the end of the 12th century,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Carles2012-36) by Ali al-Ghumari[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Carles2012-36) from the [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") period, almost square in plan, with a pool in the center[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33) and arcaded arches on each side of the courtyard, on which there is rich decoration. On the south side there are caliphal columns that support arches with decoration (_[sebka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebka "Sebka")_) of plaster.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-37) This decoration covers a porch. In the porch there is an entrance consisting of two horseshoe arches with a column in the center.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-38) On the lintel of this entrance there are two windows. On the opposite wall there is a walled exit with three horseshoe arches in the Córdoban caliphal style. This patio has undergone several alterations throughout its history. The entire wall where the _sebka_ arches were located was found covered. It was discovered by [Francisco María Tubino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Mar%C3%ADa_Tubino?action=edit&redlink=1 "Francisco María Tubino (page does not exist)") in 1890.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-39)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Carles2012-36) The [Marquis of Vega-Inclán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_de_la_Vega-Incl%C3%A1n?action=edit&redlink=1 "Benigno de la Vega-Inclán (page does not exist)"), then curator of the Alcázar, commissioned in 1912 its recovery and restoration to the architect José Gómez Millán. In the courtyard of the old [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque"), the arches were uncovered, the capitals were cleaned, and the floor of the courtyard were excavated at the foot of the columns.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-40) The courtyard although restored, the walls and horshoe arcades are well preserved with their Almohad ornamentation.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33)

### Patio de la Montería

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Patio de la Montería")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_Sevilla_%2842052074324%29.jpg/250px-Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_Sevilla_%2842052074324%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla,_Sevilla_(42052074324).jpg)

Palace of Peter to the left and the Casa de Contratación to the right.

Patio de la Montería (Courtyard of the Hunt). This is the main courtyard, and was built when Palace of Peter was built in 1364,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-sevilla.org-41) and is presided over by the door of the palace of [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile"). In the walls there are semicircular arches that were walled up in the 15th century.

To the right are the rooms of the [Casa de Contratación](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contrataci%C3%B3n "Casa de Contratación"), who built in 1503[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-sevilla.org-41) and there met the merchants who made contracts there when there was a boom in trade from Seville with Spanish America and the Philippines.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-42) The Casa de Contratación has a porticoed gallery from the 17th century made by Antón Sánchez Hurtado, the eastern side of the Casa de Contratación was built by the Belgian architect Sebastian Van der Borcht in 1755, after the [Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-sevilla.org-41)

Halls faces the square courtyard, its area was occupied by a [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") sunken garden at a level of 1.5 meters beneath the halls, it had two walkways, and had a channel to irrigate the garden.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Arnold-43) In 1997, other Alhomad palace was discovered beneath the Patio de la Montería, the building was built around 1150, it was demolished in 1356 for the construction of the Palace of Peter of Castile.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Arnold-43)

### _Patio de las Doncellas_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Patio de las Doncellas")]

The name, meaning "The Courtyard of the Maidens", is a reference to the apocryphal story that the Muslim rulers demanded an annual tribute of 100 virgins from the Christian kingdoms of Iberia.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Tremlett-44)

The courtyard was part of the Mudéjar palace built by Pedro I in the 1360s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The ground level of the building still dates to this period and contains Arabic inscriptions that refer to Pedro I as "Sultan Don Bidru".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-45) The upper story of the courtyard was an addition made by [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor"). The addition was designed by [Luis de Vega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_Vega "Luis de Vega") in the style of the [Italian Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Renaissance "Italian Renaissance") although he did include both Renaissance and mudéjar plaster work in the decorations. Construction of the addition began in 1540 and ended in 1572.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-N%C3%BA%C3%B1ezMorales199952-46)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Alcazar_de_S%C3%A9ville_-_Patio_de_la_Doncellas.JPG/250px-Alcazar_de_S%C3%A9ville_-_Patio_de_la_Doncellas.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazar_de_S%C3%A9ville_-_Patio_de_la_Doncellas.JPG)

The patio de las Doncellas in 2000, with the marble pavement laid in 1581–1584.

At ground level, several reception rooms are arranged around a long rectangular reflecting pool that runs the entire length of the patio, creating a water line.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47) This pool is surrounded by promenades covered with a red brick pavement decorated with green ceramic borders, similar to the pavement that adorns the perimeter of the garden.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47) The pool and its promenades are bordered by two flowerbeds located one meter beneath the pavement[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Doaks-48) whose sides are decorated with a frieze of interlaced semi-circular arches.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The current appearance of the courtyard garden is the result of a reconstruction carried out in the 21st century following the excavations carried out between 2002 and 2005 by a team of archaeologists led by Miguel Ángel Tabales.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Tabales-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-ElPais-50) The garden and the pool, built between 1356 and 1366, were buried between 1581 and 1584 when the courtyard was paved by Juan Bautista de Zumárraga with a white and black marble pavement and an alabaster fountain in the center.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Doaks-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Tabales-49) The patio maintained this appearance until its original structure was discovered[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Real-51) and the hidden garden was uncovered after the 2002–2005 excavations, which revealed the good state of conservation of the area under the patio.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-ElPais-50) The ancient [Mudejar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") garden was restored after being hidden for centuries under a marble floor.

### _Los Baños de Doña María de Padilla_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Los Baños de Doña María de Padilla")]

The _Baños de Doña María de Padilla_ ("Baths of Lady María de Padilla") is a chamber located in a basement beneath the _Patio del Crucero_. It is named after [María de Padilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_de_Padilla "María de Padilla"), the mistress of Pedro I, although the structure itself is unrelated to her and dates instead to the Gothic palace of Alfonso X. It consists of an elongated water basin, or [cistern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cistern "Cistern"), roofed by a series of Gothic cross-ribbed vaults.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13)

### _Salón de los Embajadores_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Salón de los Embajadores")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Alc%C3%A1zar_di_Siviglia_arco.jpg/250px-Alc%C3%A1zar_di_Siviglia_arco.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alc%C3%A1zar_di_Siviglia_arco.jpg)

One of the archway entrances to _Salón de los Embajadores_ (Hall of Ambassadors).

The Hall of the Ambassadors (_Salon de los Embajadores_) dates from the 14th century, when Pedro I of Castile made it a centerpiece of his new royal palace.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) One hypothesis states that Pedro reused and remodeled a much older hall, known as the Hall of the Pleiades, built by the Abbadid ruler al-Mu'tamid, but this theory has not been widely accepted.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:0-3)

The hall has a square shape and is covered by a dome, analogical to the _[qubba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubba "Qubba")_-type structures of Islamic architecture.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) During Pedro's construction, the orientation of the hall was changed from facing [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca "Mecca") (to the east) to the northeast, where it opens to the _Patio de las Doncellas_ through a central doorway.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-halll-52) At the middle of each of the other three sides of the hall is a central doorway consisting of a triple [horseshoe arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_arch "Horseshoe arch") supported by marble columns. Each of the triple arches is enclosed by a decorative rectangular frame (_[alfiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfiz "Alfiz")_), which in turn is enclosed by a semi-circular frame within a larger rectangular frame.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:322-53) Beyond each of these archways is a wide rectangular room, leading in turn to other rooms.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:322-53) The lower walls of the Hall of Ambassadors are decorated with a [dado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dado_(architecture) "Dado (architecture)") of tiles, while the walls above are decorated with rich plasterwork. A row of windows with delicate stucco [grilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grille_(architecture) "Grille (architecture)") runs along the top of the walls, below the dome.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Alc%C3%A1zar_Seville_April_2019-11.jpg/250px-Alc%C3%A1zar_Seville_April_2019-11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alc%C3%A1zar_Seville_April_2019-11.jpg)

Dome ceiling in the Hall of Ambassadors.

The hall's decoration was finished in 1366, as recorded by an Arabic inscription on a set of wooden doors that was made by artisans from [Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo,_Spain "Toledo, Spain").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The current dome over the hall was rebuilt in 1427 to replace the original dome. The balconies in the upper walls were added in the 16th century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) In 1526, Emperor [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") V and [Isabella of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_Portugal "Isabella of Portugal") celebrated their marriage in this room.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-54)

## The gardens

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: The gardens")]

All the palaces of [Al Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Andalus "Al Andalus") had garden orchards with fruit trees, horticultural produce and a wide variety of fragrant flowers. The garden-orchards not only supplied food for the palace residents but had the aesthetic function of bringing pleasure. Water was ever present in the form of irrigation channels, runnels, jets, ponds and pools.

The gardens adjoining the Alcázar of Seville have undergone many changes. In the 17th century during the reign of Philip III the Italian designer Vermondo Resta introduced the Italian Mannerist style. Resta was responsible for the Galeria de Grutesco (Grotto Gallery) transforming the old Muslim wall into a [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia") from which to admire the view of the palace gardens.

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

*   In 1962 the Alcázar was used as a set for [_Lawrence of Arabia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Arabia_(film) "Lawrence of Arabia (film)").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-55)
*   The Alcázar was used as the set for the court of the [King of Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Jerusalem "King of Jerusalem") in the 2005 movie [_Kingdom of Heaven_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Heaven_(film) "Kingdom of Heaven (film)").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-56)
*   Part of the [fifth season of _Game of Thrones_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_Thrones_(season_5) "Game of Thrones (season 5)") was shot in several locations in the province of Seville, including the Alcázar.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-57)

The **Alcázar of Seville**, officially called **Royal Alcázar of Seville** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Real Alcázar de Sevilla or Reales Alcázares de Sevilla_),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-1) is a historic royal palace in [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") and one of the official residences of the [Spanish royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_royal_family "Spanish royal family"). It was formerly the site of the [Islamic-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus") citadel of the city, begun in the 10th century under the [Umayyads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_state_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Umayyad state of Córdoba") and then developed into a larger palace complex by the [Abbadid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbadid_dynasty "Abbadid dynasty") (11th century) and the [Almohads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") (12th to early 13th centuries). After the [Castilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile") conquest of the city in 1248, the site was progressively rebuilt and replaced by new palaces and gardens. Among the most important of these is a richly decorated [Mudéjar-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") palace built by [Pedro I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") during the 1360s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:0-3)

The palace is a preeminent example of Mudéjar style in the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula") and also includes sections with [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") and [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture") elements. The upper storeys of the Alcázar are still occupied by the [royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_royal_family "Spanish royal family") when they visit Seville and are administered by the [Patrimonio Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrimonio_Nacional "Patrimonio Nacional"). It was registered in 1987 by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"), along with the adjoining [Seville Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral") and the [General Archive of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Archive_of_the_Indies "General Archive of the Indies").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-unesco-4)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The Spanish term _[Alcázar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar "Alcázar")_ (pronounced[[alˈkaθaɾ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) comes from [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): اَلْقَصْر, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-qaṣr_ ([اَلْقَصْر](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%82%D8%B5%D8%B1#Noun "wikt:قصر"), "a large stone building from which power is projected"), which is ultimately from Latin _[castrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castrum "Castrum")_ "fort".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Houtsma1993-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-al-Q%C5%AB%E1%B9%AD%C4%AByahJames2009-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-BloomBlair2009-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

### Islamic era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Islamic era")]

In the year 712, Seville was conquered by the [Umayyad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate"). In the year 913–914, after a revolt against the government of Córdoba, the first [emir of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_state_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Umayyad state of Córdoba"), [Abd al-Rahman III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahman_III "Abd al-Rahman III"), built a fortified construction in place of a [Visigothic Christian basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigothic_art_and_architecture "Visigothic art and architecture").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9) It was a quadrangular, roughly square enclosure about 100 metres (330 ft) long on each side, fortified with walls and rectangular towers, and annexed to the city walls.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

In the 11th century, during the [Taifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa "Taifa"), the [Abbadid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbadid_dynasty "Abbadid dynasty") ruler [al-Mu'tamid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mu'tamid_ibn_Abbad "Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad") expanded the complex southwards and eastwards,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10) with a new southern enclosure measuring approximately 70 by 80 metres (230 by 260 ft).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) This new palace was called _al-Mubarak_ "the Blessed" (المبارك).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) Various additions to the construction such as stables and warehouses were also carried out.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9)

Towards 1150, the [Almohad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") began to develop [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville") as their capital in al-Andalus. The Almohad governor extended the fortified complex to the west, nearly doubling its size. At least six new courtyard palaces were constructed in the old enclosures, and nine palaces were added in the western extensions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) In 1163 the caliph [Abu Yaʿqub Yusuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Yaqub_Yusuf "Abu Yaqub Yusuf") made the Alcazar his main residence in the region.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) He further expanded and embellished the palace complex in 1169, adding six new enclosures to the north, south, and west sides of the existing palaces. The works were carried out by architects [Ahmad Ben Baso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Ben_Baso?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ahmad Ben Baso (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad%20Ben%20Baso "es:Ahmad Ben Baso")] and Ali al-Ghumari.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11) With the exception of the walls, nearly all previous buildings were demolished, and a total of approximately twelve palaces were built.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10) Among the new structures was a very large garden courtyard, now known as the _Patio del Crucero_, which stood in the old Abbadid enclosure. Between 1171 and 1198, an enormous new [congregational mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_mosque "Congregational mosque") was built on the north side of the Alcazar (later transformed into the current [Cathedral of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral")). A shipyard was also built nearby in 1184, and a textile market was established in 1196.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

There are few remnants of these Islamic-era constructions today. Archaeological remains of the Al Mubarak Palace are currently preserved under the _Patio de la Monteria_. Several wall painting fragments were found that are now exhibited in the _Palacio del Yeso_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9) The courtyard buildings now known as the _Palacio del Yeso_ (or _Patio del Yeso_), the _Palacio de la Contratación_, and the _Patio del Crucero_ all preserve remains from the Almohad period.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Palacio_g%C3%B3tico_001.jpg/250px-Palacio_g%C3%B3tico_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Palacio_g%C3%B3tico_001.jpg)

The _Sala de las Bóvedas_ preserves elements of [Alfonso X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile "Alfonso X of Castile")'s [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") palace (13th century).

### Christian era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Christian era")]

Seville was [conquered in 1248](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Seville "Siege of Seville") by [Ferdinand III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_III_of_Castile "Ferdinand III of Castile") of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile"). The former Moorish palace-citadel was taken over by the Castilian monarchs and underwent significant reconstruction and modification, such that most of the Islamic-era structure has since disappeared.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Urqu%C3%ADzar-Herrera2017-12)

A [Gothic-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") palace was built on the site in 1258 for [Alfonso X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile "Alfonso X of Castile") (Ferdinand's successor).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:0-3) It stood on the site of the present-day _Patio del Crucero_, incorporating and preserving parts of the Almohad-era courtyard that was found here, including the Islamic-style garden divided into quadrants by two intersecting paths. Over these paths and around the courtyard, Gothic-style vaults and pointed arches were added, along with a hall divided into several naves. Corners towers containing spiral staircases granted access to an upper terrace.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13) Of the Gothic palace today, only the upstairs _Sala de las Bóvedas_ and the _Baños de María de Padilla_, with their Gothic [cross-ribbed vaults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault "Rib vault"), have been preserved or partially preserved.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13)

In the mid-14th century, [Alfonso XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XI_of_Castile "Alfonso XI of Castile") commissioned the construction of a new throne hall known as the Hall of Justice, which commemorated his victory at the [Battle of Río Salado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_R%C3%ADo_Salado "Battle of Río Salado") (1340).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) It is attached to the _Patio del Yeso_, an Almohad-era courtyard, and also serves as its antechamber. This new addition was made in a [Mudéjar style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_style "Mudéjar style"), with [stucco decoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stucco_decoration_in_Islamic_architecture "Stucco decoration in Islamic architecture") and an overall arrangement of elements directly based on contemporary [Islamic Andalusi architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Bild_fr%C3%A5n_Johanna_Kempes_f._Wallis_resa_genom_Spanien%2C_Portugal_och_Marocko_18_Mars_-_5_Juni_1895_-_Hallwylska_museet_-_103318.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Bild_fr%C3%A5n_Johanna_Kempes_f._Wallis_resa_genom_Spanien%2C_Portugal_och_Marocko_18_Mars_-_5_Juni_1895_-_Hallwylska_museet_-_103318.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bild_fr%C3%A5n_Johanna_Kempes_f._Wallis_resa_genom_Spanien,_Portugal_och_Marocko_18_Mars_-_5_Juni_1895_-_Hallwylska_museet_-_103318.tif)

1895 photo of a [Mudéjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar "Mudéjar") room in the palace

In the 1360s, much of the complex was rebuilt by [Pedro I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") in an ornate Mudéjar style.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The palace includes a monumental façade, a courtyard (the present-day _Patio de las Doncellas_), and a great domed hall known as the Hall of the Ambassadors (_Salon de los Embajadores_). A Latin inscription on the palace façade includes the year 1364 while an Arabic inscription in the Hall of Ambassadors gives the year 1366, which indicate the probable dates for the start and completion of construction, respectively.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The architecture of Pedro I's palace has strong similarities to the contemporary [Nasrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty") palaces of the [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra") in [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada "Granada"), although the complicated chronology of construction and renovations at both sites makes it difficult to determine what roles they might have played in influencing each other's designs.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) It is likely that Muhammad V, the Nasrid ruler of Granada and Pedro I's ally, sent craftsmen to Seville to help assist in the palace's construction and decoration.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-14) Under the [Catholic Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs_of_Spain "Catholic Monarchs of Spain"), [Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") (d. 1504) and [Fernando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") (d. 1516), the upper floor of the palace was extended and transformed into their main residence.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-esp-9)

The palace was the birthplace of [Infanta Maria Antonietta of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infanta_Maria_Antonietta_of_Spain "Infanta Maria Antonietta of Spain") (1729–1785), daughter of [Philip V of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Spain "Philip V of Spain") and [Elisabeth Farnese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Farnese "Elisabeth Farnese"), when the king was in the city to oversee the signing of the [Treaty of Seville (1729)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Seville_(1729) "Treaty of Seville (1729)") which ended the [Anglo-Spanish War (1727)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Spanish_War_(1727) "Anglo-Spanish War (1727)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10) Much of the old Gothic Palace of Alfonso X was destroyed during the [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13)

The Real Alcázar is situated near the [Seville Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral") and the [General Archive of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Archive_of_the_Indies "General Archive of the Indies") in one of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia")'s most emblematic areas.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-reales-10)

### Tiles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Tiles")]

The palace is renowned for its ornate tile decoration, with tiles being either _arista_ or _majolica_. In the arista technique, each tile is created by pressing clay into a mould—a process which creates tiles that have raised ridges and a three dimensional effect. By contrast, majolica tiles are flat and are created by painting design and color directly onto an opaque white background glaze. This technique was developed later than the arista process, during the 15th–16th centuries. As an important trade center, Seville had easy access to a wealth of producers of tiles which were mainly of geometric design inspired by arabesque ornamentation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-de_Viguerie_et_al_2019-15)

In the 16th century, the Catholic Monarchs commissioned an Italian artist from Pisa, Francisco Niculoso (called Pisano) to make two majolica tile altarpieces for their private chapel in the palace.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-(N.M.)2003-16) One still exists in the oratory of the royal apartments, the other one is missing. Later, the artist Cristóbal de Augusta created a tile-work in the Palacio Gotico. It features animals, cherubs and floral designs and gives the palace a bright tapestry look.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-17)

### Puerta del León

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Puerta del León")]

The Puerta del León (Gate of the Lion), located in the outer wall of the complex, is the main access to the enclosure. Between the [lintel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lintel "Lintel") of this gate and under a machicolation there was a painting of a lion, whose origin is unknown, although it appears in the drawings made by [Richard Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Ford_(English_writer) "Richard Ford (English writer)") in 1832.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-19) The painting was likely painted over in 1876 when [Joaquín Domínguez Bécquer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaqu%C3%ADn_Dom%C3%ADnguez_B%C3%A9cquer "Joaquín Domínguez Bécquer"), the director of the painting and gilding at the time, may have considered it to be in bad condition and beyond repair.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Ignacio-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Gestoso1889-21)

In 1892 the painting was replaced by a panel of [azulejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azulejo "Azulejo") designed by Manuel Tortosa y Fernández, with the historical advice of [José Gestoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Gestoso_y_P%C3%A9rez?action=edit&redlink=1 "José Gestoso y Pérez (page does not exist)"). The azulejo was made in the [Mensaque factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Mensaque_y_Vera?action=edit&redlink=1 "José Mensaque y Vera (page does not exist)")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Mensaque-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-23) and also represents a lion,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Mensaque-22) in Gothic style, which appears holding a crucifix with its right claw and with a flag under its left claw. On the chest there is a [tefillin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tefillin "Tefillin") reading in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")_Ad utrumque_, which means "for one thing and for another", the word 'paratus' would be missing; _Ad utrumque paratus_,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Ignacio-20) thus meaning "prepared for one thing and for another".

The name "Puerta del León" dates to the 19th century and derives from the heraldic lion in this panel of tilework which is above the gateway and under a defensive [machicolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolation "Machicolation").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-N%C3%BA%C3%B1ezMorales199914-25) Historically, this gate had been known as Puerta de la Montería (Gate of the Hunt).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Amador_de_los_R%C3%ADos1884-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Amador_de_los_R%C3%ADos1876-27) According to [Ortiz de Zúñiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Ortiz_de_Z%C3%BA%C3%B1iga "Diego Ortiz de Zúñiga") (17th century) it was named this way as it was the gate used by King [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") and his men when they went hunting.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-29) The fact that Peter's father, [Alfonso XI of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XI_of_Castile "Alfonso XI of Castile"), was an avid hunter who even wrote a book on hunting lends credence to this hypothesis. According to José Gestoso, the gate's name derives from the hunting-themed decoration that is found here.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-30) On the left side of the arch there are reliefs of two worn poly-lobed medallions. One of them depicts what appears to be a four-legged animal. After passing through the gate, one enters the [Patio del León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patio_del_Le%C3%B3n?action=edit&redlink=1 "Patio del León (page does not exist)"). At the back of the courtyard, facing the entrance, is a stretch of Almohad defensive wall pierced by three arches. This wall has a masonry facade behind which is found unfaced rubble. The two outer arches were originally horseshoe-shaped arches which were transformed into rounded arches during the Christian period. Theatrical plays from the Spanish Golden Age were performed in a theatre, the Corral de Montería (Enclosure of the Hunt), that once stood here. It was established in 1625 and destroyed by a fire on 3 May 1691. Behind the stretch of wall is the Patio de la Montería, which faces the Palacio del Rey Don Pedro.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-N%C3%BA%C3%B1ezMorales199914-25)

### Sala de Justicia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Sala de Justicia")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Sala_de_la_Justicia.jpg/250px-Sala_de_la_Justicia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sala_de_la_Justicia.jpg)

Sala de Justicia

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Sala_de_la_Justicia%2C_Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_techumbre.jpg/250px-Sala_de_la_Justicia%2C_Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_techumbre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sala_de_la_Justicia,_Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla,_techumbre.jpg)

[Artesonado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artesonado "Artesonado") of the Sala de la Justicia, Mudéjar hall ordered to be built by Alfonso XI of Castile[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-31) (1340). First Mudéjar structure in Seville[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Colum-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33)

The Sala de Justicia (courtroom of Justice) is accessed through the Patio del León.

It has a square floor plan, is [Mudéjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") in style and was built in the reign of [Alfonso XI of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XI_of_Castile "Alfonso XI of Castile"). It is a square room with an [artesonado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artesonado "Artesonado") ([qubba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubba "Qubba")). In it there is a shield of the [Order of the Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Band "Order of the Band"), created by Alfonso XI around 1340. The room would have been built in 1340.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Colum-32) However, although the room was dated in the reign of Alfonso XI thanks, among other details, to this shield, the shield of that order also appears in other parts of the palace decorated in the reign of his son, [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile"). It is similar to the Sala de Comares of the [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra"). In the 16th and 17th centuries it was known as the Sala de los Consejos.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-34) It is most likely that it was an Almohad room[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-35) used to gather a council (_maswar_) and that it was reformed with [Mudéjar art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") by the Christians, who continued to use it for the same purpose. This was probably the room where the court presided by Peter was located, although there are other hypotheses about its possible location. In this court there were three brick steps with a stone throne, although this structure was demolished before the visit of [Philip II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain") in 1570. This action displeased Philip II, who was a great admirer of King Don Peter and who was the first to indicate that he should be called "the Avenger".

In the centre of the hall is a fountain with a shallow drain down to the Patio del Yeso, and round the walls are brick and tile benches.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33)

### Patio del Yeso

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Patio del Yeso")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Patio_del_Yeso_%28P%C3%B3rtico%29._Reales_Alc%C3%A1zares_de_Sevilla.jpg/250px-Patio_del_Yeso_%28P%C3%B3rtico%29._Reales_Alc%C3%A1zares_de_Sevilla.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patio_del_Yeso_(P%C3%B3rtico)._Reales_Alc%C3%A1zares_de_Sevilla.jpg)

The south portico of the Patio del Yeso (Courtyard of the Plaster), one of the few remaining elements from the [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate")-era palace (end of the 12th century).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:32-11)

From the Sala de Justicia one enters the Patio del Yeso, which was built at the end of the 12th century,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Carles2012-36) by Ali al-Ghumari[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Carles2012-36) from the [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") period, almost square in plan, with a pool in the center[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33) and arcaded arches on each side of the courtyard, on which there is rich decoration. On the south side there are caliphal columns that support arches with decoration (_[sebka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebka "Sebka")_) of plaster.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-37) This decoration covers a porch. In the porch there is an entrance consisting of two horseshoe arches with a column in the center.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-38) On the lintel of this entrance there are two windows. On the opposite wall there is a walled exit with three horseshoe arches in the Córdoban caliphal style. This patio has undergone several alterations throughout its history. The entire wall where the _sebka_ arches were located was found covered. It was discovered by [Francisco María Tubino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Mar%C3%ADa_Tubino?action=edit&redlink=1 "Francisco María Tubino (page does not exist)") in 1890.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-39)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Carles2012-36) The [Marquis of Vega-Inclán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_de_la_Vega-Incl%C3%A1n?action=edit&redlink=1 "Benigno de la Vega-Inclán (page does not exist)"), then curator of the Alcázar, commissioned in 1912 its recovery and restoration to the architect José Gómez Millán. In the courtyard of the old [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque"), the arches were uncovered, the capitals were cleaned, and the floor of the courtyard were excavated at the foot of the columns.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-40) The courtyard although restored, the walls and horshoe arcades are well preserved with their Almohad ornamentation.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Companion-33)

### Patio de la Montería

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Patio de la Montería")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_Sevilla_%2842052074324%29.jpg/250px-Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla%2C_Sevilla_%2842052074324%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Real_Alc%C3%A1zar_de_Sevilla,_Sevilla_(42052074324).jpg)

Palace of Peter to the left and the Casa de Contratación to the right.

Patio de la Montería (Courtyard of the Hunt). This is the main courtyard, and was built when Palace of Peter was built in 1364,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-sevilla.org-41) and is presided over by the door of the palace of [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile"). In the walls there are semicircular arches that were walled up in the 15th century.

To the right are the rooms of the [Casa de Contratación](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contrataci%C3%B3n "Casa de Contratación"), who built in 1503[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-sevilla.org-41) and there met the merchants who made contracts there when there was a boom in trade from Seville with Spanish America and the Philippines.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-42) The Casa de Contratación has a porticoed gallery from the 17th century made by Antón Sánchez Hurtado, the eastern side of the Casa de Contratación was built by the Belgian architect Sebastian Van der Borcht in 1755, after the [Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-sevilla.org-41)

Halls faces the square courtyard, its area was occupied by a [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") sunken garden at a level of 1.5 meters beneath the halls, it had two walkways, and had a channel to irrigate the garden.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Arnold-43) In 1997, other Alhomad palace was discovered beneath the Patio de la Montería, the building was built around 1150, it was demolished in 1356 for the construction of the Palace of Peter of Castile.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Arnold-43)

### _Patio de las Doncellas_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Patio de las Doncellas")]

The name, meaning "The Courtyard of the Maidens", is a reference to the apocryphal story that the Muslim rulers demanded an annual tribute of 100 virgins from the Christian kingdoms of Iberia.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Tremlett-44)

The courtyard was part of the Mudéjar palace built by Pedro I in the 1360s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The ground level of the building still dates to this period and contains Arabic inscriptions that refer to Pedro I as "Sultan Don Bidru".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-45) The upper story of the courtyard was an addition made by [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor"). The addition was designed by [Luis de Vega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_Vega "Luis de Vega") in the style of the [Italian Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Renaissance "Italian Renaissance") although he did include both Renaissance and mudéjar plaster work in the decorations. Construction of the addition began in 1540 and ended in 1572.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-N%C3%BA%C3%B1ezMorales199952-46)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Alcazar_de_S%C3%A9ville_-_Patio_de_la_Doncellas.JPG/250px-Alcazar_de_S%C3%A9ville_-_Patio_de_la_Doncellas.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcazar_de_S%C3%A9ville_-_Patio_de_la_Doncellas.JPG)

The patio de las Doncellas in 2000, with the marble pavement laid in 1581–1584.

At ground level, several reception rooms are arranged around a long rectangular reflecting pool that runs the entire length of the patio, creating a water line.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47) This pool is surrounded by promenades covered with a red brick pavement decorated with green ceramic borders, similar to the pavement that adorns the perimeter of the garden.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47) The pool and its promenades are bordered by two flowerbeds located one meter beneath the pavement[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Doaks-48) whose sides are decorated with a frieze of interlaced semi-circular arches.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The current appearance of the courtyard garden is the result of a reconstruction carried out in the 21st century following the excavations carried out between 2002 and 2005 by a team of archaeologists led by Miguel Ángel Tabales.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Tabales-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-ElPais-50) The garden and the pool, built between 1356 and 1366, were buried between 1581 and 1584 when the courtyard was paved by Juan Bautista de Zumárraga with a white and black marble pavement and an alabaster fountain in the center.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Doaks-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Tabales-49) The patio maintained this appearance until its original structure was discovered[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Real-51) and the hidden garden was uncovered after the 2002–2005 excavations, which revealed the good state of conservation of the area under the patio.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-Fidalgo-47)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-ElPais-50) The ancient [Mudejar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") garden was restored after being hidden for centuries under a marble floor.

### _Los Baños de Doña María de Padilla_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Los Baños de Doña María de Padilla")]

The _Baños de Doña María de Padilla_ ("Baths of Lady María de Padilla") is a chamber located in a basement beneath the _Patio del Crucero_. It is named after [María de Padilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_de_Padilla "María de Padilla"), the mistress of Pedro I, although the structure itself is unrelated to her and dates instead to the Gothic palace of Alfonso X. It consists of an elongated water basin, or [cistern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cistern "Cistern"), roofed by a series of Gothic cross-ribbed vaults.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:1-13)

### _Salón de los Embajadores_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Salón de los Embajadores")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Alc%C3%A1zar_di_Siviglia_arco.jpg/250px-Alc%C3%A1zar_di_Siviglia_arco.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alc%C3%A1zar_di_Siviglia_arco.jpg)

One of the archway entrances to _Salón de los Embajadores_ (Hall of Ambassadors).

The Hall of the Ambassadors (_Salon de los Embajadores_) dates from the 14th century, when Pedro I of Castile made it a centerpiece of his new royal palace.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) One hypothesis states that Pedro reused and remodeled a much older hall, known as the Hall of the Pleiades, built by the Abbadid ruler al-Mu'tamid, but this theory has not been widely accepted.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:0-3)

The hall has a square shape and is covered by a dome, analogical to the _[qubba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubba "Qubba")_-type structures of Islamic architecture.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) During Pedro's construction, the orientation of the hall was changed from facing [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca "Mecca") (to the east) to the northeast, where it opens to the _Patio de las Doncellas_ through a central doorway.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-halll-52) At the middle of each of the other three sides of the hall is a central doorway consisting of a triple [horseshoe arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_arch "Horseshoe arch") supported by marble columns. Each of the triple arches is enclosed by a decorative rectangular frame (_[alfiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfiz "Alfiz")_), which in turn is enclosed by a semi-circular frame within a larger rectangular frame.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:322-53) Beyond each of these archways is a wide rectangular room, leading in turn to other rooms.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-:322-53) The lower walls of the Hall of Ambassadors are decorated with a [dado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dado_(architecture) "Dado (architecture)") of tiles, while the walls above are decorated with rich plasterwork. A row of windows with delicate stucco [grilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grille_(architecture) "Grille (architecture)") runs along the top of the walls, below the dome.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Alc%C3%A1zar_Seville_April_2019-11.jpg/250px-Alc%C3%A1zar_Seville_April_2019-11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alc%C3%A1zar_Seville_April_2019-11.jpg)

Dome ceiling in the Hall of Ambassadors.

The hall's decoration was finished in 1366, as recorded by an Arabic inscription on a set of wooden doors that was made by artisans from [Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo,_Spain "Toledo, Spain").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) The current dome over the hall was rebuilt in 1427 to replace the original dome. The balconies in the upper walls were added in the 16th century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-general2-2) In 1526, Emperor [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") V and [Isabella of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_Portugal "Isabella of Portugal") celebrated their marriage in this room.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-54)

## The gardens

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: The gardens")]

All the palaces of [Al Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Andalus "Al Andalus") had garden orchards with fruit trees, horticultural produce and a wide variety of fragrant flowers. The garden-orchards not only supplied food for the palace residents but had the aesthetic function of bringing pleasure. Water was ever present in the form of irrigation channels, runnels, jets, ponds and pools.

The gardens adjoining the Alcázar of Seville have undergone many changes. In the 17th century during the reign of Philip III the Italian designer Vermondo Resta introduced the Italian Mannerist style. Resta was responsible for the Galeria de Grutesco (Grotto Gallery) transforming the old Muslim wall into a [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia") from which to admire the view of the palace gardens.

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

*   In 1962 the Alcázar was used as a set for [_Lawrence of Arabia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Arabia_(film) "Lawrence of Arabia (film)").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-55)
*   The Alcázar was used as the set for the court of the [King of Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Jerusalem "King of Jerusalem") in the 2005 movie [_Kingdom of Heaven_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Heaven_(film) "Kingdom of Heaven (film)").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-56)
*   Part of the [fifth season of _Game of Thrones_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_Thrones_(season_5) "Game of Thrones (season 5)") was shot in several locations in the province of Seville, including the Alcázar.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville#cite_note-57)
