**São Jorge Castle** ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Castelo de São Jorge_; Portuguese pronunciation:[[kɐʃˈtɛlu dɨ sɐ̃w̃ˈʒɔɾʒɨ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese")), sometimes known in English as **Saint George's Castle**, is a historic [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle") in the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") capital of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), located in the _[freguesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freguesia "Freguesia")_ of [Santa Maria Maior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria_Maior_(Lisbon) "Santa Maria Maior (Lisbon)"). Human occupation of the castle hill dates to at least the 8th century BC[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-2) while the oldest fortifications on the site date from the 2nd century BC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-3) The hill on which Saint George's Castle stands has played an important part in the [history of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lisbon "History of Lisbon"), having served as the location of fortifications occupied successively by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia"), [Carthaginians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"), and [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors"), before its conquest by the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people") in the [1147 Siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon"). Since the 12th century, the castle has variously served as a [royal palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_palace "Royal palace"), a [military barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barracks "Barracks"), home of the [Torre do Tombo National Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_do_Tombo_National_Archive "Torre do Tombo National Archive"), and now as a [national monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_monuments_of_Portugal "List of national monuments of Portugal") and museum.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg/250px-Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg)

A 16th-century illuminated manuscript of Lisbon, in the _Crónica de D. Afonso Henriques_ by [Duarte Galvão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duarte_Galv%C3%A3o "Duarte Galvão"), depicting the castle and walls, including the Royal Palace (_Alcáçova_) (1505)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg/250px-Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg)

Caravels and carracks in the Tagus River, with the castle in the centre distance, unknown artist (1572)

Although the first fortifications on this hilltop date from the 1st century BC, [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") excavations have identified a human presence in the Tagus valley as far back as the 8th century BC. The first fortification was, presumably, erected in 48 BC, when Lisbon was classified as a Roman municipality.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Bellard2003-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Arruda2002-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Laidlar1997-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

The hill was first used by [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celt "Celt") tribes, then by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia"), followed by [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") and later the [Carthaginians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage") as a defensive outpost that was later expropriated successively by the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), the [Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi"), the [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoths "Visigoths"), and the [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors"). During the 10th century, the fortifications were built by [Berber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers "Berbers") forces; these included the walls or _Cerca Moura_ ("Moorish Encirclement").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

### Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Kingdom")]

In the context of the [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians")_[Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_, the castle and the city of Lisbon was conquered from the Moorish [Almoravid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravid_dynasty "Almoravid dynasty") in 1147 by [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques") and northern European knights in the [Siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon") during the [Second Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Crusade "Second Crusade"); this victory was the only notable success of that failed crusade.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) According to an oft-repeated [legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legend "Legend"), the [knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight "Knight")[Martim Moniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martim_Moniz "Martim Moniz"), noticing that one of the doors to the castle was open, prevented the Moors from closing it by throwing his own body into the breach, thus allowing Christian soldiers to enter at the cost of his own life. With the taking of the castle Christian forces were able to maintain the defense of Lisbon until the end of the 12th century.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-8)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG/250px-Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG)

The castle walls and towers, constructed during the Moorish occupation of Lisbon

When Lisbon became the capital of the [Kingdom of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") in 1255, the castle served as the _alcáçova_, a fortified residence for [Afonso III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_III_of_Portugal "Afonso III of Portugal"), in his role as governor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) It was extensively renovated around 1300 by [King Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_of_Portugal "Denis of Portugal"), transforming the Moorish alcáçova into the Royal Palace of the Alcáçova.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) Between 1373 and 1375, King [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_Portugal "Ferdinand I of Portugal") ordered the building of the _Cerca Nova_ or _Cerca Fernandina_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-silva1987-9):20–21 the walled compound that enclosed all but the north flank of the castle.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-silva1987-9)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-10) The master builders João Fernandes and Vasco Brás were responsible for its construction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) This wall, which partially replaced the old Moorish walls, was designed to encircle previously unprotected parts of the city. Completed in two years, it had 77 towers, 34 or 38 gates,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Norwich2016-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-PortuguesesCidade1997-12) and a perimeter of 5,400 metres (17,700 ft).

The castle and the city resisted the forces of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") several times during the 14th century (notably in 1373 and in 1383–1384). It was during this period (the late 14th century) that the castle was dedicated to [Saint George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George "Saint George") by King [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal"), who had married the English princess [Philippa of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_of_Lancaster "Philippa of Lancaster").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) Saint George, the warrior-saint, was normally represented slaying a dragon, and was very popular in both countries.

From 1378 onwards many of the kingdom's records were housed in the _[Torre do Tombo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre\_do\_Tombo "Torre do Tombo")_ (literally, "Tower of the Archive"), also known as the _Torre Albarrã_, until the [earthquake of 1755](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake_of_1755 "Earthquake of 1755") (a tower that is known today as _Tower of [Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus")_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) The Portuguese Royal Archive, where the eminent Portuguese [chroniclers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle "Chronicle")[Fernão Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fern%C3%A3o_Lopes "Fernão Lopes"), [Gomes Eanes de Zurara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gomes_Eanes_de_Zurara "Gomes Eanes de Zurara") and [Damião de Góis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A3o_de_G%C3%B3is "Damião de Góis") once worked, is still referred to as the _Torre do Tombo_, due to its original location in one of the towers of the Lisbon Castle. On 9 December 1448, Gil Pires was named the castle master builder to replace Afonso Esteves, being paid 400 [réis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_real "Portuguese real") for his work.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) Between 1448 and 1451, the master builder was paid several stipends for his work on the palace. Similarly, the mason João de Alverca was paid a substantial sum for stonework. These public works continued from 1449 until 1452, with additional payments being made for labor and materials to convert the building from a fortified castle to a royal residence.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

In the beginning of the 15th century, a [royal menagerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menagerie "Menagerie") was established in the Royal Palace of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), located nearby the Castle of Saint George. Following the [conquest of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Ceuta "Conquest of Ceuta") in 1415, King [John I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal") brought back to Lisbon two [Barbary lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_lion "Barbary lion"), and they were installed in a large room inside his Palace in the Citadel of Lisbon. This area of the Palace came to be known as _Casa dos Leões_ (the "Lions' House"); today the area is occupied by a famed restaurant with the same name.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Castelo-13) Later that century, German [humanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanist "Humanist")[Hieronymus Münzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymus_M%C3%BCnzer "Hieronymus Münzer") spent five days in Lisbon in [1494](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1494 "1494"), and learned about the lions, claiming to be the most beautiful wild beasts he had ever seen.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Muenzer-14)

As the royal palace, the castle was the setting for the reception by King [Manuel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") of the navigator [Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama "Vasco da Gama") when he returned from discovering the maritime route to India in 1498. The castle also served as a theater in 1502 when pioneering playwright [Gil Vicente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Vicente "Gil Vicente") staged his _Monólogo do Vaqueiro_ to honor the birth of Manuel I's son and heir, the future [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III_of_Portugal "John III of Portugal").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

Around the early 16th century, following the construction of the [Ribeira Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeira_Palace "Ribeira Palace") beside the [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus") river, the Palace of Alcáçova began to lose its importance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) An [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1531_Lisbon_earthquake "1531 Lisbon earthquake") occurring in 1531 further damaged the old castle, contributing further to its decay and neglect.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) In 1569, King [Sebastian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastiao_I_of_Portugal "Sebastiao I of Portugal") ordered the rebuilding of the royal apartments in the castle, intending to use it as his official residence. As part of the rebuilding, in 1577 Filippo Terzi demolished one of the towers near the principal facade of the Church of Loreto.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) However, many of the works were never completed after the young king's apparent death during the [Battle of Alcácer Quibir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Alc%C3%A1cer_Quibir "Battle of Alcácer Quibir"). The following [Portuguese dynastic crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_for_the_throne_of_Portugal "Struggle for the throne of Portugal") opened the way for [sixty years of Spanish rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Union "Iberian Union") and the castle was converted into military barracks and a prison.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) On 30 December 1642, Teodósio de Frias the Younger was appointed master builder to continue the works begun by his father, Luís de Frias, and his grandfather, Teodósio de Frias. This was part of a greater plan by the Spanish forces to recommission the fortification.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_%2829762148847%29.jpg/500px-Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_%2829762148847%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_(29762148847).jpg)

Lisbon seen from São Jorge Castle

However, after Portugal regained its independence following the [Portuguese Restoration War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Restoration_War "Portuguese Restoration War"), the works were taken over by the Portuguese government. On 6 November 1648, Nicolau de Langres was called upon to take over the design, execution and construction of a new fortification that would surround the Castle of Saint George and the city walls of Lisbon. In 1650 the military architect Mateus do Couto was named master builder of the project and reconstruction took on a new formality: although the military engineer João Gillot built new walls in 1652, construction again followed Couto's plans between 1657 and 1733. In 1673, the Soldiers' Hospital, dedicated to _São João de Deus_ (St John of God), was installed on the grounds beside the Rua do Recolhimento. At the end of the 17th century the _Recolhimento do Castelo_ ("Castle Shelter") was constructed along the southeast angle of the courtyard, and in 1733, new projects were initiated by master Custódio Vieira.

The [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake") severely damaged the castle and contributed to its continuing decay: apart from the walls of the old castle, the soldier's hospital and the _Recolhimento_ were left in ruins. The necessity of maintaining a supporting military force within the capital city required expansion of the site's role of garrison and presidio. From 1780 to 1807, the charitable institution [Casa Pia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_Pia "Casa Pia"), dedicated to the education of poor children, was established in the citadel, while soldiers continued to be garrisoned on site. Inspired by the events of the earthquake and the following tsunami, the first [geodetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesy "Geodesy") observatory in Portugal was constructed in 1788 at the top of one of the towers of the castle, later referred to as the _Torre do Observatório_ (Observatory Tower).

### Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Republic")]

By the 1930s, the Castle had all but disappeared as a distinguishable landmark from Lisbon's skyline, being almost entirely obscured behind and under later annexes and additions.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-15) As part of the commemorative celebrations marking the foundation of nationhood and restoration of independence ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Fundação da Nacionalidade e da Restauração da Independência_), the government of [António de Oliveira Salazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_de_Oliveira_Salazar "António de Oliveira Salazar") initiated extensive renovations at the site (as it did with similar castles, such as the ones in [Sintra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sintra "Sintra") and [Silves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silves,_Portugal "Silves, Portugal")). Most of the incongruous structures added to the castle compound in previous centuries were demolished, under the supervision of the DGEMN, and there was a partial restoration of the _Recolhimento_. In addition, on 25 October 1947, a monument dedicated to [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques"), presented by the city of Porto, of a replica created by Soares dos Reis (in 1887) was installed on the grounds.

On 31 May 1942 the castle's operations began to be handled by the city government of Lisbon, which was reaffirmed on 8 June 1979.

In 1998, the semi-rectangular spaces, columns and cistern were adapted into the museum _Olissipónia_.

On 22 August 2006, Direcção Regional de Cultura Lisboa (DRCLisboa) defined a special protection zone, that included the Castle of São Jorge and the rest of the walls of Lisbon, the _Baixa Pombalina_ and various properties that were already classified as cultural heritage. The _Conselho Nacional de Cultura_ (National Council of Culture) proposed shelving this definition on 10 October 2011, which was supported by [IGESPAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGESPAR "IGESPAR").

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/CastleSaintGeorge.jpg/960px-CastleSaintGeorge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CastleSaintGeorge.jpg)

A panorama of the entire Castle of São Jorge

The castle is in the centre of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), on a hill, while many of its walls extend around the citadel into the civil parishes that surround it to the east and south.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg/250px-S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg)

The map helps tourist find areas of interest in the castle

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg/250px-Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg)

Bridge over the current dry moat

The castle's plan is roughly square, and it was originally encircled by a wall, to form a [citadel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citadel "Citadel"). The castle complex consists of the castle itself (the _castelejo_), some ancillary buildings (including the ruins of the royal palace), gardens, and a large terraced square from which an impressive panorama of Lisbon is visible. The main entrance to the citadel is a 19th-century gate surmounted by the [coat-of-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat-of-arms "Coat-of-arms") of Portugal, the name of [Queen Maria II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_II_of_Portugal "Maria II of Portugal"), and the date 1846. This gate permits access to the main square (_Praça d'Armas_), which is decorated with old cannons and a bronze statue of [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques"), the Portuguese monarch who took the castle from the Moors. This statue is a copy of the 19th-century original, by the [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") sculptor [António Soares dos Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Soares_dos_Reis "António Soares dos Reis"), which is located near [Guimarães Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guimar%C3%A3es_Castle "Guimarães Castle") in northern Portugal.

The remnants of the royal palace are located near the main square, but all that is left are some walls and a few rebuilt rooms such as the _Casa Ogival_. It now hosts the _Olissipónia_, a multimedia show about the history of Lisbon.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg/250px-Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg)

View from the interior of the castle

The medieval castle is located toward the northwest corner of the citadel, at its highest point. Hypothetically, during a [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege"), if attackers managed to enter the citadel, the castle was the last stronghold, the last place in which to take refuge. It is rectangular, with ten towers. A wall with a tower and a connecting door divides the castle courtyard into halves. A series of stairways allow visitors to reach the walkway atop the wall and the towers, from which magnificent views of Lisbon can be enjoyed. The Tower of Ulysses (where the [_Torre do Tombo_ archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_do_Tombo "Torre do Tombo") used to be) had a [camera obscura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camera_obscura "Camera obscura") installed in 1998[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-16) that allows spectators a 360-degree view of the city and [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River").

Apart from its main walls, the castle is protected, on its southern and eastern sides, by a [barbican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbican "Barbican") (_barbacã_), a low wall that prevented [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engines "Siege engines") from approaching the main castle walls. The northern and western sides of the castle, on the other hand, were naturally protected by the steep hillside sloping downward from the castle's foundations. The castle is also partially encircled by a [moat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moat "Moat"), now dry. The main entrance is fronted by a stone bridge across the moat. On the west side, there is a long curtain wall extending downhill, ending at a tower (the _Torre de São Lourenço_).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-silva1987-9):33–35 This tower guarded a gate in the _Cerca Fernandina_.

**São Jorge Castle** ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Castelo de São Jorge_; Portuguese pronunciation:[[kɐʃˈtɛlu dɨ sɐ̃w̃ˈʒɔɾʒɨ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese")), sometimes known in English as **Saint George's Castle**, is a historic [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle") in the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") capital of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), located in the _[freguesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freguesia "Freguesia")_ of [Santa Maria Maior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria_Maior_(Lisbon) "Santa Maria Maior (Lisbon)"). Human occupation of the castle hill dates to at least the 8th century BC[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-2) while the oldest fortifications on the site date from the 2nd century BC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-3) The hill on which Saint George's Castle stands has played an important part in the [history of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lisbon "History of Lisbon"), having served as the location of fortifications occupied successively by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia"), [Carthaginians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"), and [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors"), before its conquest by the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people") in the [1147 Siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon"). Since the 12th century, the castle has variously served as a [royal palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_palace "Royal palace"), a [military barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barracks "Barracks"), home of the [Torre do Tombo National Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_do_Tombo_National_Archive "Torre do Tombo National Archive"), and now as a [national monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_monuments_of_Portugal "List of national monuments of Portugal") and museum.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg/250px-Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg)

A 16th-century illuminated manuscript of Lisbon, in the _Crónica de D. Afonso Henriques_ by [Duarte Galvão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duarte_Galv%C3%A3o "Duarte Galvão"), depicting the castle and walls, including the Royal Palace (_Alcáçova_) (1505)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg/250px-Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg)

Caravels and carracks in the Tagus River, with the castle in the centre distance, unknown artist (1572)

Although the first fortifications on this hilltop date from the 1st century BC, [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") excavations have identified a human presence in the Tagus valley as far back as the 8th century BC. The first fortification was, presumably, erected in 48 BC, when Lisbon was classified as a Roman municipality.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Bellard2003-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Arruda2002-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Laidlar1997-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

The hill was first used by [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celt "Celt") tribes, then by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia"), followed by [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") and later the [Carthaginians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage") as a defensive outpost that was later expropriated successively by the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), the [Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi"), the [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoths "Visigoths"), and the [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors"). During the 10th century, the fortifications were built by [Berber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers "Berbers") forces; these included the walls or _Cerca Moura_ ("Moorish Encirclement").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

### Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Kingdom")]

In the context of the [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians")_[Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_, the castle and the city of Lisbon was conquered from the Moorish [Almoravid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravid_dynasty "Almoravid dynasty") in 1147 by [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques") and northern European knights in the [Siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon") during the [Second Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Crusade "Second Crusade"); this victory was the only notable success of that failed crusade.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) According to an oft-repeated [legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legend "Legend"), the [knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight "Knight")[Martim Moniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martim_Moniz "Martim Moniz"), noticing that one of the doors to the castle was open, prevented the Moors from closing it by throwing his own body into the breach, thus allowing Christian soldiers to enter at the cost of his own life. With the taking of the castle Christian forces were able to maintain the defense of Lisbon until the end of the 12th century.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-8)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG/250px-Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG)

The castle walls and towers, constructed during the Moorish occupation of Lisbon

When Lisbon became the capital of the [Kingdom of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") in 1255, the castle served as the _alcáçova_, a fortified residence for [Afonso III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_III_of_Portugal "Afonso III of Portugal"), in his role as governor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) It was extensively renovated around 1300 by [King Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_of_Portugal "Denis of Portugal"), transforming the Moorish alcáçova into the Royal Palace of the Alcáçova.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) Between 1373 and 1375, King [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_Portugal "Ferdinand I of Portugal") ordered the building of the _Cerca Nova_ or _Cerca Fernandina_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-silva1987-9):20–21 the walled compound that enclosed all but the north flank of the castle.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-silva1987-9)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-10) The master builders João Fernandes and Vasco Brás were responsible for its construction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) This wall, which partially replaced the old Moorish walls, was designed to encircle previously unprotected parts of the city. Completed in two years, it had 77 towers, 34 or 38 gates,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Norwich2016-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-PortuguesesCidade1997-12) and a perimeter of 5,400 metres (17,700 ft).

The castle and the city resisted the forces of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") several times during the 14th century (notably in 1373 and in 1383–1384). It was during this period (the late 14th century) that the castle was dedicated to [Saint George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George "Saint George") by King [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal"), who had married the English princess [Philippa of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_of_Lancaster "Philippa of Lancaster").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) Saint George, the warrior-saint, was normally represented slaying a dragon, and was very popular in both countries.

From 1378 onwards many of the kingdom's records were housed in the _[Torre do Tombo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre\_do\_Tombo "Torre do Tombo")_ (literally, "Tower of the Archive"), also known as the _Torre Albarrã_, until the [earthquake of 1755](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake_of_1755 "Earthquake of 1755") (a tower that is known today as _Tower of [Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus")_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) The Portuguese Royal Archive, where the eminent Portuguese [chroniclers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle "Chronicle")[Fernão Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fern%C3%A3o_Lopes "Fernão Lopes"), [Gomes Eanes de Zurara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gomes_Eanes_de_Zurara "Gomes Eanes de Zurara") and [Damião de Góis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A3o_de_G%C3%B3is "Damião de Góis") once worked, is still referred to as the _Torre do Tombo_, due to its original location in one of the towers of the Lisbon Castle. On 9 December 1448, Gil Pires was named the castle master builder to replace Afonso Esteves, being paid 400 [réis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_real "Portuguese real") for his work.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) Between 1448 and 1451, the master builder was paid several stipends for his work on the palace. Similarly, the mason João de Alverca was paid a substantial sum for stonework. These public works continued from 1449 until 1452, with additional payments being made for labor and materials to convert the building from a fortified castle to a royal residence.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

In the beginning of the 15th century, a [royal menagerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menagerie "Menagerie") was established in the Royal Palace of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), located nearby the Castle of Saint George. Following the [conquest of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Ceuta "Conquest of Ceuta") in 1415, King [John I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal") brought back to Lisbon two [Barbary lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_lion "Barbary lion"), and they were installed in a large room inside his Palace in the Citadel of Lisbon. This area of the Palace came to be known as _Casa dos Leões_ (the "Lions' House"); today the area is occupied by a famed restaurant with the same name.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Castelo-13) Later that century, German [humanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanist "Humanist")[Hieronymus Münzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymus_M%C3%BCnzer "Hieronymus Münzer") spent five days in Lisbon in [1494](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1494 "1494"), and learned about the lions, claiming to be the most beautiful wild beasts he had ever seen.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-Muenzer-14)

As the royal palace, the castle was the setting for the reception by King [Manuel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") of the navigator [Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama "Vasco da Gama") when he returned from discovering the maritime route to India in 1498. The castle also served as a theater in 1502 when pioneering playwright [Gil Vicente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Vicente "Gil Vicente") staged his _Monólogo do Vaqueiro_ to honor the birth of Manuel I's son and heir, the future [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III_of_Portugal "John III of Portugal").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7)

Around the early 16th century, following the construction of the [Ribeira Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeira_Palace "Ribeira Palace") beside the [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus") river, the Palace of Alcáçova began to lose its importance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) An [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1531_Lisbon_earthquake "1531 Lisbon earthquake") occurring in 1531 further damaged the old castle, contributing further to its decay and neglect.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) In 1569, King [Sebastian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastiao_I_of_Portugal "Sebastiao I of Portugal") ordered the rebuilding of the royal apartments in the castle, intending to use it as his official residence. As part of the rebuilding, in 1577 Filippo Terzi demolished one of the towers near the principal facade of the Church of Loreto.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) However, many of the works were never completed after the young king's apparent death during the [Battle of Alcácer Quibir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Alc%C3%A1cer_Quibir "Battle of Alcácer Quibir"). The following [Portuguese dynastic crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_for_the_throne_of_Portugal "Struggle for the throne of Portugal") opened the way for [sixty years of Spanish rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Union "Iberian Union") and the castle was converted into military barracks and a prison.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-SIPA-7) On 30 December 1642, Teodósio de Frias the Younger was appointed master builder to continue the works begun by his father, Luís de Frias, and his grandfather, Teodósio de Frias. This was part of a greater plan by the Spanish forces to recommission the fortification.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_%2829762148847%29.jpg/500px-Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_%2829762148847%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_(29762148847).jpg)

Lisbon seen from São Jorge Castle

However, after Portugal regained its independence following the [Portuguese Restoration War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Restoration_War "Portuguese Restoration War"), the works were taken over by the Portuguese government. On 6 November 1648, Nicolau de Langres was called upon to take over the design, execution and construction of a new fortification that would surround the Castle of Saint George and the city walls of Lisbon. In 1650 the military architect Mateus do Couto was named master builder of the project and reconstruction took on a new formality: although the military engineer João Gillot built new walls in 1652, construction again followed Couto's plans between 1657 and 1733. In 1673, the Soldiers' Hospital, dedicated to _São João de Deus_ (St John of God), was installed on the grounds beside the Rua do Recolhimento. At the end of the 17th century the _Recolhimento do Castelo_ ("Castle Shelter") was constructed along the southeast angle of the courtyard, and in 1733, new projects were initiated by master Custódio Vieira.

The [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake") severely damaged the castle and contributed to its continuing decay: apart from the walls of the old castle, the soldier's hospital and the _Recolhimento_ were left in ruins. The necessity of maintaining a supporting military force within the capital city required expansion of the site's role of garrison and presidio. From 1780 to 1807, the charitable institution [Casa Pia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_Pia "Casa Pia"), dedicated to the education of poor children, was established in the citadel, while soldiers continued to be garrisoned on site. Inspired by the events of the earthquake and the following tsunami, the first [geodetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesy "Geodesy") observatory in Portugal was constructed in 1788 at the top of one of the towers of the castle, later referred to as the _Torre do Observatório_ (Observatory Tower).

### Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Republic")]

By the 1930s, the Castle had all but disappeared as a distinguishable landmark from Lisbon's skyline, being almost entirely obscured behind and under later annexes and additions.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-15) As part of the commemorative celebrations marking the foundation of nationhood and restoration of independence ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Fundação da Nacionalidade e da Restauração da Independência_), the government of [António de Oliveira Salazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_de_Oliveira_Salazar "António de Oliveira Salazar") initiated extensive renovations at the site (as it did with similar castles, such as the ones in [Sintra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sintra "Sintra") and [Silves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silves,_Portugal "Silves, Portugal")). Most of the incongruous structures added to the castle compound in previous centuries were demolished, under the supervision of the DGEMN, and there was a partial restoration of the _Recolhimento_. In addition, on 25 October 1947, a monument dedicated to [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques"), presented by the city of Porto, of a replica created by Soares dos Reis (in 1887) was installed on the grounds.

On 31 May 1942 the castle's operations began to be handled by the city government of Lisbon, which was reaffirmed on 8 June 1979.

In 1998, the semi-rectangular spaces, columns and cistern were adapted into the museum _Olissipónia_.

On 22 August 2006, Direcção Regional de Cultura Lisboa (DRCLisboa) defined a special protection zone, that included the Castle of São Jorge and the rest of the walls of Lisbon, the _Baixa Pombalina_ and various properties that were already classified as cultural heritage. The _Conselho Nacional de Cultura_ (National Council of Culture) proposed shelving this definition on 10 October 2011, which was supported by [IGESPAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGESPAR "IGESPAR").

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/CastleSaintGeorge.jpg/960px-CastleSaintGeorge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CastleSaintGeorge.jpg)

A panorama of the entire Castle of São Jorge

The castle is in the centre of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), on a hill, while many of its walls extend around the citadel into the civil parishes that surround it to the east and south.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg/250px-S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg)

The map helps tourist find areas of interest in the castle

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg/250px-Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg)

Bridge over the current dry moat

The castle's plan is roughly square, and it was originally encircled by a wall, to form a [citadel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citadel "Citadel"). The castle complex consists of the castle itself (the _castelejo_), some ancillary buildings (including the ruins of the royal palace), gardens, and a large terraced square from which an impressive panorama of Lisbon is visible. The main entrance to the citadel is a 19th-century gate surmounted by the [coat-of-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat-of-arms "Coat-of-arms") of Portugal, the name of [Queen Maria II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_II_of_Portugal "Maria II of Portugal"), and the date 1846. This gate permits access to the main square (_Praça d'Armas_), which is decorated with old cannons and a bronze statue of [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques"), the Portuguese monarch who took the castle from the Moors. This statue is a copy of the 19th-century original, by the [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") sculptor [António Soares dos Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Soares_dos_Reis "António Soares dos Reis"), which is located near [Guimarães Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guimar%C3%A3es_Castle "Guimarães Castle") in northern Portugal.

The remnants of the royal palace are located near the main square, but all that is left are some walls and a few rebuilt rooms such as the _Casa Ogival_. It now hosts the _Olissipónia_, a multimedia show about the history of Lisbon.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg/250px-Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg)

View from the interior of the castle

The medieval castle is located toward the northwest corner of the citadel, at its highest point. Hypothetically, during a [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege"), if attackers managed to enter the citadel, the castle was the last stronghold, the last place in which to take refuge. It is rectangular, with ten towers. A wall with a tower and a connecting door divides the castle courtyard into halves. A series of stairways allow visitors to reach the walkway atop the wall and the towers, from which magnificent views of Lisbon can be enjoyed. The Tower of Ulysses (where the [_Torre do Tombo_ archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_do_Tombo "Torre do Tombo") used to be) had a [camera obscura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camera_obscura "Camera obscura") installed in 1998[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-16) that allows spectators a 360-degree view of the city and [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River").

Apart from its main walls, the castle is protected, on its southern and eastern sides, by a [barbican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbican "Barbican") (_barbacã_), a low wall that prevented [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engines "Siege engines") from approaching the main castle walls. The northern and western sides of the castle, on the other hand, were naturally protected by the steep hillside sloping downward from the castle's foundations. The castle is also partially encircled by a [moat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moat "Moat"), now dry. The main entrance is fronted by a stone bridge across the moat. On the west side, there is a long curtain wall extending downhill, ending at a tower (the _Torre de São Lourenço_).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_of_Sao_Jorge#cite_note-silva1987-9):33–35 This tower guarded a gate in the _Cerca Fernandina_.

**St George's Church** is the only English-speaking [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism") congregation in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal"). It is located at Rua São Jorge 6, north of the Estrela Garden.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1654 a treaty between Lord Protector [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") and King [John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV_of_Portugal "John IV of Portugal") of [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") (signed on his behalf by [João Rodrigues de Sá e Menezes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_Rodrigues_de_S%C3%A1_e_Menezes "João Rodrigues de Sá e Menezes"), [Count of Penaguião](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Penagui%C3%A3o "Count of Penaguião")) allowed English residents in Portugal to _"profess their own Religion in private houses... and that finally a Place be allowed for them to bury their dead"_. A chaplaincy was established, with services held in the home of the British Envoy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-GLC-1)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Chapelle_Anglaise_-_Clementine_Brelaz_%28Museu_de_Lisboa%29.png/250px-Chapelle_Anglaise_-_Clementine_Brelaz_%28Museu_de_Lisboa%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chapelle_Anglaise_-_Clementine_Brelaz_(Museu_de_Lisboa).png)

The original church, built in 1822 and destroyed by a fire in 1886.

## Cemetery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cemetery")]

Main article: [British Cemetery, Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Cemetery,_Lisbon "British Cemetery, Lisbon")

Although a burial ground had been promised by the 1654 treaty, implementation was thwarted by the [Portuguese Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Inquisition "Portuguese Inquisition"). Land was finally leased in 1717;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-2) the first burial was that of Francis La Roche, a [Huguenot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenot "Huguenot") refugee, who died in 1724.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-3)

Notable burials in the cemetery include the tombs of the writer [Henry Fielding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fielding "Henry Fielding"), of hymn-writer [Philip Doddridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Doddridge "Philip Doddridge"), of merchant [David de Pury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_de_Pury "David de Pury"), astronomer [Carl Ludwig Christian Rümker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Ludwig_Christian_R%C3%BCmker "Carl Ludwig Christian Rümker"), Field Marshal of the Portuguese land army [Christian August, Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_August,_Prince_of_Waldeck_and_Pyrmont "Christian August, Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-4) and diplomat [Thomas Barclay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Barclay_(diplomat) "Thomas Barclay (diplomat)").

The cemetery includes 31 [Commonwealth War Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission"): five from the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and 26 from the [Second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-5) 29 are in individual plots; two are in private family vaults. They include members of the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army"), [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy"), [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"), [Royal Canadian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Air_Force "Royal Canadian Air Force"), [Merchant Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Navy_(United_Kingdom) "Merchant Navy (United Kingdom)") and [British Overseas Airways Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Overseas_Airways_Corporation "British Overseas Airways Corporation").

Count [Miklós Horthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikl%C3%B3s_Horthy "Miklós Horthy"), a [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Church_in_Hungary "Reformed Church in Hungary") former [Vice Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Admiral "Vice Admiral") in the [Austro-Hungarian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Navy "Austro-Hungarian Navy") and [Regent of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1920-1946) "Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946)"), died in exile in Portugal and was buried in the cemetery, along with his wife and son. In 1993 they were exhumed, and re-interred in the Horthy family mausoleum in [Kenderes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenderes "Kenderes").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-6)

## Church building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Church building")]

Anglicans in Portugal petitioned for permission to build a church, but until the early 19th century the Portuguese Inquisition prevailed on the monarch not to grant it. A church of St George the Martyr was built in the cemetery in 1822. That church was consecrated in 1843[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-7) but was damaged by earthquake in 1859.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-8) It was rebuilt, but burnt down in 1886. The present church was designed by the London-based architects [John Medland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Medland?action=edit&redlink=1 "John Medland (page does not exist)") and [Charles Edward Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Edward_Powell?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charles Edward Powell (page does not exist)") and consecrated in 1889.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-GLC-1) It is a [Romanesque Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanesque_Revival_architecture "Romanesque Revival architecture") building with a [narthex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narthex "Narthex"), [blind arcades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_arcade "Blind arcade") and [rose window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_window "Rose window") on its west front. The windows are by [Lavers & Westlake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavers,_Barraud_and_Westlake "Lavers, Barraud and Westlake").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-9)

## Anglican Church of St George and St Paul, Lisbon

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Anglican Church of St George and St Paul, Lisbon")]

In 1984, St George's Church, Lisbon was amalgamated with St Paul's Church, Estoril to form the Greater Lisbon Chaplaincy,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-GLC-1) and is part of the [Diocese in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_in_Europe "Diocese in Europe") of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"). It is now named the Anglican Church of St George and St Paul, Lisbon.

## Fincham pipe organ

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Fincham pipe organ")]

When the existing church was designed, traditional choir stalls were included in front of the Sanctuary and Henry Fincham of London built and installed a two-manual pipe organ for £526.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-23) It has 25 ranks with 61-note compass of the manuals and 30-note compass of the pedals. There were two minor changes to the Great organ which, in its original state, did not include mutation stops. The organ was restored in 1971.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-24)

This is the current disposition of the organ after 125 years of use:

**Great – I**

*   8' Open Diapason
*   8' Lieblich Gedacht
*   8' Gambe
*   4' Principal
*   2 2⁄3' Nazard
*   2' Fifteenth
*   1 3⁄5' Tierce
*   8' Corno de Bassetto
*   8' Trumpet

**Pedal**

*   16' Grande Open Diapason
*   16' Bourdon

**Swell – II**

*   16' Double Open Diapason
*   8' Horn Diapason
*   8' Stopped Diapason
*   8' Vox Angelica
*   8' Voix Celeste
*   4' Principal
*   4' Flûte a Cheminee
*   2' Fifteenth
*   III Mixture
*   8' Cornopean
*   8' Hautboy
*   8' Vox Humana
*   Swell Tremulant
*   Swell to Great Super
*   Swell to Great
*   Swell to Pedal
*   Great to Pedal
*   Swell shades open catch mechanism
*   5 pre-set piston shoes

**St George's Church** is the only English-speaking [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism") congregation in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal"). It is located at Rua São Jorge 6, north of the Estrela Garden.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1654 a treaty between Lord Protector [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") and King [John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV_of_Portugal "John IV of Portugal") of [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") (signed on his behalf by [João Rodrigues de Sá e Menezes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_Rodrigues_de_S%C3%A1_e_Menezes "João Rodrigues de Sá e Menezes"), [Count of Penaguião](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Penagui%C3%A3o "Count of Penaguião")) allowed English residents in Portugal to _"profess their own Religion in private houses... and that finally a Place be allowed for them to bury their dead"_. A chaplaincy was established, with services held in the home of the British Envoy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-GLC-1)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Chapelle_Anglaise_-_Clementine_Brelaz_%28Museu_de_Lisboa%29.png/250px-Chapelle_Anglaise_-_Clementine_Brelaz_%28Museu_de_Lisboa%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chapelle_Anglaise_-_Clementine_Brelaz_(Museu_de_Lisboa).png)

The original church, built in 1822 and destroyed by a fire in 1886.

## Cemetery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cemetery")]

Main article: [British Cemetery, Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Cemetery,_Lisbon "British Cemetery, Lisbon")

Although a burial ground had been promised by the 1654 treaty, implementation was thwarted by the [Portuguese Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Inquisition "Portuguese Inquisition"). Land was finally leased in 1717;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-2) the first burial was that of Francis La Roche, a [Huguenot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenot "Huguenot") refugee, who died in 1724.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-3)

Notable burials in the cemetery include the tombs of the writer [Henry Fielding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fielding "Henry Fielding"), of hymn-writer [Philip Doddridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Doddridge "Philip Doddridge"), of merchant [David de Pury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_de_Pury "David de Pury"), astronomer [Carl Ludwig Christian Rümker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Ludwig_Christian_R%C3%BCmker "Carl Ludwig Christian Rümker"), Field Marshal of the Portuguese land army [Christian August, Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_August,_Prince_of_Waldeck_and_Pyrmont "Christian August, Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-4) and diplomat [Thomas Barclay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Barclay_(diplomat) "Thomas Barclay (diplomat)").

The cemetery includes 31 [Commonwealth War Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission"): five from the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and 26 from the [Second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-5) 29 are in individual plots; two are in private family vaults. They include members of the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army"), [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy"), [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"), [Royal Canadian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Air_Force "Royal Canadian Air Force"), [Merchant Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Navy_(United_Kingdom) "Merchant Navy (United Kingdom)") and [British Overseas Airways Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Overseas_Airways_Corporation "British Overseas Airways Corporation").

Count [Miklós Horthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikl%C3%B3s_Horthy "Miklós Horthy"), a [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Church_in_Hungary "Reformed Church in Hungary") former [Vice Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Admiral "Vice Admiral") in the [Austro-Hungarian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Navy "Austro-Hungarian Navy") and [Regent of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1920-1946) "Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946)"), died in exile in Portugal and was buried in the cemetery, along with his wife and son. In 1993 they were exhumed, and re-interred in the Horthy family mausoleum in [Kenderes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenderes "Kenderes").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-6)

## Church building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Church building")]

Anglicans in Portugal petitioned for permission to build a church, but until the early 19th century the Portuguese Inquisition prevailed on the monarch not to grant it. A church of St George the Martyr was built in the cemetery in 1822. That church was consecrated in 1843[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-7) but was damaged by earthquake in 1859.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-8) It was rebuilt, but burnt down in 1886. The present church was designed by the London-based architects [John Medland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Medland?action=edit&redlink=1 "John Medland (page does not exist)") and [Charles Edward Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Edward_Powell?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charles Edward Powell (page does not exist)") and consecrated in 1889.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-GLC-1) It is a [Romanesque Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanesque_Revival_architecture "Romanesque Revival architecture") building with a [narthex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narthex "Narthex"), [blind arcades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_arcade "Blind arcade") and [rose window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_window "Rose window") on its west front. The windows are by [Lavers & Westlake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavers,_Barraud_and_Westlake "Lavers, Barraud and Westlake").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-9)

## Anglican Church of St George and St Paul, Lisbon

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Anglican Church of St George and St Paul, Lisbon")]

In 1984, St George's Church, Lisbon was amalgamated with St Paul's Church, Estoril to form the Greater Lisbon Chaplaincy,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-GLC-1) and is part of the [Diocese in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_in_Europe "Diocese in Europe") of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"). It is now named the Anglican Church of St George and St Paul, Lisbon.

## Fincham pipe organ

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St_George%27s_Church,_Lisbon&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Fincham pipe organ")]

When the existing church was designed, traditional choir stalls were included in front of the Sanctuary and Henry Fincham of London built and installed a two-manual pipe organ for £526.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-23) It has 25 ranks with 61-note compass of the manuals and 30-note compass of the pedals. There were two minor changes to the Great organ which, in its original state, did not include mutation stops. The organ was restored in 1971.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_Church,_Lisbon#cite_note-24)

This is the current disposition of the organ after 125 years of use:

**Great – I**

*   8' Open Diapason
*   8' Lieblich Gedacht
*   8' Gambe
*   4' Principal
*   2 2⁄3' Nazard
*   2' Fifteenth
*   1 3⁄5' Tierce
*   8' Corno de Bassetto
*   8' Trumpet

**Pedal**

*   16' Grande Open Diapason
*   16' Bourdon

**Swell – II**

*   16' Double Open Diapason
*   8' Horn Diapason
*   8' Stopped Diapason
*   8' Vox Angelica
*   8' Voix Celeste
*   4' Principal
*   4' Flûte a Cheminee
*   2' Fifteenth
*   III Mixture
*   8' Cornopean
*   8' Hautboy
*   8' Vox Humana
*   Swell Tremulant
*   Swell to Great Super
*   Swell to Great
*   Swell to Pedal
*   Great to Pedal
*   Swell shades open catch mechanism

The **Alcazaba of Almería** is a fortified complex in [Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa "Almería"), southern [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"). The word _[alcazaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba "Alcazaba")_, from the Arabic word (القَصَبَة; _[\_al-qaṣabah\_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasbah "Kasbah")_), signifies a walled fortification in a city.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 955, Almería was given the title of _medina_ ("city") by the [Caliph of Cordoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliph_of_Cordoba "Caliph of Cordoba")[Abd ar-Rahman III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_ar-Rahman_III "Abd ar-Rahman III"), when the construction of the defensive citadel located in the upper sector of the city began.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-ciudadela-1) Provided not only with walls and towers but also with squares, houses, and a mosque, it was to be the seat of the local government, commanding the city and the nearby sea.

The complex was enlarged under caliph [Al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mansur_Ibn_Abi_Aamir "Al-Mansur Ibn Abi Aamir") and again under [Khayran as-Saqlabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khayran_as-Saqlabi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Khayran as-Saqlabi (page does not exist)")[[ar](https://ar.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AE%D9%8A%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B5%D9%82%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%8A "ar:خيران الصقلبي")], the first king of the independent [taifa of Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Almer%C3%ADa "Taifa of Almería").

Its purpose was to protect the area's largest city at the time, [Pechina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechina "Pechina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-ciudadela-1)

Most of the objects from the [archaeological site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological_site "Archaeological site") at the Alcazaba are kept in the [Museo de Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_de_Almer%C3%ADa "Museo de Almería"), but some are in the Museo de la Alhambra.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-2)

The renowned Muslim scholar [Abul Walid Al-Baji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_al-Walid_al-Baji "Abu al-Walid al-Baji") was reported to be buried within the grounds of the citadel according to the biographical work of [Ibn Bashkawal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Bashkuwal "Ibn Bashkuwal") writing around 50-60 years later.

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Description")]

[![Image 9: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(March 2026)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

The first line of walls is a wide enclosure corresponding to the first Muslim military camp, used as shelter for the population in case of siege. For this task it was provided with large [cisterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cistern "Cistern").

The first enclosure is separated by the second one by the so-called _Muro de la Vela_ ("Wall of the Sail"), taking its name from a bell that warned the population in case of events such as the arrival of a ship in the port, danger, fires etc. This wall was built by King [Charles III of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain").

In the second enclosure was the residence for the governors, their soldiers and their servants. It included also the mosque, baths, tanks, tents etc.

The third enclosure, the most external, is also the most modern in the complex. After the Christian reconquest of Almería, the [Catholic monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_monarchs "Catholic monarchs")[Isabella I of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") and [Ferdinand II of Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") had a castle built in the most elevated sector of the town, more apt to resist the new gunpowder [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery").

## Cinema

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Cinema")]

The Alcazaba has been used to film _[Conan the Barbarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan\_the\_Barbarian\_(1982\_film) "Conan the Barbarian (1982 film)")_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-3)_[Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana\_Jones\_and\_the\_Last\_Crusade "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade")_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-4)_[Never Say Never Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never\_Say\_Never\_Again "Never Say Never Again")_,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-5) and most recently _[Wonder Woman 1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonder\_Woman\_1984 "Wonder Woman 1984")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-8) The syndicated TV series _[Queen of Swords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen\_of\_Swords\_(TV\_series) "Queen of Swords (TV series)")_ used the inner courtyard and gardens.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-9)

The [sixth season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_Thrones_(season_6) "Game of Thrones (season 6)") of the TV series _[Game of Thrones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_of\_Thrones "Game of Thrones")_ was shot in locations from Andalusia to Catalonia, including the Muralla de Jayrán,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-10) and the Alcazaba fortress, which is the capital of [Dorne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorne "Dorne"), the kingdom of the [House Martell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Martell "House Martell").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-11)

The **Alcazaba of Almería** is a fortified complex in [Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa "Almería"), southern [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"). The word _[alcazaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba "Alcazaba")_, from the Arabic word (القَصَبَة; _[\_al-qaṣabah\_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasbah "Kasbah")_), signifies a walled fortification in a city.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 955, Almería was given the title of _medina_ ("city") by the [Caliph of Cordoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliph_of_Cordoba "Caliph of Cordoba")[Abd ar-Rahman III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_ar-Rahman_III "Abd ar-Rahman III"), when the construction of the defensive citadel located in the upper sector of the city began.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-ciudadela-1) Provided not only with walls and towers but also with squares, houses, and a mosque, it was to be the seat of the local government, commanding the city and the nearby sea.

The complex was enlarged under caliph [Al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mansur_Ibn_Abi_Aamir "Al-Mansur Ibn Abi Aamir") and again under [Khayran as-Saqlabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khayran_as-Saqlabi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Khayran as-Saqlabi (page does not exist)")[[ar](https://ar.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AE%D9%8A%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B5%D9%82%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%8A "ar:خيران الصقلبي")], the first king of the independent [taifa of Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Almer%C3%ADa "Taifa of Almería").

Its purpose was to protect the area's largest city at the time, [Pechina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechina "Pechina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-ciudadela-1)

Most of the objects from the [archaeological site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological_site "Archaeological site") at the Alcazaba are kept in the [Museo de Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_de_Almer%C3%ADa "Museo de Almería"), but some are in the Museo de la Alhambra.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-2)

The renowned Muslim scholar [Abul Walid Al-Baji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_al-Walid_al-Baji "Abu al-Walid al-Baji") was reported to be buried within the grounds of the citadel according to the biographical work of [Ibn Bashkawal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Bashkuwal "Ibn Bashkuwal") writing around 50-60 years later.

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alcazaba_of_Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Description")]

[![Image 9: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**.
