**São Jorge Castle** ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Castelo de São Jorge_; Portuguese pronunciation:[[kɐʃˈtɛlu dɨ sɐ̃w̃ˈʒɔɾʒɨ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese")), sometimes known in English as **Saint George's Castle**, is a historic [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle") in the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") capital of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), located in the _[freguesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freguesia "Freguesia")_ of [Santa Maria Maior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria_Maior_(Lisbon) "Santa Maria Maior (Lisbon)"). Human occupation of the castle hill dates to at least the 8th century BC[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-2) while the oldest fortifications on the site date from the 2nd century BC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-3) The hill on which Saint George's Castle stands has played an important part in the [history of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lisbon "History of Lisbon"), having served as the location of fortifications occupied successively by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia"), [Carthaginians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"), and [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors"), before its conquest by the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people") in the [1147 Siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon"). Since the 12th century, the castle has variously served as a [royal palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_palace "Royal palace"), a [military barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barracks "Barracks"), home of the [Torre do Tombo National Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_do_Tombo_National_Archive "Torre do Tombo National Archive"), and now as a [national monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_monuments_of_Portugal "List of national monuments of Portugal") and museum.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg/250px-Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castle-DuarteGalvao3.jpg)

A 16th-century illuminated manuscript of Lisbon, in the _Crónica de D. Afonso Henriques_ by [Duarte Galvão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duarte_Galv%C3%A3o "Duarte Galvão"), depicting the castle and walls, including the Royal Palace (_Alcáçova_) (1505)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg/250px-Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbona._Olisipo_..._vulgo_Lisbona_Florentissimum_Portugalliae_Emporiu.jpg)

Caravels and carracks in the Tagus River, with the castle in the centre distance, unknown artist (1572)

Although the first fortifications on this hilltop date from the 1st century BC, [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") excavations have identified a human presence in the Tagus valley as far back as the 8th century BC. The first fortification was, presumably, erected in 48 BC, when Lisbon was classified as a Roman municipality.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-Bellard2003-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-Arruda2002-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-Laidlar1997-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7)

The hill was first used by [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celt "Celt") tribes, then by [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia"), followed by [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") and later the [Carthaginians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage") as a defensive outpost that was later expropriated successively by the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), the [Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi"), the [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoths "Visigoths"), and the [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors"). During the 10th century, the fortifications were built by [Berber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers "Berbers") forces; these included the walls or _Cerca Moura_ ("Moorish Encirclement").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7)

### Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Kingdom")]

In the context of the [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians")_[Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_, the castle and the city of Lisbon was conquered from the Moorish [Almoravid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravid_dynasty "Almoravid dynasty") in 1147 by [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques") and northern European knights in the [Siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon") during the [Second Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Crusade "Second Crusade"); this victory was the only notable success of that failed crusade.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) According to an oft-repeated [legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legend "Legend"), the [knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight "Knight")[Martim Moniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martim_Moniz "Martim Moniz"), noticing that one of the doors to the castle was open, prevented the Moors from closing it by throwing his own body into the breach, thus allowing Christian soldiers to enter at the cost of his own life. With the taking of the castle Christian forces were able to maintain the defense of Lisbon until the end of the 12th century.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-8)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG/250px-Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castelo_Sao_Jorge_Lisboa_1.JPG)

The castle walls and towers, constructed during the Moorish occupation of Lisbon

When Lisbon became the capital of the [Kingdom of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") in 1255, the castle served as the _alcáçova_, a fortified residence for [Afonso III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_III_of_Portugal "Afonso III of Portugal"), in his role as governor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) It was extensively renovated around 1300 by [King Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_of_Portugal "Denis of Portugal"), transforming the Moorish alcáçova into the Royal Palace of the Alcáçova.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) Between 1373 and 1375, King [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_Portugal "Ferdinand I of Portugal") ordered the building of the _Cerca Nova_ or _Cerca Fernandina_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-silva1987-9):20–21 the walled compound that enclosed all but the north flank of the castle.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-silva1987-9)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-10) The master builders João Fernandes and Vasco Brás were responsible for its construction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) This wall, which partially replaced the old Moorish walls, was designed to encircle previously unprotected parts of the city. Completed in two years, it had 77 towers, 34 or 38 gates,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-Norwich2016-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-PortuguesesCidade1997-12) and a perimeter of 5,400 metres (17,700 ft).

The castle and the city resisted the forces of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") several times during the 14th century (notably in 1373 and in 1383–1384). It was during this period (the late 14th century) that the castle was dedicated to [Saint George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George "Saint George") by King [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal"), who had married the English princess [Philippa of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_of_Lancaster "Philippa of Lancaster").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) Saint George, the warrior-saint, was normally represented slaying a dragon, and was very popular in both countries.

From 1378 onwards many of the kingdom's records were housed in the _[Torre do Tombo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre\_do\_Tombo "Torre do Tombo")_ (literally, "Tower of the Archive"), also known as the _Torre Albarrã_, until the [earthquake of 1755](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake_of_1755 "Earthquake of 1755") (a tower that is known today as _Tower of [Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus")_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) The Portuguese Royal Archive, where the eminent Portuguese [chroniclers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle "Chronicle")[Fernão Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fern%C3%A3o_Lopes "Fernão Lopes"), [Gomes Eanes de Zurara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gomes_Eanes_de_Zurara "Gomes Eanes de Zurara") and [Damião de Góis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A3o_de_G%C3%B3is "Damião de Góis") once worked, is still referred to as the _Torre do Tombo_, due to its original location in one of the towers of the Lisbon Castle. On 9 December 1448, Gil Pires was named the castle master builder to replace Afonso Esteves, being paid 400 [réis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_real "Portuguese real") for his work.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) Between 1448 and 1451, the master builder was paid several stipends for his work on the palace. Similarly, the mason João de Alverca was paid a substantial sum for stonework. These public works continued from 1449 until 1452, with additional payments being made for labor and materials to convert the building from a fortified castle to a royal residence.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7)

In the beginning of the 15th century, a [royal menagerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menagerie "Menagerie") was established in the Royal Palace of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), located nearby the Castle of Saint George. Following the [conquest of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Ceuta "Conquest of Ceuta") in 1415, King [John I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal") brought back to Lisbon two [Barbary lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_lion "Barbary lion"), and they were installed in a large room inside his Palace in the Citadel of Lisbon. This area of the Palace came to be known as _Casa dos Leões_ (the "Lions' House"); today the area is occupied by a famed restaurant with the same name.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-Castelo-13) Later that century, German [humanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanist "Humanist")[Hieronymus Münzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymus_M%C3%BCnzer "Hieronymus Münzer") spent five days in Lisbon in [1494](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1494 "1494"), and learned about the lions, claiming to be the most beautiful wild beasts he had ever seen.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-Muenzer-14)

As the royal palace, the castle was the setting for the reception by King [Manuel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") of the navigator [Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama "Vasco da Gama") when he returned from discovering the maritime route to India in 1498. The castle also served as a theater in 1502 when pioneering playwright [Gil Vicente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Vicente "Gil Vicente") staged his _Monólogo do Vaqueiro_ to honor the birth of Manuel I's son and heir, the future [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III_of_Portugal "John III of Portugal").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7)

Around the early 16th century, following the construction of the [Ribeira Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeira_Palace "Ribeira Palace") beside the [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus") river, the Palace of Alcáçova began to lose its importance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) An [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1531_Lisbon_earthquake "1531 Lisbon earthquake") occurring in 1531 further damaged the old castle, contributing further to its decay and neglect.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) In 1569, King [Sebastian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastiao_I_of_Portugal "Sebastiao I of Portugal") ordered the rebuilding of the royal apartments in the castle, intending to use it as his official residence. As part of the rebuilding, in 1577 Filippo Terzi demolished one of the towers near the principal facade of the Church of Loreto.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) However, many of the works were never completed after the young king's apparent death during the [Battle of Alcácer Quibir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Alc%C3%A1cer_Quibir "Battle of Alcácer Quibir"). The following [Portuguese dynastic crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_for_the_throne_of_Portugal "Struggle for the throne of Portugal") opened the way for [sixty years of Spanish rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Union "Iberian Union") and the castle was converted into military barracks and a prison.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-SIPA-7) On 30 December 1642, Teodósio de Frias the Younger was appointed master builder to continue the works begun by his father, Luís de Frias, and his grandfather, Teodósio de Frias. This was part of a greater plan by the Spanish forces to recommission the fortification.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_%2829762148847%29.jpg/500px-Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_%2829762148847%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_(29762148847).jpg)

Lisbon seen from São Jorge Castle

However, after Portugal regained its independence following the [Portuguese Restoration War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Restoration_War "Portuguese Restoration War"), the works were taken over by the Portuguese government. On 6 November 1648, Nicolau de Langres was called upon to take over the design, execution and construction of a new fortification that would surround the Castle of Saint George and the city walls of Lisbon. In 1650 the military architect Mateus do Couto was named master builder of the project and reconstruction took on a new formality: although the military engineer João Gillot built new walls in 1652, construction again followed Couto's plans between 1657 and 1733. In 1673, the Soldiers' Hospital, dedicated to _São João de Deus_ (St John of God), was installed on the grounds beside the Rua do Recolhimento. At the end of the 17th century the _Recolhimento do Castelo_ ("Castle Shelter") was constructed along the southeast angle of the courtyard, and in 1733, new projects were initiated by master Custódio Vieira.

The [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake") severely damaged the castle and contributed to its continuing decay: apart from the walls of the old castle, the soldier's hospital and the _Recolhimento_ were left in ruins. The necessity of maintaining a supporting military force within the capital city required expansion of the site's role of garrison and presidio. From 1780 to 1807, the charitable institution [Casa Pia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_Pia "Casa Pia"), dedicated to the education of poor children, was established in the citadel, while soldiers continued to be garrisoned on site. Inspired by the events of the earthquake and the following tsunami, the first [geodetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesy "Geodesy") observatory in Portugal was constructed in 1788 at the top of one of the towers of the castle, later referred to as the _Torre do Observatório_ (Observatory Tower).

### Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Republic")]

By the 1930s, the Castle had all but disappeared as a distinguishable landmark from Lisbon's skyline, being almost entirely obscured behind and under later annexes and additions.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-15) As part of the commemorative celebrations marking the foundation of nationhood and restoration of independence ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Fundação da Nacionalidade e da Restauração da Independência_), the government of [António de Oliveira Salazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_de_Oliveira_Salazar "António de Oliveira Salazar") initiated extensive renovations at the site (as it did with similar castles, such as the ones in [Sintra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sintra "Sintra") and [Silves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silves,_Portugal "Silves, Portugal")). Most of the incongruous structures added to the castle compound in previous centuries were demolished, under the supervision of the DGEMN, and there was a partial restoration of the _Recolhimento_. In addition, on 25 October 1947, a monument dedicated to [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques"), presented by the city of Porto, of a replica created by Soares dos Reis (in 1887) was installed on the grounds.

On 31 May 1942 the castle's operations began to be handled by the city government of Lisbon, which was reaffirmed on 8 June 1979.

In 1998, the semi-rectangular spaces, columns and cistern were adapted into the museum _Olissipónia_.

On 22 August 2006, Direcção Regional de Cultura Lisboa (DRCLisboa) defined a special protection zone, that included the Castle of São Jorge and the rest of the walls of Lisbon, the _Baixa Pombalina_ and various properties that were already classified as cultural heritage. The _Conselho Nacional de Cultura_ (National Council of Culture) proposed shelving this definition on 10 October 2011, which was supported by [IGESPAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGESPAR "IGESPAR").

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/CastleSaintGeorge.jpg/960px-CastleSaintGeorge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CastleSaintGeorge.jpg)

A panorama of the entire Castle of São Jorge

The castle is in the centre of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), on a hill, while many of its walls extend around the citadel into the civil parishes that surround it to the east and south.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg/250px-S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle_map_for_tourists.jpg)

The map helps tourist find areas of interest in the castle

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg/250px-Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge_BW_2018-10-03_11-13-09.jpg)

Bridge over the current dry moat

The castle's plan is roughly square, and it was originally encircled by a wall, to form a [citadel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citadel "Citadel"). The castle complex consists of the castle itself (the _castelejo_), some ancillary buildings (including the ruins of the royal palace), gardens, and a large terraced square from which an impressive panorama of Lisbon is visible. The main entrance to the citadel is a 19th-century gate surmounted by the [coat-of-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat-of-arms "Coat-of-arms") of Portugal, the name of [Queen Maria II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_II_of_Portugal "Maria II of Portugal"), and the date 1846. This gate permits access to the main square (_Praça d'Armas_), which is decorated with old cannons and a bronze statue of [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques"), the Portuguese monarch who took the castle from the Moors. This statue is a copy of the 19th-century original, by the [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") sculptor [António Soares dos Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Soares_dos_Reis "António Soares dos Reis"), which is located near [Guimarães Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guimar%C3%A3es_Castle "Guimarães Castle") in northern Portugal.

The remnants of the royal palace are located near the main square, but all that is left are some walls and a few rebuilt rooms such as the _Casa Ogival_. It now hosts the _Olissipónia_, a multimedia show about the history of Lisbon.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg/250px-Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_BW_2018-10-03_11-16-40.jpg)

View from the interior of the castle

The medieval castle is located toward the northwest corner of the citadel, at its highest point. Hypothetically, during a [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege"), if attackers managed to enter the citadel, the castle was the last stronghold, the last place in which to take refuge. It is rectangular, with ten towers. A wall with a tower and a connecting door divides the castle courtyard into halves. A series of stairways allow visitors to reach the walkway atop the wall and the towers, from which magnificent views of Lisbon can be enjoyed. The Tower of Ulysses (where the [_Torre do Tombo_ archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_do_Tombo "Torre do Tombo") used to be) had a [camera obscura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camera_obscura "Camera obscura") installed in 1998[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-16) that allows spectators a 360-degree view of the city and [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River").

Apart from its main walls, the castle is protected, on its southern and eastern sides, by a [barbican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbican "Barbican") (_barbacã_), a low wall that prevented [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engines "Siege engines") from approaching the main castle walls. The northern and western sides of the castle, on the other hand, were naturally protected by the steep hillside sloping downward from the castle's foundations. The castle is also partially encircled by a [moat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moat "Moat"), now dry. The main entrance is fronted by a stone bridge across the moat. On the west side, there is a long curtain wall extending downhill, ending at a tower (the _Torre de São Lourenço_).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle#cite_note-silva1987-9):33–35 This tower guarded a gate in the _Cerca Fernandina_.

**Almería** ([UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English "British English"): [/ˌ æ l m ə ˈ r iː ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-4)[US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English") also [/ˌ ɑː l-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-6)Spanish:[[almeˈɾi.a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/c/c6/Pronunciation_of_Almer%C3%ADa_in_Spanish.ogg/Pronunciation_of_Almer%C3%ADa_in_Spanish.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pronunciation_of_Almer%C3%ADa_in_Spanish.ogg "File:Pronunciation of Almería in Spanish.ogg")) is a city and [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_in_Spain "Municipalities in Spain") of [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), located in [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia"). It is the capital of the [province of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Almer%C3%ADa "Province of Almería"). The city lies in southeastern [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"), extending primarily in between the eastern fringes of the [Sierra de Gádor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_de_G%C3%A1dor "Sierra de Gádor") and the [Andarax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andarax "Andarax") riverbed along the coastline of the [Gulf of Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Almer%C3%ADa "Gulf of Almería"), a large inlet of the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"). The municipality has a population of 201,946.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-population-3)

Caliph [Abd al-Rahman III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahman_III "Abd al-Rahman III") founded the city in 955.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-7) The city grew wealthy during the Islamic era, becoming a [world city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_city "World city") throughout the 11th and 12th centuries.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMazzoli-Guintard2016249-8) It enjoyed an active port that traded [silk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADan_silk "Almerían silk"), oil, and raisins.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-9) This period was brought to an end with the [1147 conquest of the city by a Christian coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Almer%C3%ADa_(1147) "Siege of Almería (1147)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-10) Control over Almería switched hands over the rest of the middle ages. In the early modern period, with the onset of Barbary piracy, the ethnic cleansing of _[moriscos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moriscos "Moriscos")_ in the [Kingdom of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Granada_(Crown_of_Castile) "Kingdom of Granada (Crown of Castile)"), and several natural calamities, urban decay accrued. The 19th-century reactivation of mining activity ([lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead")) in the hinterland fostered commercial activity and demographic growth.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-11)

Key road routes include the [A-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autov%C3%ADa_A-7 "Autovía A-7") connecting Almería to the rest of the Spanish Mediterranean coast and the [A-92](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autov%C3%ADa_A-92 "Autovía A-92") connecting the city to [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada "Granada") and inner Andalusia. Almería is served by [a medium-sized airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa_Airport "Almería Airport") and [a port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Almeria "Port of Almeria") with a growing specialization in passenger and [ro-ro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roll-on/roll-off "Roll-on/roll-off") transport with the North of Africa (Algeria and Morocco).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-12)

Being adjacent to a small desert,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-13) Almería has an exceptionally dry climate by European standards.

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The name "Almería" comes from the city's former Arabic name, مدينة المرية: _Madīnat al-Mariyya_, meaning "city of the watchtower".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-:0522-14) As the settlement was originally the port or coastal suburb of [Pechina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechina "Pechina"), it was initially known as مريّة البجّانة : _Mariyyat al-Bajjāna_ (_Bajjāna_ being the Arabic name for Pechina).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-:052-15)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

See also: [Timeline of Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Almer%C3%ADa "Timeline of Almería")

The origin of Almería is connected to the 9th-century establishment of the so-called Republic of Pechina (Bajjana) some kilometres to the north, which was for a time autonomous from the [Cordobese central authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Emirate of Córdoba"): the settlement of current-day Almería initially developed as a humble trading port of Pechina known as Al-Mariyya Bajjana.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTES%C3%A1nchez_Sedano1985163-16) Pechina and its maritime port experienced divergent fortunes, and while the former progressively depopulated, the latter became the base of the [Caliphal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") navy after 933, during the rule of [Abd-ar-Rahman III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd-ar-Rahman_III "Abd-ar-Rahman III").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTES%C3%A1nchez_Sedano1985163%E2%80%93164-17) The port suffered a devastating [Fatimid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatimid "Fatimid") naval attack in 955 that exposed the Caliphate's defensive shortcomings.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-18) Also in 955, Abd-ar-Rahman III decided to erect the [walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_walls "City walls").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAziz_Salem1979%E2%80%9319808-19) A [silk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk "Silk") industry consisting of hundreds of looms and feeding itself from the [mulberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulberry "Mulberry") trees planted in the region, fostered Almería's economy.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTES%C3%A1nchez_Sedano1985164-20) Almería also became an important [slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery "History of slavery") hub during the caliphal period.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMazzoli-Guintard2016246-21)

In the wake of the [collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitna_of_al-Andalus "Fitna of al-Andalus") in the early 11th century, Almería detached from Cordobese authority towards 1014 and became ruled as an independent [taifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa "Taifa") under [Slavic kinglets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saqaliba "Saqaliba").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera_Molins201429,_32-22) It submitted to the [Taifa of Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Valencia "Taifa of Valencia") in 1038, yet it soon became independent as a new taifa,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera_Molins201432-23) ruled by the Arab [Banu Sumadih](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Sumadih "Banu Sumadih") until 1091, when it fell to Almoravid control. This allowed the city's economy to insert itself into the trade networks of the [Almoravid empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravid_empire "Almoravid empire").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMazzoli-Guintard2016245-24) Building upon the previous development during the caliphal period, Almería reached a degree of historical relevance unmatched in the rest of its history throughout the 11th and 12th centuries,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMazzoli-Guintard2016244-25) becoming the third-largest city of [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMazzoli-Guintard2016245-24) It was the largest industrial centre in all Andalus, boasting over 800 workshops for the manufacture of [Tiraz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiraz "Tiraz") textiles.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-26) Importing [indigo dye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo_dye "Indigo dye") and [wool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wool "Wool") from the Maghreb and [linen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linen "Linen") from Egypt, while it exported [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") to [Fez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fez,_Morocco "Fez, Morocco") and [Tlemcen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tlemcen "Tlemcen") as well as its highly sought textiles.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMazzoli-Guintard2016246-21) It was also frequented by merchants from as far as [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant "Levant") and had a strong silk and metal trade with [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria "Alexandria").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-27)

See also: [Siege of Almería (1147)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Almer%C3%ADa_(1147) "Siege of Almería (1147)")

Contested by the emirs of Granada and Valencia, Almería experienced many sieges, including one especially fierce siege when Christians, called to the [Second Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Crusade "Second Crusade") by [Pope Eugene III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Eugene_III "Pope Eugene III"), were also encouraged to counter the Muslim forces on a more familiar coast. On that occasion [Alfonso VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_VII_of_Le%C3%B3n_and_Castile "Alfonso VII of León and Castile"), starting on 11 July 1147, at the head of mixed armies of Catalans, Genoese, Pisans and Franks, led a crusade against the rich city, and Almería was captured on 17 October 1147,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers201036-28) marking the breakup of the city's period of splendor in the Middle Ages.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVillanueva_Mu%C3%B1oz1981269-29)

Within a decade, in 1157, Almería had passed to the control of Muslim [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_dynasty "Almohad dynasty") rulers.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers201036-28) Almería soon passed by the temporary overarching control of rebel Murcian emir [Ibn Mardanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ab%C5%AB_%CA%BFAbd_All%C4%81h_Mu%E1%B8%A5ammad_ibn_Sa%CA%BFd_ibn_Mardan%C4%ABsh "Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Saʿd ibn Mardanīsh") (1165–1169), hindering the early efforts of recovery in the city,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-30) that under the decade of Christian occupation reportedly had been left depopulated and, by and large, quite destroyed.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarc%C3%ADa_L%C3%B3pezCara_BarrionuevoOrtiz_Soler199091-31) During Almohad rule, the city did not return to its previous splendor, although the port remained trading with the [Crown of Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Aragon "Crown of Aragon") and the Italian republics.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolina_L%C3%B3pez199020-32)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Almeriastamp750.svg/250px-Almeriastamp750.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Almeriastamp750.svg)

A [block printed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarsh "Tarsh") commercial stamp stating: "Stamp of the Almería Qaysarīya (warehouse), Year 750 (1349-1350 CE)" - It seems to have been used to indicate property ownership or potentially as proof that required taxes had been assessed on goods entering the city.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-33)

Following the rebellion against Almohad rule heralded by the likes of the Banu Hud and the Banu Mardanis, Almería submitted to the authority of [Ibn Hud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Hud "Ibn Hud"), who had raised the [black banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Standard "Black Standard") and pledged nominal allegiance to [Abbasid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") authorities by 1228.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMelo20196-34) After Ibn Hud's assassination in Almería in 1238,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMelo20197-35)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolina_L%C3%B3pez199020-32) the bulk of the remaining Muslim-controlled territories in the Iberian Peninsula passed to the control of rival ruler [Ibn al-Aḥmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_I_of_Granada "Muhammad I of Granada") (sultan since 1232), who had set the capital of his emirate in Granada by 1238,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMelo20197-35) constituting the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"), to which Almería belonged from then on. While relatively languishing throughout the Nasrid period, Almería still remained a key strategic port of the emirate together with [Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), as well as a haven for pirates and political dissidents.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolina_L%C3%B3pez199021-36) It sustained intense trading relations with Aragon and the African port of [Honaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honaine "Honaine").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolina_L%C3%B3pez199021-36) Almería endured [a brutal siege by Aragonese forces in 1309](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Almer%C3%ADa_(1309) "Siege of Almería (1309)") that, while eventually unsuccessful, left the city battered.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolina_L%C3%B3pez199021-36)

The city submitted to the sovereignty of the [Catholic Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs "Catholic Monarchs") on 22 December 1489.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-37) Relatively isolated and within the range of attacks from [Barbary pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_pirates "Barbary pirates"), the hitherto mercantile city entered modernity by undergoing a process of heavy ruralization that imperiled its very same continued existence as a city.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-38)

Historically, there was a [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") community in Almería dating to the 10th century, where members of the community mostly engaged in maritime trade. When the [Jews were expelled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_the_Jews_from_Spain "Expulsion of the Jews from Spain") in 1492, many living in Almería fled to North Africa.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-39)

The 16th century was for Almería a century of natural and human catastrophes; for there were at least four [earthquakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquakes "Earthquakes"), of which the one in 1522 was especially violent, devastating the city. The people who had remained [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") were expelled from Almería after the [War of Las Alpujarras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpujarras "Alpujarras") in 1568 and scattered across the Crown of Castile. Landings and attacks by [Barbary pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_pirates "Barbary pirates") were also frequent in the 16th century, and continued until the early 18th century. At that time, huge iron mines were discovered and French and British companies set up business in the area, bringing renewed prosperity and returning Almería to a position of relative importance within Spain.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

View of Almería during the [Second Spanish Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Spanish_Republic "Second Spanish Republic") (1931–39)

During the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War") the city was [shelled by the German Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardment_of_Almer%C3%ADa "Bombardment of Almería"), with news reaching the London and Parisian press about the "criminal bombardment of Almería by German planes".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-40) Almería surrendered in 1939, being the last Andalusian main city to fall to [Francoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Franco_Bahamonde "Francisco Franco Bahamonde") forces.

In the second half of the 20th century, Almería witnessed spectacular economic growth due to tourism and intensive agriculture, with crops grown year-round in massive _invernaderos_– plastic-covered "greenhouses" – for intensive vegetable production.

After Franco's death and popular approval of the new Spanish Constitution, the people of southern Spain were called on to approve an autonomous status for Andalusia region in a referendum. The referendum were approved with 118,186 votes for and 11,092 votes against in Almería province,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-41) which represented 42% of all registered voters.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-42)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/%28Almer%C3%ADa%29_Greenhouses_of_Almer%C3%ADa%2C_Spain_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-%28Almer%C3%ADa%29_Greenhouses_of_Almer%C3%ADa%2C_Spain_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:(Almer%C3%ADa)_Greenhouses_of_Almer%C3%ADa,_Spain_(cropped).jpg)

Satellite view centered on Almería

Due to its arid landscape, numerous [Spaghetti Westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaghetti_Western "Spaghetti Western") were filmed in Almería and some of the sets still remain as a tourist attraction.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-44) These sets are located in the [desert of Tabernas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabernas_Desert "Tabernas Desert"). The town and region were also used by [David Lean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lean "David Lean") in _[Lawrence of Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence\_of\_Arabia\_(film) "Lawrence of Arabia (film)")_ (1962), [John Milius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Milius "John Milius") in _[The Wind and the Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wind\_and\_the\_Lion "The Wind and the Lion")_ (1975), _[The Gospel of John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gospel\_of\_John\_(film) "The Gospel of John (film)")_ (2003) and others.

One of Almería's most famous natural spots is the [Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_de_Gata-N%C3%ADjar_Natural_Park "Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park"). This park is of volcanic origin,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-45) and is the largest and most ecologically significant marine-terrestrial space in the European Western [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park runs through the municipal areas of [Níjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADjar "Níjar"), [Almerimar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almerimar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Almerimar (page does not exist)") and [Carboneras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboneras "Carboneras"). Its villages, previously dedicated to [fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing "Fishing"), have become [tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism "Tourism") spots. The beaches of Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park are also an attraction.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-46)

Almería has one islet that it administers as a part of its territory in the Alboran Sea, [Alboran Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alboran_Island "Alboran Island"). The island has a small cemetery, a harbor, and a lighthouse, built in the 19th century.

See also: [Sierra de Gádor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_de_G%C3%A1dor "Sierra de Gádor")

### Crystal cave

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Crystal cave")]

In 2000, a team of geologists found a cave filled with giant [gypsum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gypsum "Gypsum") crystals in an abandoned silver mine near Almería. The cavity, which measures 8 by 1.8 by 1.7 metres (26.2 ft ×5.9 ft ×5.6 ft), may be the largest [geode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geode "Geode") ever found.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-47) The entrance of the cave was blocked by five tons of rocks, and was under police protection (to prevent looters from entering). According to geological models, the cave was formed during the [Messinian salinity crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinian_salinity_crisis "Messinian salinity crisis") 6 million years ago, when the Mediterranean sea evaporated and left thick layers of salt sediments ([evaporites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaporite "Evaporite")).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The site is currently open for tourists under guided tours.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Climate")]

According to the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), Almería has a [hot desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_desert_climate "Hot desert climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_BWh_; [Trewartha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trewartha_climate_classification "Trewartha climate classification"): _BWal_).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-:0-48) Almería is the driest city in Europe and it is the only one with a hot desert climate, starting in the south-eastern outskirts of the city (still inside the municipality of Almería) until the [Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_de_Gata-N%C3%ADjar_Natural_Park "Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park") located east of the city.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-50)

The BWh climate is present in the city of Almería, in nearby areas of Almería province (such as the [Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_de_Gata-N%C3%ADjar_Natural_Park "Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park"), the [Andarax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andarax "Andarax")/[Almanzora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almanzora_(river) "Almanzora (river)") river valleys), the only region in Europe to have this climate.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-51) This arid climatic region spreads along the coastline around Almería to [Torrevieja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrevieja "Torrevieja"), in the northeast.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-:0-48) The nearby Faro del Cabo in the [Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_de_Gata-N%C3%ADjar_Natural_Park "Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park"), has the lowest annual precipitation on the European continent (156 millimetres (6.1 in)) in the period 1961-1990 and around 140 millimetres (5.5 in) since 2010.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-54) With over 3,000 hours of sunshine across 320 days per year on average, Almería is considered one of the sunniest cities in Europe.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-55)

Almería is the only city in [Continental Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Europe "Continental Europe") that has never registered any temperature below freezing in its recorded weather history.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-57) The coldest temperature recorded was 0.1°C (32.2°F) at the airport in January 2005.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-58) Before that, the previous record was 0.2°C (32.4°F) on 9 February 1935.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-59) Settled snow is unknown since 1935, although during the 20th century, light flurries (without settling) occurred on few occasions.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-62) The most important settled snowfall event occurred in 1926 and the snow arrived even at the coastline of the city.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-63) The last event with settled snowfall happened on 9 February 1935.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-64)

During the winter, daily maximum temperatures tend to stay around 17–18°C (63–64°F). At night, the minimum temperature is usually around 8–10°C (46–50°F). This makes the city of Almería one of the warmest in winter in [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-65) The city only receives yearly precipitation of just 200 mm (7.9 in) and 26 days of precipitation annually; so while no month could be described as truly wet, there are strong seasonal differences in terms of precipitation and temperature, with coastal parts of the city (such as the [Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_de_Gata-N%C3%ADjar_Natural_Park "Cabo de Gata-Níjar Natural Park")) receiving a precipitation amount of 156 mm (6.1 in), and an annual temperature of 19.1°C (66.4°F), while mountainous areas (such as the [Tabernas Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabernas_Desert "Tabernas Desert")) receive a precipitation amount of 220 mm (8.7 in) per year, and an average temperature of 17.9°C (64.2°F), so it would be classified as a [cold desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_desert_climate "Cold desert climate") (_BWk_) bordering a [cold semi-arid climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_semi-arid_climate "Cold semi-arid climate") (_BSk_).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-:0-48)

Inland areas of the Almería province are believed to have reached temperatures above 45°C (113°F) in summer.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-66) Though temperatures above 40°C (104°F) are very rare in the city of Almería.

During the summer, the skies are usually sunny and almost no rainfall occurs. The typical daily temperatures are around 30°C (86°F) during the day while the minimum temperatures stay around 22°C (72°F) during July and August. As is the case for most of coastal Iberia, heatwaves in Almería are much less common than in the interior because of its coastal location; The hottest temperature recorded was 42.0°C (107.6°F) in August 2022.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-67) The highest minimum temperature ever recorded was 33.2°C (91.8°F) on 31 July 2001, which is also the highest ever recorded in [peninsular Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_Spain "Peninsular Spain") and [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-69)

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Almeria_Puerta_de_Purchena_%28fcm%29.jpg/250px-Almeria_Puerta_de_Purchena_%28fcm%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Almeria_Puerta_de_Purchena_(fcm).jpg)

House of the Butterflies

Famous natives of Almería include [Nicolás Salmerón y Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Salmer%C3%B3n_y_Alonso "Nicolás Salmerón y Alonso"), who in 1873 was the third president of the [First Spanish Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Spanish_Republic "First Spanish Republic"), as well as several musicians, including the composer José Padilla Sánchez, whose music was declared of "universal interest" by Unesco in 1989, the popular folk singer [Manolo Escobar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manolo_Escobar "Manolo Escobar"), renowned Flamenco guitar player [José Tomás "Tomatito"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomatito "Tomatito") and Grammy Award winner [David Bisbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bisbal "David Bisbal"); the champion motorcyclist [Antonio Maeso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Maeso "Antonio Maeso") moved to Almería as a child.

The Irish folk-rock group [The Pogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pogues "The Pogues") paid tribute to Almería in "Fiesta", a song on the band's third album, _If I Should Fall from Grace with God_.

In 1989, English electronic band [Depeche Mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depeche_Mode "Depeche Mode") filmed the video for their song "[Personal Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_Jesus "Personal Jesus")" in Almería.

Tourism increased and hotels were all occupied from January to February during the filming of the [sixth season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_Thrones_(season_6) "Game of Thrones (season 6)") of the TV series _[Game of Thrones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_of\_Thrones "Game of Thrones")_.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-79)

### Festivities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Festivities")]

## Notable locations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Notable locations")]

*   The Alcazaba, a medieval fortress that was begun in the 10th century but destroyed by an earthquake in 1522. It includes a triple line of walls, a majestic [keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep") and large gardens. It commands a city quarter with buildings dressed in pastel colors, of Muslim-age aspect. It is the second largest among the Muslim fortresses of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia"), after the [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   [Almería air raid shelters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa_air_raid_shelters "Almería air raid shelters"), underground galleries for civilian protection during the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War"), currently the longest in Europe open for tourists.
*   [The Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa_Cathedral "Almería Cathedral") has a fortress-like appearance due to its towers, merlons and protected paths, created to defend it from Mediterranean pirates. Originally designated as a mosque, it was later converted into a Christian church, before being destroyed in the 1522 earthquake. In the 16th century it was rebuilt in the Renaissance style, whilst keeping some of its defensive features.
*   Renaissance church of Santiago, built in 1533, with tower and portal decorated with reliefs.
*   _Chanca_, a group of houses carved into rocks.
*   Castle of _San Cristobal_, now in ruins. It is connected to the Alcazaba by a line of walls.
*   Museum of Almería. Includes findings from Prehistoric, Iberic, Roman, Greek ages and Muslim objects, mostly from the Alcazaba.
*   _Paseo de Coches_, a modern seaside promenade with gardens and palms.
*   _Cable Inglés_ (English Pier), 1904 iron railway pier built to transfer iron ore, copper, and silver produced by British- and French-run mines in Granada from trains to waiting cargo ships.

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Greenhouses_near_El_Ejido.jpg/250px-Greenhouses_near_El_Ejido.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greenhouses_near_El_Ejido.jpg)

Greenhouses near Almería

Intensive agriculture has been the most important economic sector of Almería for the last 50 years.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-81) Nowadays, greenhouse production, handling and commercialisation of vegetables, and the supply industry of the sector, represent almost 40% of Almería's GDP. Directly, agricultural production accounts for 18.2% of the provincial GDP. In Andalusia, the average contribution is 6.6% and in Spain it is only 2.9%.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-82)

This situation is the result of an innovative dynamic model, which can continually incorporate new technologies: using soil sanding, plastic covers, drip irrigation systems, hybrid seeds, soil-less cultivation, irrigation programs, new greenhouse structures, and so on. They all allowed to improve production and increase commercialisation calendars, assuring the profitability and quality of the crops and the competitiveness of the markets.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-83) Moreover, Almería's economy has an important exporting function:[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-84) 75% of production was sold abroad in 2018, with a value of 2,400 million euros.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-85)

This development is explained by familiar investment, as subsidies have been limited or non-existent. In this sense, the horticultural sector receives the least European aid from the Common Agricultural Policy: 1.9% of total income. This figure is much lower than that received by other sectors such as olive groves (33%) or cereals (53%).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-86)

The production of this area is based on fair competition with officially a just remuneration of employees, with similar salaries than the ones in the same sector in Europe: 8% higher than Italy and 11% than Belgium.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-87) This avoids the social dumping exerted by non-EU countries, like Morocco, with salaries up to 90% lower than those of Almería. However, there is well-documented widespread exploitation of workers from North Africa who work and live in terrible conditions, earning much lower than the minimum wage.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-88)

From a social point of view, Almería and Granada are an example of family-owned and smallholder agriculture, with small farms and little concentration of land.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-ifapa-89) This social nature generates high equity in the level of income and welfare: social cohesion is produced, and inequality is reduced.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-90) Concretely, Almería is made up of 12,500 farms with an average of 2.5 hectares and 30% of familiar labour. The high education levels of the farmers are also significant, which demonstrates an innovative and receptive character towards continuing education: 81.2% of farmers have some type of formal academic training.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-ifapa-89)

At the same time, a commercial system based on social economy enterprises has been developed, e.g. as cooperative societies. These companies represent 62% of production and sales.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-91)They assure the access to the market in optimal conditions, because they increase its position inside the agri-food supply chain, facilitate financing, technical advice, and incorporation of technology. Moreover, local ties increase environmental sustainability.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa#cite_note-92)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almer%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Transport")]

See also: [Port of Almeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Almeria "Port of Almeria")

By land, Almería can be reached by the [A-7 Mediterranean Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autov%C3%ADa_A-7 "Autovía A-7"), which connects the Mediterranean area with the [Spanish A-92](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autov%C3%ADa_A-92 "Autovía A-92") that unites it with the rest of Andalusia. [Almería railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa_railway_station "Almería railway station") is served by [Renfe Operadora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renfe_Operadora "Renfe Operadora") with direct rail services to [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_railway_station "Granada railway station"), and [Madrid Atocha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid_Atocha_railway_station "Madrid Atocha railway station") using a branch off the [Alcázar de San Juan–Cádiz railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_de_San_Juan%E2%80%93C%C3%A1diz_railway "Alcázar de San Juan–Cádiz railway"); the [Linares Baeza–Almería railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linares_Baeza%E2%80%93Almer%C3%ADa_railway "Linares Baeza–Almería railway"). In the future, [high-speed rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-speed_rail "High-speed rail")[AVE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AVE "AVE") services will [link Almería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murcia%E2%80%93Almer%C3%ADa_high-speed_rail_line "Murcia–Almería high-speed rail line") to Madrid via [Murcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murcia "Murcia"). The central railway station has been closed for several months and it is not known exactly when it will re-open. Passengers currently start their journey by being bussed a few kilometres to Huercal de Almería station.

By sea, the port of Almería has connections to [Melilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melilla "Melilla"), [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria"), [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco"), and tourist cruises in the Mediterranean. It also has a marina with moorings for pleasure boats. Currently the port of Almería is being expanded with new docks and transformed into a container port to take large-scale international shipping and thereby increase its freight traffic. It normally connects with the following destinations:

*   [Acciona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acciona_Trasmediterr%C3%A1nea "Acciona Trasmediterránea"): Ghazaouet (Algeria), [Oran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oran "Oran") (Algeria), [Nador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nador_Port "Nador Port") ([Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco")) and [Melilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melilla "Melilla").
*   [Comarit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comarit "Comarit"): Nador.
*   [Comanav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnie_Marocaine_de_Navigation "Compagnie Marocaine de Navigation"): Nador.

By air, Almería is served by [Almería Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almer%C3%ADa_Airport "Almería Airport"), the fourth largest in Andalusia.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The winter timetable includes flights to [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid"), [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), [Melilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melilla "Melilla"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), and Seville, with international connections to [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"), [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin") and Swiss, German and other EU airports being added during the summer.
