### The other façades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: The other façades")]

The longest of all, the one running south along Via Acton, was built in different phases: its eastern half at the beginning of the 17th century according to Fontana's designs and the eastern half, including the central belvedere, from 1837 to 1844 by Gaetano Genovese. The north façade facing Piazza Trieste e Trento was also by the same architect, completed between 1841 and 1843 after the demolition of the Viceregal Palace. While the architects [Francesco Gavaudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Gavaudan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Francesco Gavaudan (page does not exist)") and [Pietro Gesuè](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Gesu%C3%A8?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pietro Gesuè (page does not exist)") were responsible for the connection to the [San Carlo Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Carlo_Theatre "San Carlo Theatre").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:9-59)

Both façades imitate the architectural articulation designed by Fontana for the main façade, and both are C-shaped and contain a garden in their centre, the south façade the so-called Hanging Gardens and the north the Italian Garden, in the centre of which is the statue of _Liberty_, made by [Francesco Liberti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Liberti?action=edit&redlink=1 "Francesco Liberti (page does not exist)") in 1861, a clear reference to the [Italian unification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_of_Italy "Unification of Italy").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio36-60) In addition, this north façade is partially porticoed to support a terrace. It has a glass entrance leading directly onto the grand staircase, decorated with two pairs of plaster statues from the [Palazzo degli Studi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Naples "National Archaeological Museum of Naples") and placed there during Genovese's restoration. These are copies of the _[Farnese Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farnese\_Hercules "Farnese Hercules")_ and the _Farnesian Flora_ on one side, and of the _Minerva_ and of _Pyrrhus and [Astyanax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astyanax "Astyanax")_ on the other.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio36-37-61)

### The courtyards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: The courtyards")]

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_01.JPG/250px-N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_01.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_01.JPG)

The courtyard of honour.

According to Domenico Fontana's original project, three [courtyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard") were to be opened in front of each entrance, which would be connected to each other by vaulted corridors. However, only the central entrance courtyard was ultimately built, the so-called [Courtyard of honour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_honor_(architecture) "Court of honor (architecture)")(_Cortile D'Onore_), which is square in shape, with five arches on each side.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-sasso250-62) The central arch on each side is a [segmental arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segmental_arch "Segmental arch") of larger dimensions than the others. Around the courtyard, on the first floor, there is a [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia"), originally open, but which was finally closed with large windows. In a niche in the eastern part of the courtyard there was originally a cistern, which was replaced during the 1940s by a fountain decorated with a statue of _Fortuna_. The fountain, made in 1742 by Giuseppe Canart, was commissioned by Charles of Bourbon and was originally located near the port. Following an investigation, brick paving in the shape of a [herringbone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herringbone_pattern "Herringbone pattern") has been discovered in some places.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio41-63)

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_03.JPG/250px-N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_03.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_03.JPG)

The fountain with the statue of _Fortuna_.

During the construction of the new southern arm of the palace between 1758 and 1760, two new courtyards were created: one on the same axis as the courtyard of honour, just behind it, which is called the Courtyard of the Carriages, while the other is the Courtyard of the Belvedere.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio42-64)

Despite having been built in different periods, the Courtyard of the Carriages (_Cortile delle Carrozze_), so called because it contained the coach houses, is architecturally close to the style that Domenico Fontana gave to the palace, although there are no lack of different elements such as the use of [stucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stucco "Stucco") instead of piperno and the angular [pilasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilaster "Pilaster").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio42-64) The courtyard is rectangular in shape, and has an elliptical marble cistern in the centre. It is connected to the courtyard of honour and the esplanade of the bastions by two service corridors with lowered arches. The coach house, built in 1832 by [Giacinto Passaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacinto_Passaro?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giacinto Passaro (page does not exist)"), replaced the one existing from the previous century, the work of [Ferdinando Sanfelice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinando_Sanfelice "Ferdinando Sanfelice"), mainly for aesthetic reasons, since the new one was aligned with the facade of the palace while the previous one was situated obliquely. The new coach house is a space dominated by a central line of nine columns of the [Doric order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doric_order "Doric order"), on which you can still admire red shields with the crown of [Umberto I of Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_I_of_Italy "Umberto I of Italy"). The window layout was modified by Genovese in 1837 to adapt it to the requirements of the Belvedere Courtyard.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio43-65)

The [Belvedere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belvedere_(structure) "Belvedere (structure)") (_Cortile del Belvedere_) was born as a boundary towards the sea of the first nucleus of the palace and was originally C-shaped. It was closed by a loggia, which would be modified as a consequence of the construction of the new bodies of the palace in the 18th century,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio43-65) with the insertion of lowered arches in the eastern part. Later, the courtyard underwent modifications between 1837 and 1840, when, for access to the courtyard, a triumphal arch with Ionic and Corinthian semi-columns of false piperno was created. Between the ground and first floors, the courtyard is decorated with a Doric band with [metopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metope "Metope"), also in false piperno, and [triglyphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triglyph "Triglyph").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio48-66) From the Belvedere Courtyard, you can access different areas of the palace: on the left is the Guest Staircase, which leads to the Vestibule (room XX) of the Royal Apartment and to the small bridge, destroyed in the bombings of the Second World War and rebuilt on the same supports, which links it directly to the hanging gardens.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio48-66) From the courtyard, you can also access a private apartment with Pompeian-style decorations, originally reserved for official meetings of [Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies"), which later became the seat of the superintendency; and also to a bridge that, overcoming the defensive ditch, led to the bastion of the [Castel Nuovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castel_Nuovo "Castel Nuovo") and to a slope that led to the [stables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stables "Stables").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio4849-67)

## The Royal Apartments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: The Royal Apartments")]

The Royal Apartments ([Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language"): _Appartamento Reale_) are the part currently open to visitors and is located on the _[piano nobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano\_nobile "Piano nobile")_ of the western core of the palace. Throughout its history it has undergone several changes of use and name: from 1616 to 1734 it was used as the apartments of the [Spanish and Austrian viceroys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_viceroys_of_Naples "List of viceroys of Naples") and their consorts; from 1734 to 1806 it was the public and private apartment of the [king and queen of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_of_Naples "List of monarchs of Naples"); from 1806 to 1815 it served as the "honorary" and "ordinary" apartment of [Joseph Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bonaparte "Joseph Bonaparte") and [Joachim Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Murat "Joachim Murat"); It was later called the "Grand Apartment of His Majesty the King" and [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies") and [Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies") were the last to inhabit it. After the 1837–1844 renovation by Gaetano Genovese, it was called the "Etiquette Apartment of the King and Queen" and was used only for receptions, as the sovereigns moved to the second floor of the eastern wing.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:4-30) In the travel guides of the beginning of the century it was simply called the "Gala Apartment", and could be visited from Thursday to Sunday from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. upon request for a permit.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:5-44)

When the palace ceased to be property of the Crown and passed to the State in 1919, the Royal Apartment became one of the _institutes of antiquities and art_ (now called _Italian national museums_). Its present museum appearance is due to the restoration carried out between 1950 and 1954 to alleviate the damage suffered during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), when several ceilings were damaged by Allied bombing and the silk hangings of twenty rooms were removed when the apartment was transformed into a _Welfare Club_ (social club) for the occupying English troops.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-68)

Originally, to access the king's rooms, silver and gold keys were used, guarded by the [gentlemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentlemen "Gentlemen") of the chamber, some of which are in the [Museo Civico Filangieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_Civico_Filangieri "Museo Civico Filangieri") donated by Neapolitan nobles.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7072-69)

### The collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: The collections")]

The current decoration represents the tastes of the different dynasties and historical figures who have lived there, as well as different political messages typical of a building that represented the pinnacle of power in the kingdom. The reference date is the inventory made by the Savoy family in 1874, which describes the rooms after the late Bourbon modifications (1837–1844) and some slight changes introduced after the Unification in 1860.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7273-70)

First of all, the frescoes stand out. These essentially cover the viceregal period with works by [Belisario Corenzio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belisario_Corenzio "Belisario Corenzio") of Roman Renaissance inspiration or [Giovanni Battista Caracciolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Caracciolo "Giovanni Battista Caracciolo") in a more [Caravagesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravaggisti "Caravaggisti") line; the Baroque period of Charles of Bourbon with large allegorical frescoes with [trompe l'oeil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trompe_l'oeil "Trompe l'oeil") by Solimena, Vaccaro or de Mura; and finally historicist and neo-medieval works from the mid-19th century.

The paintings in the rooms also correspond to different periods, highlighting the northern and European schools of the 16th and 17th centuries from the Farnesio collection inherited by Charles of Bourbon; Caravaggesque paintings and the Dutch portraits that Domenico Venuti bought for [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies") and the large court portraits of the royal family.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7374-71) There are also more intimate and contemporary paintings from the apartments in the east wing, such as _troubadour_ paintings commissioned by the Murats from artists such as [Louis Nicolas Philippe Auguste de Forbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Nicolas_Philippe_Auguste_de_Forbin "Louis Nicolas Philippe Auguste de Forbin") or the chronicle paintings of the great moments of the reigns of Francis I and Ferdinand II by [Salvatore Fergola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvatore_Fergola "Salvatore Fergola") and [Frans Vervloet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frans_Vervloet?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frans Vervloet (page does not exist)"). However, due to the sending of the most important paintings to the [Real Museo Borbonico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Naples "National Archaeological Museum of Naples") between 1829 and 1832 and the transfer of paintings to the [Capodimonte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Capodimonte "National Museum of Capodimonte") from 1862 onwards, the palace's collection of paintings today appears more scattered and impoverished than before, with its series and iconographies fragmented. In the 1874 inventory, the paintings were given special importance, together with the furniture, tapestries, flowered hangings and large neo-baroque mirrors, as creating a sumptuous atmosphere.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-72)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:7-73)

The furniture, in the [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque"), [Rococo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rococo "Rococo") and historicist style, was made by Neapolitan cabinetmakers between the 18th and 19th centuries or brought from [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_French_Empire "First French Empire") during Murat's stay in Naples, together with carpets and [tapestries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapestry "Tapestry"), some of them woven in the Royal Tapestry Factory of Naples. Also of note are the French clocks, the porcelain, especially [Sèvres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A8vres_porcelain "Sèvres porcelain"), Chinese and Russian; bronze and marble sculptures and works in hard stone. Many of the exhibits come from other parts of the palace, especially the eastern wing, which was completely stripped of furniture when the National Library was installed there.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7374-71)

In any case, the palace does not have a real collection, but rather loose pieces, since during the 19th century, on the initiative of the Bourbons and especially the Savoys, many works were transferred to other museums (see History).[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7273-70)

### Grand Staircase

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Grand Staircase")]

The north side of the courtyard, orthogonal to the façade, was originally occupied by a modest two-ramp staircase, the work of [Domenico Fontana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Fontana "Domenico Fontana"). However, after the [anti-Spanish revolt of 1647](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neapolitan_Republic_(1647) "Neapolitan Republic (1647)"), the viceroy [Iñigo Vélez de Guevara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8D%C3%B1igo_V%C3%A9lez_de_Guevara_el_Mozo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Íñigo Vélez de Guevara el Mozo (page does not exist)") commissioned a new and monumental staircase from Francesco Antonio Picchiatti. The new space was built between 1650 and 1670 in Piperno, and was inspired by the immense staircase of the Real [Alcázar of Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Toledo "Alcázar of Toledo"), built by [Alonso de Covarrubias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonso_de_Covarrubias "Alonso de Covarrubias") and [Juan de Herrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_de_Herrera "Juan de Herrera") between 1550 and 1605.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-74) The new staircase, which occupied an entire side of the courtyard of honour, was built in accordance with the importance that the Austrian ceremony gave to these spaces. [Montesquieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montesquieu "Montesquieu") described it in 1729 as the most beautiful in Europe,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida4-75) however it had to be rebuilt after the fire in February 1837.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:9-59)

The staircase today, note the absence of several torches. 

The new design in a grandiose late neoclassical style was the work of [Gaetano Genovese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaetano_Genovese "Gaetano Genovese"). In 1841 the problem of the staircase's luminosity was resolved with the demolition of the viceregal palace annex, the creation of the Piazza Trieste e Trento and the opening of large iron-framed windows. However, it was not until 1858 that Francesco Gavaudan completed the decoration[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:9-59) characterized by sumptuous marbles such as pink marble, the _porto venere_, the red of [Vitulano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitulano "Vitulano"), the _breccia rosata_ of [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily"), the marble of [Mondragone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mondragone "Mondragone") and the _lumachino_ of [Trapani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trapani "Trapani").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida4-75) For its part, the [cloister vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloister_vault "Cloister vault") that covers it is decorated with white stuccos on a gray background, representing garlands and the shields of the [Kingdom of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Naples "Kingdom of Naples"), of the [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Sicily "Kingdom of Sicily"), of [Basilicata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilicata "Basilicata"), of [Calabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabria "Calabria") and, although it was added later, of the [House of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy "House of Savoy").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida4-75) Finally, the side walls are decorated with sculptures of the [cardinal virtues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_virtues "Cardinal virtues"): on one side, the _Fortitude_ by [Antonio Calì](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Cal%C3%AC?action=edit&redlink=1 "Antonio Calì (page does not exist)") and the _Justice_ by [Gennaro Calì](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gennaro_Cal%C3%AC "Gennaro Calì"); on the other, the _Clemencia_ by [Tito Angelini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tito_Angelini "Tito Angelini") and the _Prudencia_ by Tommaso Scolari;[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida124-56) and, flanking the central section, two [bas-reliefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bas-relief "Bas-relief") in Carrara marble representing the _Victory between the Genius of Fame and Courage_, by [Salvatore Irdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvatore_Irdi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Salvatore Irdi (page does not exist)"), and the _Glory between the symbols of Justice, War, Science, Art and Industry_, by [Francesco Liberti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Liberti?action=edit&redlink=1 "Francesco Liberti (page does not exist)").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida4-75)

### Ambulatory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Ambulatory")]

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Ambulacro_%28Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli%29_001.jpg/250px-Ambulacro_%28Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli%29_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ambulacro_(Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli)_001.jpg)

A corridor of the ambulatory.

The ambulatory on the first floor is made up of four corridors surrounding the courtyard of honour: originally it was an open loggia which, during the restoration in the 19th century, was closed off by means of large windows. At this time the vaults were decorated with stuccoes by Gaetano Genovese.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida5-76) The rooms of the royal apartment open off the ambulatory: in the first arm, which runs parallel to the façade towards the [Piazza del Plebiscito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piazza_del_Plebiscito "Piazza del Plebiscito"), are the court theatre and the audience chambers; in the second are the private rooms of the former private apartment, which overlook the hanging garden; in the third, facing east, are the Hall of Hercules and the royal chapel; and finally, the fourth arm leads to the grand staircase, from which one can see through a stained glass window the [Piazza Trieste e Trento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piazza_Trieste_e_Trento?action=edit&redlink=1 "Piazza Trieste e Trento (page does not exist)"), with a view, in the distance, of the [Carthusian monastery of San Martino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthusian_monastery_of_San_Martino?action=edit&redlink=1 "Carthusian monastery of San Martino (page does not exist)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio25-18) This layout has been preserved unchanged, as it was designed by Domenico Fontana. The doors leading to the ambulatory are [lacquered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacquered "Lacquered") in white, are in a neoclassical style and were built in the 1930s.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-77)

### The King's Apartment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: The King's Apartment")]

[![Image 41](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Teatrino_di_Corte_%28Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli%29_001.jpg/250px-Teatrino_di_Corte_%28Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli%29_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Teatrino_di_Corte_(Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli)_001.jpg)

The Court Theatre.

The Court Theatre (Room I) was originally the "Sala Regia" or "Sala Maggiore" and was the largest room according to Fontana's project. From the beginning it was used for balls, comedies and festivities, and from 1648 Picchiatti decorated its ceiling with sumptuous gilded stucco and paintings by order of the viceroy [Count of Oñate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8D%C3%B1igo_V%C3%A9lez_de_Guevara_el_Mozo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Íñigo Vélez de Guevara el Mozo (page does not exist)"). This renovation ran parallel to the creation of another large ceremonial room in the palace, the "Sala de los Virreyes" (now the Hall of Hercules). During the reign of [Charles of Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") it was regularly used for theatrical performances and a large stage was set up on it.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-78) Its current appearance, however, dates back to 1768, when on the occasion of the wedding of [Ferdinand IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies") and [Maria Carolina of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Carolina_of_Austria "Maria Carolina of Austria") it was completely remade by [Ferdinando Fuga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinando_Fuga "Ferdinando Fuga") in a classi
