The **Royal Palace of Naples** ([Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language"): _Palazzo Reale di Napoli_) is a historic building located in [Piazza del Plebiscito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piazza_del_Plebiscito "Piazza del Plebiscito"), in the historic center of [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples "Naples"), Italy. Although the main entrance is located in this square, there are other accesses to the complex, which also includes the gardens and the [Teatro di San Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teatro_di_San_Carlo "Teatro di San Carlo"), from the Piazza Trieste e Trento, Piazza del Municipio and Via Acton.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Napoli_2019_-Royal_Palace_-_San_Francesco_di_Paola-_by-RaBoe_074.jpg/250px-Napoli_2019_-Royal_Palace_-_San_Francesco_di_Paola-_by-RaBoe_074.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Napoli_2019_-Royal_Palace_-_San_Francesco_di_Paola-_by-RaBoe_074.jpg)

The Royal Palace of Naples

The palace was built from 1600 onwards by the architect [Domenico Fontana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Fontana "Domenico Fontana") as the residence of the Spanish [viceroys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_viceroys_of_Naples "List of viceroys of Naples"), and in the mid-17th century [Francesco Antonio Picchiatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Antonio_Picchiatti "Francesco Antonio Picchiatti") made numerous improvements and interventions, such as the staircase and the chapel. [Charles of Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") made it, from 1734, the main residence of the [Bourbons of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Bourbon-Two_Sicilies "House of Bourbon-Two Sicilies") for more than a hundred years, first as [kings of Naples and Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Naples "Kingdom of Naples") (1734–1816) and later as [kings of the Two Sicilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Kingdom of the Two Sicilies") (1816–1861). It was also the residence of [Joseph Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_I_Bonaparte "Joseph I Bonaparte") and [Joachim Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Murat "Joachim Murat") during [French rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Naples_(Napoleonic) "Kingdom of Naples (Napoleonic)") (1806–1815), under which extensive redecorations were carried out.

The Bourbons made important and constant modifications to the interiors of the palace, relying on great artists such as [Francesco de Mura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_de_Mura "Francesco de Mura") or [Francesco Solimena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Solimena "Francesco Solimena"). However, after the fire of 1837, the palace had to be almost completely rebuilt by [Gaetano Genovese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaetano_Genovese "Gaetano Genovese"), who finished the unfinished wings and gave a homogeneous appearance to the entire complex.

After the [Italian unification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_of_Italy "Unification of Italy") (1861) it passed into the hands of the [Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy "House of Savoy"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio69-1) until [Victor Emmanuel III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Emmanuel_III "Victor Emmanuel III") ceded it to the state in 1919. From the late 19th century, the western half of the palace was opened to the public as a museum of the Royal Apartment, and in 1924 its eastern half became the home of the [National Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_of_Naples "National Library of Naples"), uses that continue today.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Braun_Napoli_UBHD.jpg/250px-Braun_Napoli_UBHD.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Braun_Napoli_UBHD.jpg)

Map of Naples in the 16th century.

At the end of the [Aragonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Aragon "Crown of Aragon") domination, the [Kingdom of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Naples "Kingdom of Naples") entered into the expansionist objectives of the French and the Spanish: both powers divided the territory with the signing of the [Treaty of Granada (1500)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Granada_(1500) "Treaty of Granada (1500)"). In any case, the treaty was not respected and under the command of the Great Captain [Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonzalo_Fern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba "Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba") the Spanish conquered the kingdom in 1503, thus beginning the [Spanish viceroyalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_viceroys_of_Naples "List of viceroys of Naples").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-vic1-2) Although this period, which lasted more than two hundred years, has been considered a dark and devolutionary period, but in fact the city enjoyed a notable cultural ferment and a dynamic bourgeoisie, as well as a cutting-edge merchant fleet, capable of competing with those of [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville") and [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio13-3)

Under the command of [Pedro Álvarez de Toledo y Zúñiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_de_Toledo_(1484-1553)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pedro de Toledo (1484-1553) (page does not exist)"), the construction of a viceregal palace was decided, designed by the architects [Ferdinando Manlio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinando_Manlio "Ferdinando Manlio") and [Giovanni Benincasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Benincasa?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giovanni Benincasa (page does not exist)"). The construction of the palace began in 1543 and was completed shortly afterwards.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio17-4) The new palace was born at a time when the viceroys dedicated their efforts to the urban reorganization of Italian cities: in Naples, the walls and forts were remodeled and the so-called _[Quartieri Spagnoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartieri\_Spagnoli "Quartieri Spagnoli")_ were built.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio17-4)

### Construction (1600–1616)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Construction (1600–1616)")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Fernando_Ruiz_de_Castro_conde_de_Lemos.jpg/250px-Fernando_Ruiz_de_Castro_conde_de_Lemos.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fernando_Ruiz_de_Castro_conde_de_Lemos.jpg)

Fernando Ruiz de Castro, count of Lemos.

When [Fernando Ruiz de Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Ruiz_de_Castro_Andrade_y_Portugal "Fernando Ruiz de Castro Andrade y Portugal"), count of Lemos, arrived in the city as viceroy Together with his wife, Catalina de Zúñiga,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida2-5) he decided to build a new palace. The official argument to justify its construction was to honor [Philip III of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_III_of_Spain "Philip III of Spain") by hosting him solemnly in view of an imminent visit by the monarch that, in the end, never took place.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida122-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-Raneo-7) However, contemporary analysis indicates that the viceroy knew that Philip III had never intended to move his court to Naples and that the palace was actually built to satisfy the viceroy's own wishes.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-8)

The area chosen for the new construction was located at the western end of the city, on the hill of Pizzofalcone, in a position that allowed the port to be dominated and that would facilitate an escape route for the king in case of an enemy attack. There it would be next to the Viceregal Palace, using, in fact, part of its gardens, and next to the [Castel Nuovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castel_Nuovo "Castel Nuovo"), the former royal residence, reinforcing the courtly character of the area.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-vic1-2)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio18-9) The choice of this location was also encouraged by the fact that the city was expanding towards the west: in this way, with such an important building in the vicinity, the price of land in the areas of Pizzofalcone and [Chiaia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiaia "Chiaia") would increase.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio18-9)

The project was entrusted to [Domenico Fontana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Fontana "Domenico Fontana"), considered at the time the most prestigious architect in the western world, who held the position of chief engineer of the kingdom. Fontana had fallen into disgrace a few years earlier, due to the death of [Sixtus V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixtus_V "Sixtus V") in 1590, the pope who had commissioned him to carry out numerous works in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio18-21-10)

The first stone was laid in 1600,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-vic1-2) in the square that, in those years, bore the name of _Piazza San Luigi._ The final project for the palace was published by Fontana in 1604 under the title _Dichiarazione del Nuevo Regio Palagio._[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio21-11) However, the original plans used by the architect to begin the work were lost and, in fact, Fontana himself lamented this:[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio35-12)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Federico_Zuccari%2C_Ritratto_di_Domenico_Fontana.jpg/250px-Federico_Zuccari%2C_Ritratto_di_Domenico_Fontana.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Federico_Zuccari,_Ritratto_di_Domenico_Fontana.jpg)

Domenico Fontana, the architect of the palace.

> I have not been able to print the designs for the work I have done in this city of Naples and its kingdom due to lack of time.

—[Domenico Fontana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Fontana "Domenico Fontana")

In any case, a plan drawn by [Giovanni Giacomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Giacomo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giovanni Giacomo (page does not exist)") is preserved in Rome, probably before 1651, which shows how the palace was intended to have been according to the architect's first wishes. In any case, the original design does not seem to have differed too much from its final appearance, although undeniable modifications were made during its construction.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio26-13) In this design, both the main west and north facades were the same, while a C-shaped structure was supposed to have been built along the south side facing the sea.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio26-13) This design was so popular that, even though the palace was still under construction, the press of the time often depicted it as it was in the plans rather than as it was actually being built. Domenico Fontana was so enthusiastic about the project he had been commissioned to do that he had the following inscriptions inscribed on two columns of the façade:[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio35-12)

> Domenicus Fontana Patricius Romanus  
> Eques Auratus comes palatinus inventor

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/El_Greco%2C_Portrait_of_Juan_Alfonso_de_Pimentel_y_Herrera.jpg/250px-El_Greco%2C_Portrait_of_Juan_Alfonso_de_Pimentel_y_Herrera.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_Greco,_Portrait_of_Juan_Alfonso_de_Pimentel_y_Herrera.jpg)

[Juan Alonso Pimentel de Herrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Alonso_Pimentel_de_Herrera "Juan Alonso Pimentel de Herrera"), under whose mandate the work on the palace was slowed down.

However, only the main façade of this project was completed; while the south-east arm was not built and the south façade remained unfinished and disordered until it was completed in 1843.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio26-13)

The architectural style developed by the architect was [late Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture"), with a central courtyard and an interior [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia") on the first floor, thus adapting the project to the demands of the time; that is, to a function of ostentation rather than a fortified residence.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-vic1-2) It also had a large square located right in front of the palace for military parades and public events. The works were carried out diligently both under the mandate of the Count of Lemos and under that of his son and successor [Francisco Ruiz de Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Ruiz_de_Castro "Francisco Ruiz de Castro"). Under Viceroy [Juan Alonso Pimentel de Herrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Alonso_Pimentel_de_Herrera "Juan Alonso Pimentel de Herrera"), Count of Benavente, the works slowed down, probably due to the limited availability of resources after the wars and crises that hit [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_Spain "Habsburg Spain") or even as a matter of honour: the Pimentels showed little interest in completing a work begun by the Ruiz de Castro.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio22-14)

In 1607, after the death of his father, [Giulio Cesare Fontana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giulio_Cesare_Fontana "Giulio Cesare Fontana") took over the direction of the works. The construction of the palace continued rapidly, until in 1610 [Pedro Fernández de Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Fern%C3%A1ndez_de_Castro_y_Andrade "Pedro Fernández de Castro y Andrade"), also the son of Fernando Ruiz de Castro, was appointed viceroy.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio22-14) In 1616, the new headquarters of the [university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Naples_Federico_II "University of Naples Federico II") was built at the end of [Via Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Toledo "Via Toledo"), that is, at the opposite end to the site on which the Royal Palace was being built. It was named Palazzo degli Studi and would be the future headquarters of the [National Archaeological Museum of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Naples "National Archaeological Museum of Naples").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio18-9) Thanks to some notes by [Alessandro Beratta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Beratta?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alessandro Beratta (page does not exist)") and the writings in a [travel diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_book "Travel book") by Confalonieri, we have evidence of the state of the works in that year:[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio22-14)

> That day we saw the structure of the royal palace, which has a facade of peperino[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-15) worked. On the first floor there are twenty-one windows and three railings; on the second floor, there are as many small windows without railings. Below, at ground level, there is a large portico, which faces the street and serves as a guard, carried out by two companies of soldiers. Inside the palace is not finished. It has two large staircases and a large square courtyard with porticos, of which two sides were still uncovered.

From this writing, it is clear that the work was almost finished at that time.

Shortly afterwards, although the exact date is not known, the interior decoration work began with the execution of the paintings by [Giovanni Battista Caracciolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Caracciolo "Giovanni Battista Caracciolo"), [Belisario Corenzio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belisario_Corenzio "Belisario Corenzio") and [Giovanni Balducci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Balducci "Giovanni Balducci").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio22-14)

### The Viceregal Period (1616–1734)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Viceregal Period (1616–1734)")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Palazzo_Reale_Napoli_1700s_1.png/250px-Palazzo_Reale_Napoli_1700s_1.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Palazzo_Reale_Napoli_1700s_1.png)

The Royal Palace around 1700, with the Belvedere Pavilion attached to its south-west corner.

From the time the palace was completed, it was inhabited by 22 [Spanish viceroys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroys_of_Naples "Viceroys of Naples") and 11 Austrian viceroys. Far from remaining unchanged, the Royal Palace continued to transform itself according to the tastes of each viceroy.

The [Duke of Alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo_y_Beaumont "Antonio Álvarez de Toledo y Beaumont") (1622–1629) was commissioned to finish some vaults begun by the Count of Lemos and dedicate them to the family glories.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-16) The Palatine Chapel was completed under the Duke of Medina de las Torres, from 1646 to 1648, with a large altarpiece by [José de Ribera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_de_Ribera "José de Ribera"); in 1656 the [stucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stucco "Stucco") work on the vault of the interdeux of the windows was carried out, which had to be redone after 1688 due to an earthquake that collapsed the roof. They were not finished until 1705.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-17)

Under the government of [Íñigo Vélez de Guevara el Mozo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8D%C3%B1igo_V%C3%A9lez_de_Guevara_el_Mozo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Íñigo Vélez de Guevara el Mozo (page does not exist)"), Count of Oñate, the original two-ramp staircase of Fontana, judged undignified, was completely renovated by [Francesco Antonio Picchiatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Antonio_Picchiatti "Francesco Antonio Picchiatti"), following the wishes of the Count of Oñate, the works took place from 1651 to 1666.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio25-18) The two main rooms of the palace were also redecorated: the "Great Hall" and the "Hall of the Viceroys", which began to be adorned with portraits of the viceroys from 1503.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-19)

Exteriorly, between 1666 and 1671, when [Pedro Antonio de Aragón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Antonio_de_Arag%C3%B3n "Pedro Antonio de Aragón") was in power, the most notable addition took place with the construction of a small pavilion facing the sea, the so-called Belvedere, which would serve as a bedroom for the viceroys and later for the Bourbon sovereigns. Attached to it was a small garden terrace that grew over the decades to become the current "hanging gardens or Belvedere gardens".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida2-5)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-20)

From 18 April to 2 June 1702, [Philip V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Spain "Philip V of Spain") visited Naples, being therefore the first and only [Spanish sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Spanish_monarchs "List of Spanish monarchs") to stay in a palace originally intended to receive Philip III.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-21) In 1707 the Austrians took the city in the midst of the [War of the Spanish Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession "War of the Spanish Succession"), beginning the government of the Austrian viceroys that did not bring substantial changes to the palace.

### The first Bourbons (1734–1806)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: The first Bourbons (1734–1806)")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Gaspar_van_wittel%2C_veduta_del_palazzo_reale_di_napoli%2C_1706.jpg/250px-Gaspar_van_wittel%2C_veduta_del_palazzo_reale_di_napoli%2C_1706.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gaspar_van_wittel,_veduta_del_palazzo_reale_di_napoli,_1706.jpg)

The _Largo di Palazzo_ painted by [Gaspar van Wittel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspar_van_Wittel "Gaspar van Wittel") between 1700 and 1725.

In May 1734 [Charles of Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") entered Naples, the city became, once again, the capital of an autonomous kingdom and not a viceroyalty.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-bor1-22) The new king found the Royal Palace empty and dilapidated, since, since its construction, it had been normal for viceroys to move in with their furniture and, once their mandate had ended, to take it with them. This was done by the last [Austrian viceroys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_viceroys_of_Naples "List of viceroys of Naples"), [Giulio Visconti Borromeo Arese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giulio_Visconti_Borromeo_Arese "Giulio Visconti Borromeo Arese"), in March 1734. All that remained in the palace were the magnificent painted vaults made by Neapolitan artists of the 17th century.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-23)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Alessandro_D%27Anna_-_Napoli%2C_carnevale_a_Largo_di_Palazzo.jpg/250px-Alessandro_D%27Anna_-_Napoli%2C_carnevale_a_Largo_di_Palazzo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alessandro_D'Anna_-_Napoli,_carnevale_a_Largo_di_Palazzo.jpg)

The Royal Palace of Naples (right) and the Viceregal Palace (left) during the carnival of 1774, by Alessandro D'Anna.

The renovation works were directed by the military engineer [Giovanni Antonio Medrano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Antonio_Medrano "Giovanni Antonio Medrano"), later architect of the [Royal Palace of Portici](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Palace_of_Portici "Royal Palace of Portici"), and initially focused on the king's apartments facing the Piazza della Repubblica. Although the works were completed in 1740, by 1738, the year of Charles's wedding with [Maria Amalia of Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Amalia_of_Saxony "Maria Amalia of Saxony"), they were almost ready. The palace was then structured around two main rooms or apartments:[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:3-24)

*   the King's Apartment facing the square and composed of: the Great Hall or Royal Room, the Room of the Guard of Corps, the Room of the Officers, the Antechamber of the Titleholders, the Room of the Hand-Kissing or of the Throne, the Gallery, the Room "where His Majesty dresses", the "secret" Chapel of His Majesty, the Belvedere Room or where the king sleeps, the "toilet" and the Room "where His Majesty's valet sleeps".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:8-25)
*   the Queen's Apartment facing the sea and composed of: the Room of the Viceroys, the Room of the Guard of Corps, the Second Antechamber, the Room of the Kissing Hands, the Room of the Alcove or where the queen sleeps, the Oratory, the "toilet", the Chambermaids' Room and the Queen's Boudoir.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Abdicaci%C3%B3n_de_Carlos_III.jpg/250px-Abdicaci%C3%B3n_de_Carlos_III.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abdicaci%C3%B3n_de_Carlos_III.jpg)

Abdication of [Charles of Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") in favour of his son [Ferdinand IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies") in the Throne Room of the Royal Palace of Naples, 1759.

In general, in this first reform, the works that evoked the history of Naples and its Spanish past were preserved as a sign of historical prestige, while those that referred to the Austrian period were destroyed. From 1735 to 1738, large celebratory frescoes were commissioned from Neapolitan late Baroque painters such as [Francesco Solimena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Solimena "Francesco Solimena"), [Nicola Maria Rossi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Maria_Rossi "Nicola Maria Rossi"), [Francesco de Mura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_de_Mura "Francesco de Mura") and [Domenico Vaccaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Vaccaro "Domenico Vaccaro"). For example, Rossi painted a fresco celebrating the [taking of Gaeta in 1734](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Gaeta_(1734) "Siege of Gaeta (1734)") in the "Room where His Majesty dresses" (Room IX); Solimena painted another fresco of the king on horseback in the "Room of the Viceroys" (Room XXII), covering up an earlier one of [Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor"); and de Mura painted another fresco of large proportions in the "Room of the Guard" (Room II) celebrating marital virtues following the royal wedding. Finally, the sovereign redecorated the interior of the palace with sumptuous marble and silk hangings.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida2-5)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:3-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio28-26)

During the reign of Charles of Bourbon, the Royal Palace of Naples was a meeting place for the French lifestyle, Spanish tradition and Italian artistic culture.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-27)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/N%C3%A1poles_Teatro_Palacio_Real_07.jpg/250px-N%C3%A1poles_Teatro_Palacio_Real_07.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:N%C3%A1poles_Teatro_Palacio_Real_07.jpg)

Ceiling of the new "Court Theatre", restored after the Second World War.

During the minority of [Ferdinand IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies"), from 1759 to 1767, it is worth highlighting the progressive extension of the palace towards the east (towards the Castel Nuovo), with the construction, around 1760, of the eastern wing that ran parallel to the so-called "Steward's Apartment" facing the sea and the hanging gardens systematized around 1740. Following these extensions, two interior courtyards called "de "the Carriages" and "the Belvedere".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida2-5)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:12-28) There were also important decorative changes, such as the extension in 1763 of the Belvedere Wing facing the sea with the "daily bedroom of His Majesty", four private cabinets and the king's study; most of the rooms decorated with frescoes by [Giuseppe Bonito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Bonito "Giuseppe Bonito"). However, the most notable reform, coinciding with the end of the minority and the marriage of the King to the Archduchess [Maria Carolina of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Carolina_of_Austria "Maria Carolina of Austria") in May 1768, was the transformation of the Spanish-era "Grand Hall" into a late-baroque court theatre by [Ferdinando Fuga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinando_Fuga "Ferdinando Fuga").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio28-26)

From 1780 onwards, the interest of Ferdinand IV and Maria Carolina turned to the [Caserta Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caserta_Palace "Caserta Palace"), where their apartments had been completed. From then on, the court would spend at least half the year outside Naples.

### The Bonapartes (1806–1815)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: The Bonapartes (1806–1815)")]

The arrival of the French in 1806 and the beginning of the reigns of [Joseph Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bonaparte "Joseph Bonaparte") (1806–1808) and [Joachim Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Murat "Joachim Murat") (1808–1815) did not bring about major architectural changes to the royal palace, but it did bring about major interior and decorative transformations, most of which have now disappeared. The Napoleonic monarchs had to deal first of all with a general refurnishing of the palace, which [Ferdinand IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies") had emptied when he went into exile in Palermo in 1798 and 1806. Although some interventions had already taken place under Joseph, from 1809 to 1810 the reforms were essentially functional, to convert the palace into a habitable residence. From 1810 to 1814 the major works took place, but were never completed.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:2-29)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Carolina_Bonaparte_nel_Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli_-_1811.jpg/250px-Carolina_Bonaparte_nel_Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli_-_1811.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carolina_Bonaparte_nel_Palazzo_Reale_di_Napoli_-_1811.jpg)

Carolina Bonaparte's study in the Royal Palace of Naples, painted in 1811 by Elie Honoré de Montagny.

In addition to a joint "grand apartment of ceremony", Joachim Murat and [Caroline Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Bonaparte "Caroline Bonaparte") each had an "apartment of honour" and an "ordinary apartment", Murat's apartments were concentrated in the western core of the palace, while Caroline's were grouped in the eastern wing formerly intended for the royal princes (now the seat of the [National Library of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_of_Naples "National Library of Naples")). The Belvedere garden was the connection between the royal couple's private apartments and also a play area for their children. Among the transformations of the period, it is worth highlighting the new theatre by Caroline Murat in the eastern wing or the bedroom in the form of a military tent for Joachim in the Belvedere Wing.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:2-29)

The fall of the Bonapartes in 1815 prevented further transformations, such as the new throne room in the "Gallery of the Ambassadors" (now Room 8). However, two spaces were deeply marked by that period. On the one hand, the Royal Chapel, to which Joseph Bonaparte had already added the sumptuous altar of [pietra dura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietra_dura "Pietra dura") from _[Santa Maria degli Scalzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalzi,\_Venice "Scalzi, Venice")_, was remodelled in Byzantine style and inaugurated in 1814; although it would be rebuilt after the fire of 1837 and destroyed during the Second World War.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:2-29) On the other hand, in the "Hall of the Viceroys" the gallery of portraits of these disappeared and it was transformed into an [antiquarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquarium "Antiquarium"), adding plaster copies of the sculptures of the royal collection; due to the [Farnese Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farnese_Hercules "Farnese Hercules") the room began to be called "Hall of Hercules", the sculptures were also lost in 1837.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:4-30)

### The Bourbon Restoration (1815–1837)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: The Bourbon Restoration (1815–1837)")]

After the reconquest of Naples by the Bourbons, only cosmetic but highly symbolic modifications took place in the palace. In 1818, Ferdinand IV, now [Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies"), undertook the complete redecoration of the Throne Room, resacralizing the space after the Napoleonic interlude. Antonio de Simone designed the ceiling stuccos with fourteen allegories representing the provinces, united around the throne, of the new [Kingdom of the Two Sicilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Kingdom of the Two Sicilies") created in 1816 by unifying those of [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Naples "Kingdom of Naples") and [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Sicily "Kingdom of Sicily"). The entire room was also covered with a red velvet hanging with gilded [Bourbon lilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleur-de-lis "Fleur-de-lis").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-bor3-31)

At that time, the division of the palace into two poles devised under the Bonapartes was perpetuated. On the western side facing the [Largo di Palazzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piazza_del_Plebiscito "Piazza del Plebiscito") was the "Grand Apartment of the King", while on the eastern wing facing the [Castel Nuovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castel_Nuovo "Castel Nuovo") was the "Reception Apartment" of the [Duke of Calabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Francis I of the Two Sicilies"), who enjoyed the old little theatre of Caroline Murat, as well as his private rooms and accommodation for his children. During his brief reign, Francis I continued to inhabit these same apartments, and after his death, they were occupied by his widow, the queen mother [María Isabella of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_Isabella_of_Spain "María Isabella of Spain").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:4-30)

### The Transformation by Ferdinand II (1837–1861)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Transformation by Ferdinand II (1837–1861)")]

On 6 February 1837, at 5 am, a fire broke out in the [Queen mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_Isabella_of_Spain "María Isabella of Spain")'s chambers in the eastern wing, destroying much of the eastern half of the palace.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-32) After the disaster, a new restoration of the entire complex became necessary. King [Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies") commissioned the renovation by the architect [Gaetano Genovese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaetano_Genovese "Gaetano Genovese"), who carried out the work between 1837 and 1844, restoring the parts damaged by the fire, extending and finishing others, and redecorating the interiors. Genovese followed the [neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") and [historicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historicist_architecture "Historicist architecture") trends prevailing at the time, without abandoning the original architecture of [Domenico Fontana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Fontana "Domenico Fontana"), to give a homogeneous appearance to the whole complex.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-33)

During the course of the work, the eastern wing facing the Castel Nuovo was completely remodelled; the Belvedere wing was demolished; the unfinished south façade facing the sea was completed, uniting it with the existing Fontana-era façade and crowning the central section with a new [belvedere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belvedere_(structure) "Belvedere (structure)") of white marble; and the private apartments of Ferdinand II and [Maria Theresa of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Theresa_of_Austria,_Queen_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Maria Theresa of Austria, Queen of the Two Sicilies") were moved to the second floor, leaving the former first-floor apartments for official receptions only.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio28-26) The surroundings of the palace also underwent major transformations. Between 1841 and 1843 the Viceregal palace was demolished, creating in its place the _Piazza San Ferdinando_ (now Piazza Trieste e Trento), and [Friedrich Dehnhardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Dehnhardt "Friedrich Dehnhardt") created a new romantic rear garden by demolishing old stables and other buildings.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio18-9)

The Royal Palace was then made up of several apartments grouped around two cores. In the western one, which constitutes the original palace, were the King and Queen's Etiquette Apartment (now the Royal Apartment) and the King's Apartment on the ground floor used for private receptions (now closed).

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Biblioteca_nazionale_di_Napoli_%2807%29.jpg/250px-Biblioteca_nazionale_di_Napoli_%2807%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Biblioteca_nazionale_di_Napoli_(07).jpg)

Ceiling of one of the rooms of the "Apartment of the Festivals", now the National Library.

In the eastern wing (now the National Library), made up of the extensions of the 18th and 19th centuries, were located the Apartment of the Festivals and the Apartment of the Duke of Calabria, on the first floor; and the Palatine Library, the King's Physics Office and the Private Apartment of the King and Queen on the second floor.

The decoration of the newly created spaces, as well as the renovations to some of the old ones, moved away from [academic neoclassicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academicism "Academicism") and adopted a more eclectic and historicist approach, close to the exuberance of [Percier and Fontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percier_and_Fontaine "Percier and Fontaine").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:14-34)

Few changes took place during the short reign of Francis II, who on 6 September 1860 had to abandon the palace and the city in the face of the threat of the [Garibaldine troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_of_the_Thousand "Expedition of the Thousand"). Before leaving, the sovereign packed some of his most precious possessions, which were sent to [Capua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capua "Capua") and [Gaeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaeta "Gaeta"), among which were Raphael's prized [Pala Colonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pala_Colonna "Pala Colonna"), [Titian's portrait of Alessandro Farnese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Cardinal_Alessandro_Farnese_(Titian) "Portrait of Cardinal Alessandro Farnese (Titian)"), a marble bust of [Pope Pius IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Pius_IX "Pope Pius IX"), the relics of Saint Jasonia, sixty-six reliquaries, a portrait of [Louis XVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XVIII "Louis XVIII"), vases, porcelain, a nightstand with views of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") on [Sèvres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A8vres_porcelain "Sèvres porcelain") plates, tablecloths, household linen, mattresses and cushions, twenty-six boxes containing silverware, seven déjeuners and one hundred and fifteen silver candlesticks. However, much of Queen Maria Sophie's wardrobe and the king's personal fortune deposited in the [Banco di Napoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_di_Napoli "Banco di Napoli") were left behind.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-35)

### The Savoys (1861–1919)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: The Savoys (1861–1919)")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Umberto_and_Margherita.jpg/250px-Umberto_and_Margherita.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Umberto_and_Margherita.jpg)

Umberto and Margherita during their stay in Naples.

After the fall of the [Kingdom of the Two Sicilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Kingdom of the Two Sicilies") in 1860 and the proclamation of the [Kingdom of Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy"), the palace became the residence of the [House of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy "House of Savoy"). The new owner of the palace, [Victor Emmanuel II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Emmanuel_II "Victor Emmanuel II"), first visited the palace on 7 November 1860, just two months after [Francis II of the Two Sicilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Francis II of the Two Sicilies") had left, and it does not seem that he ever stayed there again.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:0-37) The visits of the new dynasty to the city were generally sporadic.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-38) Only from 1868 to 1870, the palace served as a permanent residence for Prince [Umberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_I_of_Italy "Umberto I of Italy") and Princess [Margherita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margherita_of_Savoy "Margherita of Savoy"), newly married in April 1868. It was in this palace that the future king [Victor Emmanuel III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Emmanuel_III "Victor Emmanuel III") was born on 11 November 1869.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida122-6) The couple left the city after the [taking of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Question "Roman Question") in September 1870.

After ascending to the throne in 1878, the new royal couple returned to Naples, but their stays were always bittersweet. In 1878 they were victims of the assassination attempt by [Giovanni Passannante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Passannante "Giovanni Passannante"), in 1883 they returned to comfort the wounded in the earthquake at [Casamicciola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casamicciola_Terme "Casamicciola Terme") and in 1885 they returned to the victims of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera"). More fortunate was the visit in 1889, following the inauguration of the [Corso Umberto I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corso_Umberto_I "Corso Umberto I"). The [Prince of Piedmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Piedmont "Prince of Piedmont"), the future Victor Emmanuel III, also resided in Naples from 1891 to 1896. However, the royal family often preferred the [Capodimonte palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Palace_of_Capodimonte "Royal Palace of Capodimonte"), which was more isolated and had a larger garden.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-40)

The first decades after the [Unification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Unification "Italian Unification") were also those of a slow process of emptying the palace's treasures: from 1862 to 1864 several modern paintings were moved to Capodimonte, in 1864 the Armory was moved and in 1873 the porcelain, both also to Capodimonte; In 1878 several tapestries were taken to the [Quirinal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirinal_Palace "Quirinal Palace"), in 1879 the instruments of the Physics Cabinet went to the [University of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Naples_Federico_II "University of Naples Federico II"), before 1884 the royal carriages left for the [Pitti Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitti_Palace "Pitti Palace"), the music archive was ceded to the Conservatory on an uncertain date and in 1921 it was the turn of the Archives of the Royal House, integrated into the [State Archives of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Archives_of_Naples "State Archives of Naples").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-41)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Sommer%2C_Giorgio_%281834-1914%29_-_n._1116_-_Napoli_-_Palazzo_Reale_%28bis%29.jpg/250px-Sommer%2C_Giorgio_%281834-1914%29_-_n._1116_-_Napoli_-_Palazzo_Reale_%28bis%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sommer,_Giorgio_(1834-1914)_-_n._1116_-_Napoli_-_Palazzo_Reale_(bis).jpg)

The main façade of the palace before the sculptures were installed in 1888.

However, it is also worth highlighting some specific interventions in the palace, such as the sumptuous neo-baroque furniture in the First Antechamber, carried out between 1862 and 1864; the coats of arms of the provinces of the new Kingdom of Italy painted in the Hall of Hercules around 1868 or the _[marouflage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marouflage "Marouflage")_ of the _Assumption_ by [Domenico Morelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Morelli "Domenico Morelli") made for the Royal Chapel in 1869.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-42) Another notable change was the replacement of the Bourbon [fleur-de-lis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleur-de-lis "Fleur-de-lis") by the Savoy cross in several places in the palace, including the main staircase, the court theatre and the throne itself. However, the most important and controversial intervention would be the installation, in 1888, in the niches of the main façade, of eight sculptures of the most important kings of Naples, including Victor Emmanuel II, despite the fact that he never held that title.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:1-43)

Likewise, the core of the palace was moved to the eastern wing, a process that had already begun with the reform of Ferdinand II. Umberto and Margherita were installed in the former apartment of [Caroline Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Bonaparte "Caroline Bonaparte"), of [duke of Calabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Francis I of the Two Sicilies") and then of Francis II. His son, Prince Victor Emmanuel (III), had it done[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_] just above, in the private apartments of [Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies"). The apartments were furnished with sumptuous new [Neo-Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_Revival_architecture "Baroque Revival architecture") and [Neo-Rococo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rococo_Revival "Rococo Revival") furniture, as well as an extensive collection of contemporary paintings that Queen Margherita had been collecting.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:0-37)

In the old heart of the palace, the western wing, the so-called "Gala Apartment", was regularly open to the public.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:5-44)

### Transfer to the State (1919–1940)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Transfer to the State (1919–1940)")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Palazzo_Reale_Napoli_colores_Wikipedia.png/250px-Palazzo_Reale_Napoli_colores_Wikipedia.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Palazzo_Reale_Napoli_colores_Wikipedia.png)

The Royal Palace of Naples after the transformations of the 1920s: in orange in the Royal Apartment, the original core of the building; in blue the eastern wing, current headquarters of the National Library.

The greatest change in the history of the Royal Palace of Naples took place in 1919, when King Victor Emmanuel III transferred the palace, along with many other royal residences, to the state. Three years later, between 1922 and 1924, following the impulse of [Benedetto Croce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedetto_Croce "Benedetto Croce"), the [National Library of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_of_Naples "National Library of Naples") was installed in the eastern wing of the palace, the one that had been occupied by the various sovereigns and their families since the mid-19th century. This installation entailed the transfer and storage of the furniture and the loss of part of the decoration to make way for the shelves of the library. Only on the west side was the "Gala Apartment", since then called the "Royal Apartment", open to the public.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida2-5)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:1-43)

In 1931, the last royals to live in the palace moved in: Crown Prince [Umberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_II_of_Italy "Umberto II of Italy") (II) and his wife Princess [Maria Jose of Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Jose_of_Belgium "Maria Jose of Belgium"). On 24 September 1934, their first-born daughter, Princess [Maria Pia of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Maria_Pia_of_Bourbon-Parma "Princess Maria Pia of Bourbon-Parma"), was born in the palace; from then on, the couple preferred the privacy of the [Villa Maria Pia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Rosebery "Villa Rosebery") in [Posillipo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posillipo "Posillipo").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-45)

### From World War II to the new century (1940-2000)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: From World War II to the new century (1940-2000)")]

During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") the palace suffered considerable damage.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida122-6) On 4 August 1943, during an Allied bombing raid, the roof of the court theatre, the chapel and the bridge in the hanging garden, among other areas, were destroyed.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-46) The palace was then used as a welfare club by Anglo-American troops from 1943 to 1945. During this period, numerous thefts of works of art took place and a large number of curtains and hangings from the Royal Apartment were destroyed. The furniture was not so unlucky, as it was moved to a safe place at the beginning of the conflict.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio70-47)

The restoration took place from 1950 to 1954: the paintings were recovered, in some cases repainted; The original furniture was reinstalled and the silk elements originally made in [San Leucio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Leucio "San Leucio") were reconstructed using the ancient looms.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio70-47)

In 1994, the seat of the [regional government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campania "Campania"), which had been located in the Royal Palace since the beginning of the 20th century, was permanently moved to another location.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio73-48) In the middle of the second decade of the 21st century the façade was restored and some areas of the Royal Apartment were renovated.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-49) among them the corte theater.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-50)

## Exterior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Exterior")]

### The main façade

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: The main façade")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/PalazzoRealediNapoli.jpg/250px-PalazzoRealediNapoli.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PalazzoRealediNapoli.jpg)

The main façade.

The main façade of the Royal Palace faces the [Piazza del Plebiscito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piazza_del_Plebiscito "Piazza del Plebiscito") and was completed in 1616. It is one hundred and sixty-nine metres long[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida122-6) and until 1843 was adjacent to that of the Viceregal Palace, which was demolished to make way for the Piazza Trieste e Trento.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio34-51) The façade is made of fired reddish clay bricks, piperno and volcanic stone from the [Phlegraean Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phlegraean_Fields "Phlegraean Fields"). The late Renaissance and [Mannerist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannerist "Mannerist") imprint can be seen in the superposition of several orders, typical of theatrical buildings of ancient Rome, such as the [Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coliseum "Coliseum") or the [Theatre of Marcellus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Marcellus "Theatre of Marcellus"); while the Mannerist can be appreciated in the modular design of the façade that could be repeated ad infinitum since it has no element that marks its beginning or its end, in the same way that, in the upper part, it does not find a conclusion due to the lack of a cornice.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio21-11) However, originally the cornice was crowned by obelisks, vases and three bell gables positioned vertically at each entrance. All of this was removed at the beginning of the 19th century, leaving only the central bell gable with the clock.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio35-12)

The architectural articulation follows the treatises of [Vitruvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitruvius "Vitruvius"): the [pilasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilaster "Pilaster") are arranged vertically and the three orders (at ground level we find the [Tuscan order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuscan_order "Tuscan order"), followed by the [Ionic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_order "Ionic order") and, finally, the [Corinthian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinthian_order "Corinthian order")) are arranged horizontally. On the other hand, the two-tone use of materials stands out to highlight the architectural elements (in grey stone) on the walls (in reddish brick), a technique that would be very successful in Naples.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio34-35-52)

Originally, the lower part had [porticos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portico "Portico") along its entire length, a very innovative decision for the time, designed by Fontana so that the people could walk around even in bad weather. However, after the [Masaniello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaniello "Masaniello") revolt and because of the structural problems of the pillars, which were being crushed, in 1753 the arches were walled up according to the project of [Luigi Vanvitelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Vanvitelli "Luigi Vanvitelli").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-cir213-53) Niches were opened in the new walls, but it was not until 1888 that statues of the main [kings of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_of_Naples "Kings of Naples") were placed in them,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida122-6) with the intention of showing a certain continuity between the [House of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy "House of Savoy") and the previous dynasties of Neapolitan history. From left to right, we can recognize _Roger II of Sicily,_ a work by Emilio Franceschi; _Frederick II of Swabia,_ by Emanuele Caggiano; _Charles of Anjou,_ by [Tommaso Solares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommaso_Solari "Tommaso Solari"); _Alfonso V of Aragon,_ by Aquiles De Osas; _Charles V of Habsburg,_ by [Vincenzo Gemito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincenzo_Gemito "Vincenzo Gemito"); _Charles of Bourbon,_ by Raffaele Belliazzi; _Joachim Murat,_ by Giovanni Battista Amendola and _Victor Emmanuel II of Savoy,_ by Francesco Jerace.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-vic2-54)

In the centre of the main façade is the entrance portal, flanked by two [coupled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupled_column "Coupled column") granite columns, and crowned with the coat of arms of [Philip III of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_III_of_Spain "Philip III of Spain"), already planned by Fontana to emphasise the public function of the palace. Next to it, on each side, are two smaller coats of arms belonging to [Juan Alonso Pimentel de Herrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Alonso_Pimentel_de_Herrera "Juan Alonso Pimentel de Herrera") and [Pedro Fernández de Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Fern%C3%A1ndez_de_Castro "Pedro Fernández de Castro"), viceroys of Naples when the palace was built.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-vic3-55) Below the balcony cornice is the coat of arms of the [Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy "House of Savoy").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida124-56) There are also two plaques: one in commemoration of the start of the works by order of [Fernando Ruiz de Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Ruiz_de_Castro_Andrade_y_Portugal "Fernando Ruiz de Castro Andrade y Portugal") and his wife [Catalina de Zúñiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalina_de_Z%C3%BA%C3%B1iga?action=edit&redlink=1 "Catalina de Zúñiga (page does not exist)"); and the other, with an inscription praising the beauty of the building. Below the plaques there were, until the beginning of the 18th century, two statues representing _Religion_ and _Justice._ The two [sentry boxs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentry_box "Sentry box") on either side of the main entrance were made in the early years of the 18th century.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-57) Along the façade and in the courtyard of honour there is, between the ground floor and the first floor, a frieze with [triglyphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triglyph "Triglyph") and [metopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metope "Metope") in which are the emblems of the [Hispanic Monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_Spain "Habsburg Spain") and its possessions in Europe, largely obtained after the 1559 [Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Cateau-Cambr%C3%A9sis "Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis"): the three-towered castle of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile"); the rampant lion of [Léon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Le%C3%B3n "Kingdom of León"); the snake devouring a captive, symbolizing the [Duchy of Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Milan "Duchy of Milan"); the shield with the four vertical bars of [Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Aragon "Crown of Aragon"); the cross with the four [Moor's heads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moor's_head "Moor's head"), symbol of the [Kingdom of Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Sardinia "Kingdom of Sardinia"); and the emblems of [Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Navarre "Kingdom of Navarre"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy"), [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal"), [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Granada_(Crown_of_Castile) "Kingdom of Granada (Crown of Castile)") and [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Jerusalem "Kingdom of Jerusalem").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-vic4-58)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida124-56)

### The other façades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: The other façades")]

The longest of all, the one running south along Via Acton, was built in different phases: its eastern half at the beginning of the 17th century according to Fontana's designs and the eastern half, including the central belvedere, from 1837 to 1844 by Gaetano Genovese. The north façade facing Piazza Trieste e Trento was also by the same architect, completed between 1841 and 1843 after the demolition of the Viceregal Palace. While the architects [Francesco Gavaudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Gavaudan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Francesco Gavaudan (page does not exist)") and [Pietro Gesuè](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Gesu%C3%A8?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pietro Gesuè (page does not exist)") were responsible for the connection to the [San Carlo Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Carlo_Theatre "San Carlo Theatre").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:9-59)

Both façades imitate the architectural articulation designed by Fontana for the main façade, and both are C-shaped and contain a garden in their centre, the south façade the so-called Hanging Gardens and the north the Italian Garden, in the centre of which is the statue of _Liberty_, made by [Francesco Liberti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Liberti?action=edit&redlink=1 "Francesco Liberti (page does not exist)") in 1861, a clear reference to the [Italian unification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_of_Italy "Unification of Italy").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio36-60) In addition, this north façade is partially porticoed to support a terrace. It has a glass entrance leading directly onto the grand staircase, decorated with two pairs of plaster statues from the [Palazzo degli Studi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Naples "National Archaeological Museum of Naples") and placed there during Genovese's restoration. These are copies of the _[Farnese Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farnese\_Hercules "Farnese Hercules")_ and the _Farnesian Flora_ on one side, and of the _Minerva_ and of _Pyrrhus and [Astyanax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astyanax "Astyanax")_ on the other.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio36-37-61)

### The courtyards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: The courtyards")]

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_01.JPG/250px-N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_01.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_01.JPG)

The courtyard of honour.

According to Domenico Fontana's original project, three [courtyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard") were to be opened in front of each entrance, which would be connected to each other by vaulted corridors. However, only the central entrance courtyard was ultimately built, the so-called [Courtyard of honour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_honor_(architecture) "Court of honor (architecture)")(_Cortile D'Onore_), which is square in shape, with five arches on each side.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-sasso250-62) The central arch on each side is a [segmental arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segmental_arch "Segmental arch") of larger dimensions than the others. Around the courtyard, on the first floor, there is a [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia"), originally open, but which was finally closed with large windows. In a niche in the eastern part of the courtyard there was originally a cistern, which was replaced during the 1940s by a fountain decorated with a statue of _Fortuna_. The fountain, made in 1742 by Giuseppe Canart, was commissioned by Charles of Bourbon and was originally located near the port. Following an investigation, brick paving in the shape of a [herringbone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herringbone_pattern "Herringbone pattern") has been discovered in some places.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio41-63)

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_03.JPG/250px-N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_03.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:N%C3%A1poles_patio_palacio_real_03.JPG)

The fountain with the statue of _Fortuna_.

During the construction of the new southern arm of the palace between 1758 and 1760, two new courtyards were created: one on the same axis as the courtyard of honour, just behind it, which is called the Courtyard of the Carriages, while the other is the Courtyard of the Belvedere.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio42-64)

Despite having been built in different periods, the Courtyard of the Carriages (_Cortile delle Carrozze_), so called because it contained the coach houses, is architecturally close to the style that Domenico Fontana gave to the palace, although there are no lack of different elements such as the use of [stucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stucco "Stucco") instead of piperno and the angular [pilasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilaster "Pilaster").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio42-64) The courtyard is rectangular in shape, and has an elliptical marble cistern in the centre. It is connected to the courtyard of honour and the esplanade of the bastions by two service corridors with lowered arches. The coach house, built in 1832 by [Giacinto Passaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacinto_Passaro?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giacinto Passaro (page does not exist)"), replaced the one existing from the previous century, the work of [Ferdinando Sanfelice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinando_Sanfelice "Ferdinando Sanfelice"), mainly for aesthetic reasons, since the new one was aligned with the facade of the palace while the previous one was situated obliquely. The new coach house is a space dominated by a central line of nine columns of the [Doric order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doric_order "Doric order"), on which you can still admire red shields with the crown of [Umberto I of Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_I_of_Italy "Umberto I of Italy"). The window layout was modified by Genovese in 1837 to adapt it to the requirements of the Belvedere Courtyard.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio43-65)

The [Belvedere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belvedere_(structure) "Belvedere (structure)") (_Cortile del Belvedere_) was born as a boundary towards the sea of the first nucleus of the palace and was originally C-shaped. It was closed by a loggia, which would be modified as a consequence of the construction of the new bodies of the palace in the 18th century,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio43-65) with the insertion of lowered arches in the eastern part. Later, the courtyard underwent modifications between 1837 and 1840, when, for access to the courtyard, a triumphal arch with Ionic and Corinthian semi-columns of false piperno was created. Between the ground and first floors, the courtyard is decorated with a Doric band with [metopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metope "Metope"), also in false piperno, and [triglyphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triglyph "Triglyph").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio48-66) From the Belvedere Courtyard, you can access different areas of the palace: on the left is the Guest Staircase, which leads to the Vestibule (room XX) of the Royal Apartment and to the small bridge, destroyed in the bombings of the Second World War and rebuilt on the same supports, which links it directly to the hanging gardens.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio48-66) From the courtyard, you can also access a private apartment with Pompeian-style decorations, originally reserved for official meetings of [Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies"), which later became the seat of the superintendency; and also to a bridge that, overcoming the defensive ditch, led to the bastion of the [Castel Nuovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castel_Nuovo "Castel Nuovo") and to a slope that led to the [stables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stables "Stables").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio4849-67)

## The Royal Apartments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: The Royal Apartments")]

The Royal Apartments ([Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language"): _Appartamento Reale_) are the part currently open to visitors and is located on the _[piano nobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano\_nobile "Piano nobile")_ of the western core of the palace. Throughout its history it has undergone several changes of use and name: from 1616 to 1734 it was used as the apartments of the [Spanish and Austrian viceroys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_viceroys_of_Naples "List of viceroys of Naples") and their consorts; from 1734 to 1806 it was the public and private apartment of the [king and queen of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_of_Naples "List of monarchs of Naples"); from 1806 to 1815 it served as the "honorary" and "ordinary" apartment of [Joseph Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bonaparte "Joseph Bonaparte") and [Joachim Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Murat "Joachim Murat"); It was later called the "Grand Apartment of His Majesty the King" and [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies") and [Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies") were the last to inhabit it. After the 1837–1844 renovation by Gaetano Genovese, it was called the "Etiquette Apartment of the King and Queen" and was used only for receptions, as the sovereigns moved to the second floor of the eastern wing.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:4-30) In the travel guides of the beginning of the century it was simply called the "Gala Apartment", and could be visited from Thursday to Sunday from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. upon request for a permit.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:5-44)

When the palace ceased to be property of the Crown and passed to the State in 1919, the Royal Apartment became one of the _institutes of antiquities and art_ (now called _Italian national museums_). Its present museum appearance is due to the restoration carried out between 1950 and 1954 to alleviate the damage suffered during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), when several ceilings were damaged by Allied bombing and the silk hangings of twenty rooms were removed when the apartment was transformed into a _Welfare Club_ (social club) for the occupying English troops.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-68)

Originally, to access the king's rooms, silver and gold keys were used, guarded by the [gentlemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentlemen "Gentlemen") of the chamber, some of which are in the [Museo Civico Filangieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_Civico_Filangieri "Museo Civico Filangieri") donated by Neapolitan nobles.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7072-69)

### The collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: The collections")]

The current decoration represents the tastes of the different dynasties and historical figures who have lived there, as well as different political messages typical of a building that represented the pinnacle of power in the kingdom. The reference date is the inventory made by the Savoy family in 1874, which describes the rooms after the late Bourbon modifications (1837–1844) and some slight changes introduced after the Unification in 1860.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7273-70)

First of all, the frescoes stand out. These essentially cover the viceregal period with works by [Belisario Corenzio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belisario_Corenzio "Belisario Corenzio") of Roman Renaissance inspiration or [Giovanni Battista Caracciolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Caracciolo "Giovanni Battista Caracciolo") in a more [Caravagesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravaggisti "Caravaggisti") line; the Baroque period of Charles of Bourbon with large allegorical frescoes with [trompe l'oeil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trompe_l'oeil "Trompe l'oeil") by Solimena, Vaccaro or de Mura; and finally historicist and neo-medieval works from the mid-19th century.

The paintings in the rooms also correspond to different periods, highlighting the northern and European schools of the 16th and 17th centuries from the Farnesio collection inherited by Charles of Bourbon; Caravaggesque paintings and the Dutch portraits that Domenico Venuti bought for [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I_of_the_Two_Sicilies "Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies") and the large court portraits of the royal family.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7374-71) There are also more intimate and contemporary paintings from the apartments in the east wing, such as _troubadour_ paintings commissioned by the Murats from artists such as [Louis Nicolas Philippe Auguste de Forbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Nicolas_Philippe_Auguste_de_Forbin "Louis Nicolas Philippe Auguste de Forbin") or the chronicle paintings of the great moments of the reigns of Francis I and Ferdinand II by [Salvatore Fergola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvatore_Fergola "Salvatore Fergola") and [Frans Vervloet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frans_Vervloet?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frans Vervloet (page does not exist)"). However, due to the sending of the most important paintings to the [Real Museo Borbonico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Naples "National Archaeological Museum of Naples") between 1829 and 1832 and the transfer of paintings to the [Capodimonte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Capodimonte "National Museum of Capodimonte") from 1862 onwards, the palace's collection of paintings today appears more scattered and impoverished than before, with its series and iconographies fragmented. In the 1874 inventory, the paintings were given special importance, together with the furniture, tapestries, flowered hangings and large neo-baroque mirrors, as creating a sumptuous atmosphere.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-72)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:7-73)

The furniture, in the [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque"), [Rococo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rococo "Rococo") and historicist style, was made by Neapolitan cabinetmakers between the 18th and 19th centuries or brought from [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_French_Empire "First French Empire") during Murat's stay in Naples, together with carpets and [tapestries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapestry "Tapestry"), some of them woven in the Royal Tapestry Factory of Naples. Also of note are the French clocks, the porcelain, especially [Sèvres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A8vres_porcelain "Sèvres porcelain"), Chinese and Russian; bronze and marble sculptures and works in hard stone. Many of the exhibits come from other parts of the palace, especially the eastern wing, which was completely stripped of furniture when the National Library was installed there.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7374-71)

In any case, the palace does not have a real collection, but rather loose pieces, since during the 19th century, on the initiative of the Bourbons and especially the Savoys, many works were transferred to other museums (see History).[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-porzio7273-70)

### Grand Staircase

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Royal_Palace_of_Naples&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Grand Staircase")]

The north side of the courtyard, orthogonal to the façade, was originally occupied by a modest two-ramp staircase, the work of [Domenico Fontana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Fontana "Domenico Fontana"). However, after the [anti-Spanish revolt of 1647](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neapolitan_Republic_(1647) "Neapolitan Republic (1647)"), the viceroy [Iñigo Vélez de Guevara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8D%C3%B1igo_V%C3%A9lez_de_Guevara_el_Mozo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Íñigo Vélez de Guevara el Mozo (page does not exist)") commissioned a new and monumental staircase from Francesco Antonio Picchiatti. The new space was built between 1650 and 1670 in Piperno, and was inspired by the immense staircase of the Real [Alcázar of Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Toledo "Alcázar of Toledo"), built by [Alonso de Covarrubias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonso_de_Covarrubias "Alonso de Covarrubias") and [Juan de Herrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_de_Herrera "Juan de Herrera") between 1550 and 1605.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-74) The new staircase, which occupied an entire side of the courtyard of honour, was built in accordance with the importance that the Austrian ceremony gave to these spaces. [Montesquieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montesquieu "Montesquieu") described it in 1729 as the most beautiful in Europe,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-guida4-75) however it had to be rebuilt after the fire in February 1837.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Reale_of_Naples#cite_note-:9-59)

The new design in a grandiose late neoclassical style was the work of [Gaetano Genovese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaetano_Genovese "Gaetano Genovese"). In 1841 the problem of the staircase's luminosity was resolved with the demolition of the viceregal palace annex, the creation of the Piazza Trieste e Trento and the opening of large iron-framed windows. From that church the sea is only a short walk further – all within the 200‑–1 km range you described.

- The Alcazaba’s page notes the presence of a *former parish church* (dates from Ferdinand & Isabella’s era) near the entrance.  
- The fortress *overlooks the port and the sea*【13†L10-L16】.

These facts match the geographical clues you gave, making the Alcazaba of Málaga the likely castle you visited.
